title: Who the Virginia Residential Landlord and Tenant Act Covers
bodyText: The Virginia Residential Landlord and Tenant Act applies to every residential rental of a single-family or multifamily dwelling unit in Virginia, including a rented manufactured home, and it cannot be waived by a lease or changed by a city or county. There is no longer any exemption or opt-out for small landlords: the old rule that let an individual owning two or fewer single-family rentals opt out in the lease ended with the 2019 recodification, and Title 55.1 Chapter 14 now covers only nonresidential rentals. The Act does not cover: residence in an institution incidental to detention or medical, geriatric, educational, counseling or religious services; fraternity or similar organization housing for members; a condominium owner or cooperative proprietary lessee; campgrounds; a tenant who pays no rent; an employee whose multifamily unit is conditioned on employment on the premises (or a former employee for under 60 days); a buyer occupying under a contract of sale; recovery residences; and hotel, motel, extended-stay or similar transient lodging unless the person has lived there as a primary residence for more than 90 consecutive days or has a written lease for more than 90 days (a lodging owner may use self-help after a five-day written nonpayment notice for residents of 90 days or less). Public housing is covered, but federal HUD rules control where they conflict. Several rules depend on how many Virginia rental units a landlord owns (see Landlord Portfolio Size Rules).

title: Landlord Portfolio Size Rules
bodyText: Virginia applies some rules only to landlords who own more than four rental dwelling units in Virginia, or more than a 10 percent interest in more than four, counting units held individually or through a business entity: 60 days' written notice of a rent increase for a renewal term and of nonrenewal (90 days for rent increases, with a tenant response deadline, from July 1, 2027); no denial of an applicant based solely on payment history or an eviction for nonpayment during the COVID-19 emergency period (with a written denial notice and a $1,000 penalty); from January 1, 2027, no ban on a tenant's plug-in solar device on the exterior of the tenant's premises; from July 1, 2027, a one-time payment-plan offer before terminating for small arrearages; and, under fair housing law, no refusal of an applicant because of the source of funds used to pay rent, such as a housing voucher. A landlord with four or fewer units may refuse debit and credit card payments, may limit the tenant to one redemption of a nonpayment eviction per lease period with written notice, and may decline to rent based on source of funds. A landlord who owns fewer than four units and receives no rental or utility assistance on the tenant's behalf is exempt from the 2027 tenant-ledger rule. Landlords with more than 200 units on one property need key-control and employee background-check policies. Any locality may require landlords with five or more units in one multifamily building to install deadbolts, peepholes and window and sliding-door locks.

title: Lease Terms Virginia Prohibits
bodyText: A Virginia lease may not make the tenant: waive rights or remedies under the Act; waive the 120-day notice for condominium or cooperative conversion or rehabilitation; authorize a confession of judgment; agree to pay the landlord's attorney fees except as the Act provides; agree to exculpate or limit the landlord's liability to the tenant arising under law, or indemnify the landlord for that liability; accept a firearm ban as a condition of public housing unless federal law requires it; prepay a security deposit plus damage and renter's insurance premiums above two months' rent; or waive Servicemembers Civil Relief Act rights before a dispute arises. Any such provision is unenforceable, and if the landlord sues to enforce it the tenant may recover actual damages and reasonable attorney fees. No landlord may charge a tenant any fee for maintenance or repair unless the tenant's violation of the Act made it necessary. A lease may allow a tenant to operate child care in an apartment building in compliance with state and local law. Releases of the landlord from negligence, casualty or pest claims, which appear in some Virginia forms, are exactly the kind of exculpatory terms the Act prohibits. A lease may make the tenant pay the landlord's attorney fees and collection costs only as the Act allows: reasonable attorney fees as the lease provides or the law allows (not awarded if the court finds the tenant's failure to pay or vacate was reasonable), costs of a proceeding only once a court action has been filed, and no more than $12 for a sheriff's or process server's service of a notice.

title: Rental Applications, Application Fees and Deposits
bodyText: A Virginia application fee may not exceed $50 ($32 for public housing or other HUD-regulated units), plus the actual out-of-pocket cost a third party charges for background, credit or other screening. A landlord may also take a refundable application deposit; if the applicant does not rent, the landlord must refund everything above the landlord's actual expenses and damages, with an itemized list, within 20 days (10 days where the landlord rejects an applicant who paid by cash, certified check, cashier's check or money order), or owe the wrongfully withheld amount and attorney fees. Money paid as a security deposit is treated as an application deposit until the lease commencement date. A landlord may copy a driver's license or similar photo ID (not a U.S. government ID where that would violate federal law) and may require a Social Security number or an ITIN. A landlord must consider evidence that an applicant is a victim of family abuse to mitigate a low credit score. A rental application may require disclosure of criminal convictions and consent to a criminal record check, charging only its exact cost. From July 1, 2027, before collecting any payment or information, the landlord must tell applicants in writing or by posting the fees and deposit and whether refundable, the selection criteria, automatic-denial criteria, other criteria that may lead to denial, the consumer reporting agency used, and the applicant's right to a free copy of the report and to dispute it. Information received with an application is a confidential tenant record.

title: Virginia Security Deposit Rules
bodyText: Virginia caps the security deposit, including any pet deposit, at two months' periodic rent, and the deposit plus any damage and renter's insurance premiums paid before the lease begins may not together exceed two months' rent. At the end of the tenancy the deposit may be applied only to accrued rent (including reasonable late charges in the lease), damages from the tenant's failure to meet statutory maintenance duties less reasonable wear and tear, other damages or charges provided in the lease, and actual damages for breach. Within 45 days after the tenancy ends or the tenant vacates, whichever is later, the landlord must give an itemized written disposition with any refund; where damages exceed the deposit and need a contractor, written notice within the 45 days buys 15 more days to itemize. The landlord must tell the tenant of the right to attend the move-out inspection, which must occur within 72 hours after possession is delivered if the tenant asks. Refunds go by one check to all tenants unless each agrees otherwise in writing; without a forwarding address the landlord holds the money and may send it to the State Treasurer as unclaimed property after a year. Deductions during the tenancy must be noticed within 30 days. A willful violation means return of the whole deposit plus actual damages and attorney fees. Landlords must keep two years of deduction records for tenant inspection, transfer deposits to a buyer on sale, and remain bound as successors. No interest is owed. Damage insurance may replace the deposit if it meets five statutory criteria, and the tenant may switch to paying the full deposit at any time.

title: No Interest on Security Deposits
bodyText: Virginia law does not require a landlord to pay interest on a security deposit or to hold it in an interest-bearing or separate account. If a deposit happens to earn interest, a seller must transfer the deposit and any accrued interest to a buyer.

title: Late Fees in Virginia
bodyText: A Virginia landlord may charge a late fee only if the written lease provides for it, and the fee can never exceed the lesser of 10 percent of the periodic rent or 10 percent of the remaining balance due and owed by the tenant. There is no statutory grace period for a written lease (without a written lease, rent is due on the first and late after the fifth). Late fees on landlord-billed utilities under submetering or ratio billing are separately capped at $5 and cannot be due sooner than 15 days after the bill. After a foreclosure, a tenant cannot be charged a late fee until the new owner says where to pay. From July 1, 2027, a landlord with more than four units that offers a statutory payment plan may not add late fees on the covered arrearage while the tenant keeps to the plan. A late fee is part of 'rent' under the Act and can be claimed in an eviction as a contracted-for late charge.

title: Rent Payments, Receipts and Statements
bodyText: Every Virginia landlord must accept rent and security deposits by check and money order and must give a written receipt whenever rent is paid in cash or by money order. A landlord may not charge a payment-processing fee unless it also offers a fee-free way to pay, and a fee for card or electronic payment may not exceed the actual third-party cost. A landlord with four or fewer units need not accept debit or credit cards. On a tenant's written request, the landlord must provide within 10 business days a written statement of all charges and payments over the tenancy or the past 12 months, whichever is shorter; from July 1, 2027, the same statement must be provided within 10 business days of a written request for tenant records (in writing or by a free portal), except by a landlord owning fewer than four Virginia rental units, or less than a 10 percent interest in more than four, that receives no state or local rental or utility assistance for the tenant, and a termination notice for nonpayment must include it. Rent paid more than one month in advance must go into a federally insured escrow account by the fifth business day after receipt. Unless the lease says otherwise, rent is payable without demand at the place the landlord designates, at the beginning of each month. Rent paid under a housing payment plan or a court-ordered plan may have to be paid by cashier's check, certified check, money order or electronic transfer.

title: Bounced Checks and Rejected Electronic Payments
bodyText: For rent paid by a check refused for no account or insufficient funds, a Virginia lease may set a processing fee of up to $50. When a rent check bounces, an electronic transfer is rejected for insufficient funds, or a stop-payment order is placed in bad faith, the landlord may serve a 14-day written notice requiring payment by cash, cashier's check, certified check or completed electronic transfer and, if not paid, terminate and seek possession. The landlord may also recover, as part of the eviction case, the face amount, legal interest, the bank's return fee, a $50 processing charge and attorney fees if awarded, and, if the payment remains unpaid 30 days after proper notice, a civil recovery of the lesser of $250 or three times the check. A holder who charges more than the law allows is liable for the lesser of $50 plus the excess or twice the excess.

title: Virginia Required Lease Disclosures and Their Timing
bodyText: Before or at signing, a Virginia landlord must: offer a written lease with the state Statement of Tenant Rights and Responsibilities and have the parties sign the state acknowledgment form (the landlord cannot sue on a lease violation until the statement is provided); put the itemized fee disclosure, with the required sentence, on the first page of the lease; give the renter's insurance and flood notice if the lease does not require renter's insurance; disclose in writing the name and address of the manager and of an owner or owner's agent; name a Virginia agent in the lease if the owner is a nonresident individual; give the federal lead-based paint disclosure and pamphlet for pre-1978 housing; and, where they apply, disclose a noise or accident potential zone near a military air installation, known unremediated defective drywall, or known uncleaned prior methamphetamine manufacture. Within five days after move-in the landlord must give a written move-in inspection report with a statement about visible mold. During the tenancy the landlord must give notice of a sale, of a lender's default or foreclosure notice on a single-family rental within five business days, 48 hours' notice before pesticide use in the unit, and a smoke alarm certificate. A termination notice to a tenant using a housing voucher must show the statewide legal aid phone number and website on its first page.

title: No Radon Disclosure Rule for Leases
bodyText: Virginia has no radon testing or disclosure requirement for residential leases. The only radon disclosure in the Code is a buyer-beware statement for home sales. If you lease a one-to-four-unit home with an option to buy, the Residential Property Disclosure Act applies, and its buyer-beware statement (which covers this subject) must be given before the contract is signed.

title: No Sex Offender Registry Notice Required in Leases
bodyText: Virginia does not require a residential lease to contain a sex offender registry notice or require a landlord to disclose registered offenders. The registry notice some Virginia lease forms include comes from the buyer-beware rules for home sales, not from landlord-tenant law.

title: No Bed Bug Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Virginia has no bed bug disclosure or treatment statute for rentals. General pest rules apply: the tenant must keep the unit free of insects and pests and report them promptly and pays for treatment made necessary by the tenant's delay or fault, and the landlord must give 48 hours' notice before applying pesticide in the unit.

title: No Separate Flood Disclosure for Leases
bodyText: Virginia has no stand-alone flood-zone or flood-history disclosure for residential leases. The only lease flood notice is inside the renter's insurance notice a landlord must give when the lease does not require renter's insurance: renter's insurance does not cover flood, and the tenant is pointed to FEMA's National Flood Insurance Program and the state Flood Risk Information System. If you lease a one-to-four-unit home with an option to buy, the Residential Property Disclosure Act applies, and its buyer-beware statement (which covers this subject) must be given before the contract is signed.

title: No Lease Rule on Deaths or Crimes in the Unit
bodyText: Virginia has no statute requiring or excusing disclosure to a prospective tenant of a death, homicide, suicide or other crime in a rental unit.

title: No Tenant Electric Vehicle Charging Right
bodyText: Virginia gives condominium unit owners and cooperative proprietary lessees a right to install electric vehicle charging stations, but gives residential tenants no statutory right to install one. Charging equipment in a rental is a matter for the lease.

title: No Tenant Flag Display Statute
bodyText: Virginia has no statute protecting a residential tenant's right to display a flag. A lease rule on signs and displays governs, subject to fair housing law's protection of religious expression.

title: No Right-to-Call-Police Statute
bodyText: Virginia has no statute that bars eviction or penalties because a tenant calls the police or emergency services. Retaliation protection covers code complaints and other listed acts, and from January 1, 2027 also complaints to the media and fair housing complaints, but not emergency calls as such.

title: Pet Deposits and Pet Rent
bodyText: A pet deposit is part of the security deposit and counts toward Virginia's two-month cap. Virginia sets no separate limit on pet rent or nonrefundable pet fees, but pet rent is 'rent' and every recurring or one-time charge must appear in the first-page fee disclosure. No pet fee, deposit or additional rent may be charged for an assistance animal or a guide, hearing or service dog.

title: Local Landlord-Tenant Rules and Rent Control
bodyText: The Virginia Residential Landlord and Tenant Act supersedes all local ordinances and regulations concerning landlord and tenant relations and the leasing of residential property, so Virginia cities and counties cannot adopt their own landlord-tenant codes or rent control; no statute authorizes local rent control. Localities may still: set up voluntary mediation commissions; enforce property maintenance codes; create rental inspection districts; require deadbolts, peepholes and window and sliding-door locks in buildings with five or more units; require smoke alarms and owner certificates; regulate towing from private lots; bring habitability lawsuits on tenants' behalf (from July 1, 2026); and require notice and a right of first refusal before affordability restrictions on publicly supported housing end (from July 1, 2026).

title: Virginia Fair Housing Law
bodyText: Virginia's Fair Housing Law protects race, color, religion (including religious dress and displays), national origin, sex, elderliness (age 55 and over), familial status (including pregnancy), source of funds (any lawful source of rent money, including housing vouchers and other assistance), sexual orientation, gender identity, military status (service members, veterans and certain dependents) and disability. It covers refusals to rent, terms and services, advertising, false unavailability, and refusals of reasonable modifications and accommodations. Exemptions: an individual owner of no more than three single-family houses renting without a broker and without discriminatory advertising; an owner-occupied building of up to four families; religious organizations and private clubs in limited cases. An owner of four or fewer Virginia rental units may decline a tenant based on source of funds, and any owner may decline if the assistance program has not approved the tenancy within 15 days of the request. Landlords may ask about criminal convictions and charge the exact cost of a record check, deny a clear and present threat, apply reasonable occupancy standards, and consider evidence of family abuse. An owner or managing agent may set occupancy standards, and a limit of two persons per bedroom is presumed reasonable, subject to fair housing law. Advertising may never indicate a preference based on a protected class, including disability. Threatening eviction or loss of housing to coerce a person into a sexual act is sexual extortion, a Class 5 felony.

title: Assistance Animals, Service Dogs and Accommodations
bodyText: In Virginia an assistance animal, including an emotional support animal, is not a pet and need not be trained or certified. The tenant must follow rules that apply to all residents so long as they do not interfere with equal use of the home. No pet fee, pet deposit or extra rent may be charged, and a person with a guide, hearing or service dog has full and equal access to housing without extra compensation, but is liable for damage the animal causes. If the disability and need are obvious or known, the landlord may not ask for verification; otherwise it may ask for reliable documentation, including from someone with a therapeutic relationship with the person (a mental health provider, a licensed or certified professional, a free peer support group member, or a caregiver or reliable third party with actual knowledge). Requests are decided case by case; if a request may impose an undue burden or fundamental alteration, the landlord must offer an interactive process to find an alternative. A specific animal may be refused only if it poses a clear and present threat of substantial harm that is not based solely on breed, size or type and cannot be reduced by another accommodation. A request for accessible parking is an accommodation request. Providers who give fraudulent documentation violate the Virginia Consumer Protection Act; fraudulently passing off a service dog to gain public access is a misdemeanor, but there is no Virginia crime for misrepresenting an assistance animal in housing.

title: Entry, Access and Temporary Relocation
bodyText: A Virginia tenant may not unreasonably refuse entry for inspections, repairs, services or showings. Except in an emergency or where impractical, the landlord gives notice of intent to enter and enters at reasonable times; unrequested routine maintenance needs at least 72 hours' notice, must be done within 14 days, and the notice must state the last possible date. Pesticide application in the unit needs 48 hours' written notice. The landlord may enter during a tenant's absence of more than seven days to protect the property. If the lease says so, a tenant who unjustifiably refuses a showing for sale or lease owes damages, costs and attorney fees. A tenant who refuses lawful access can be enjoined or have the lease terminated, with damages and fees; a landlord who enters unlawfully or harasses faces the same remedies. For a nonemergency repair that needs the unit empty, the landlord may, on 30 days' written notice, move the tenant for up to 30 days to a comparable unit or hotel at the landlord's cost (rent continues); the same is true for mold remediation. A tenant with a non-ex parte court order excluding a co-tenant may have the locks changed at the landlord's actual cost or change them, and the landlord may not give keys to the excluded person. Tenants may install security devices that cause no permanent damage, giving the landlord keys.

title: Repair Duties and Tenant Remedies
bodyText: A Virginia landlord must comply with building and housing codes affecting health and safety, keep the premises fit and habitable, keep common areas clean and safe, maintain supplied facilities and appliances (including elevators), prevent moisture and mold, provide trash receptacles and removal, and supply running water, reasonable hot water, heat in season and reasonable air conditioning if provided. Liability for failing these duties is limited to actual damages from a failure to use ordinary care. Tenant remedies: a 21-day cure notice that terminates the lease 30 days after receipt; termination within seven days if the unit is uninhabitable at the start (full refund within 15 business days); damages or substitute housing for willful or negligent loss of an essential service, which since July 1, 2026 includes central air conditioning supplied and operating when the lease took effect; a rent escrow case in general district court (from January 1, 2027 the tenant need not first pay arrears to file); a defense to a nonpayment eviction (since July 1, 2026 no longer conditioned on paying rent into court); repair-and-deduct by a licensed contractor after 14 days' written notice, up to the greater of one month's rent or $1,500; and damages, prepaid rent and deposit if the unit is condemned after the tenant reported the code violation. Since July 1, 2026, a locality may sue on tenants' behalf to enforce habitability after notice to the landlord. No landlord may charge a repair or maintenance fee unless the tenant's violation caused the need.

title: Mold
bodyText: Virginia requires a written statement about visible mold in the move-in inspection report; if mold is present the tenant may walk away, or the landlord must remediate within five business days and reinspect. During the tenancy the landlord must keep the premises free of moisture accumulation and mold growth, respond promptly to tenant reports, remediate visible mold to professional standards and reinspect, and give the tenant a summary of remediation information (and the full package on request). Once mold has been remediated to professional standards, it need not be disclosed to later tenants. The tenant must use reasonable efforts to prevent moisture and mold and report it promptly. Where mold materially affects health or safety, the landlord may relocate the tenant for up to 30 days to a comparable unit or hotel at the landlord's expense (rent continues, and the tenant cannot terminate once remediation is done); the landlord pays for relocation and remediation unless the tenant's breach caused the mold.

title: Termination Notices for Tenant Default
bodyText: Virginia notices for tenant breach: nonpayment, 14 days to pay (five days before July 1, 2026); a remediable breach, 21 days to cure with termination at least 30 days after receipt; a non-remediable breach or a repeat of a cured breach of like nature, termination at least 30 days after receipt; a criminal or willful act that is not remediable and threatens health or safety, including illegal drug activity by the tenant, an authorized occupant or a guest, immediate termination without waiting for a conviction (the tenant is presumed to know of occupants' and guests' activity). From July 1, 2027, a nonpayment notice must include a statement of charges and payments for the tenancy or the past 12 months, and a landlord with more than four units must first offer a one-time payment plan (up to six months) if the arrearage is no more than one month's rent plus late charges. A termination notice to a tenant using a housing voucher must show the statewide legal aid number and website on page one. A lease may not terminate solely because of family abuse against the tenant where the perpetrator is barred by the landlord or a court. A landlord may bar a tenant's guest for conduct violating the lease or law by written notice served personally, with a copy to the tenant, and then seek a trespass warrant. The sheriff may serve these notices for a fee of up to $12. The court will not grant possession without a proper termination notice in evidence.

title: Accepting Rent With Reservation, and the Right of Redemption
bodyText: In Virginia, a landlord that accepts full payment of rent, damages, judgment, attorney fees and costs cannot proceed with an eviction based only on nonpayment. To accept partial payments and still evict, the landlord must give the tenant written notice that payments will be accepted with reservation, using the exact statutory language (which may be included in the termination notice), and must give the court a copy for service with the unlawful detainer summons. A new written lease before the eviction makes an earlier order of possession unenforceable. The tenant may redeem by paying all amounts due at or before the first return date (or by presenting a written payment commitment from a local government or nonprofit, which triggers a 10-day continuance), and may cancel a scheduled eviction by paying everything claimed at least 48 hours before it; the landlord must then promptly tell the sheriff to cancel, and willfully failing to do so can be treated as an unlawful lockout. On written request the landlord must state the exact amount owed; redemption payments are by cashier's check, certified check or money order. A landlord with four or fewer units may limit redemption to once per lease period by written notice.

title: Eviction (Unlawful Detainer) Process
bodyText: Virginia evictions are unlawful detainer cases in general district court. The initial hearing must be held within 21 days of filing (30 at most), and the summons must be served at least 10 days before the return date. The court cannot grant possession unless a proper termination notice is in evidence (and from July 1, 2027 no unlawful detainer may be filed until a proper and effective termination notice has been given). The landlord may amend the amount owed up to the hearing, may ask for the whole month's rent for the month of the hearing only if the lease makes rent due on the first of the month in advance for the entire month (otherwise rent is prorated to the hearing date), and may split possession and money issues (not if the tenant contests the amount at the first hearing). A tenant asking for a continuance without a good-faith defense may have to pay rent into court. Appeals must be noted within 10 days; since July 1, 2026 an indigent tenant need not post an appeal bond, and other appellants must pay rent and charges into court. The sheriff serves notice at least 72 hours before executing the writ and may not evict within the 10-day appeal period. Belongings go to the public way or the landlord's storage for 24 hours (see the separate row on the tenant's belongings after an eviction). Tenants who are federal employees or contractors unpaid in a federal shutdown get a 60-day continuance on proof, unless the landlord has served a noncompliance notice for a non-rent violation. Where a general district court runs the Eviction Diversion Program, an eligible tenant who pays at least 10 percent can enter a three-month court payment plan. An owner-occupant of a single-family home with an occupant who never had a lease can get an emergency hearing within 14 days after a 72-hour written notice to vacate.

title: Eviction Record Expungement
bodyText: Virginia courts automatically expunge the records of an unlawful detainer case that was dismissed (after 30 days) or voluntarily nonsuited (after six months) where no order of possession was entered. A tenant who won the case, or whose qualifying case began before July 1, 2024, may petition, and the court must expunge without a hearing.

title: No Self-Help Eviction
bodyText: A Virginia landlord may not take possession by cutting off an essential service or locking the tenant out without a court order. A tenant who is willfully removed or excluded, has an essential service interrupted, or has the premises made unsafe can petition the general district court, which must hear the case within five days and may order the tenant restored, services resumed or the condition fixed; at a full hearing the tenant recovers actual damages, statutory damages of the greater of $5,000 or four months' rent, and attorney fees, and may end the lease with a full deposit refund. A landlord who knows the tenant has redeemed and willfully fails to cancel the eviction can be treated the same way.

title: Retaliation
bodyText: Until January 1, 2027, a Virginia landlord may not raise rent, cut services, sue or threaten to sue for possession, or terminate after knowing the tenant complained to a code agency about a health or safety violation, complained to or sued the landlord under the Act, joined or organized a tenants' organization, or testified against the landlord; market-rate increases and across-the-board service cuts are allowed, and the tenant must prove retaliatory intent. From January 1, 2027, protected acts also include complaints to the media, written complaints and fair housing complaints, tenants' organization activities and administrative testimony; prohibited retaliation also includes fee increases, selective enforcement or new rules for the tenant, threats and harassment, and refusing to renew a voucher holder; the statement placing the burden of proof on the tenant is removed. Safe harbors include tenant-caused code violations, rent default when the case is filed, repairs that require vacating, health and safety lease defaults, notices given before the protected act, rent or fee increases under the lease, and changes that apply to all tenants.

title: Holdover Remedies
bodyText: If a Virginia tenant stays after the lease ends or is terminated without the landlord's consent, the landlord may sue for possession and recover actual damages, attorney fees and court costs unless the tenant proves the failure to leave was reasonable. The lease may add liquidated damages of up to 150 percent of the daily rent (100 percent for HUD-regulated housing) for each day after the termination date in the landlord's notice. If the landlord consents to the tenant staying and no new lease is signed, the old terms continue and rent can change only by written notice taking effect on the next rent due date at least 30 days later.

title: Periodic Tenancies and Mass Nonrenewals
bodyText: Unless the lease sets a different period, a Virginia month-to-month tenancy ends on written notice served at least 30 days before the next rent due date, and a week-to-week tenancy on seven days' notice. Without a written lease, the law creates a 12-month tenancy. If a written lease is not signed and delivered by one side, accepting rent (or possession) without reservation gives it the same effect as if signed, but a term longer than one year is then effective for only one year. In a tenancy at will, a notice changing the terms is a notice to vacate. An owner of a multifamily property who declines to renew the greater of 20 or 50 percent of the month-to-month tenancies within 30 days must give each affected tenant 60 days' written notice (not needed for a tenant who is behind on rent). A landlord changing a multifamily building's use (conversion or rehabilitation of a building with four or more units) must give 120 days' written notice, which a lease cannot waive except for month-to-month tenancies (30 days' notice); the notice must be a separate writing, not part of the lease. For a landlord with more than four units, whether the 60-day renewal and nonrenewal notice applies to a lease written as month-to-month is unsettled; see the row on renewal and rent increases.

title: Renewals and Rent Increases
bodyText: Virginia has no rent control. A landlord with more than four Virginia units must give written notice of a rent increase for a renewal term, and of nonrenewal, at least 60 days before the lease ends where the lease can renew or renews automatically; from July 1, 2027 the rent-increase notice must be given 90 days ahead with a response deadline at least 30 days out. A landlord with four or fewer units has no statutory renewal-notice deadline. For a month-to-month or holdover tenancy with the landlord's consent, a new rent takes effect only on the next rent due date at least 30 days after written notice. No unilateral change to lease terms is valid without notice and both parties' written consent, and new or changed rules that substantially modify the bargain need the tenant's written consent. From January 1, 2027, a rent or fee increase made because of a tenant's protected activity is retaliation unless made under the lease terms or at market rate. That notice rule does not apply to a month-to-month tenancy that arises when a tenant stays on with the landlord's consent after the lease ends. Virginia law does not say how it applies to a lease written as month-to-month or week-to-week, where each period could be read as a new term; a landlord with more than four units is safer giving written notice at least 60 days before a nonrenewal or a rent increase takes effect (90 days for a rent increase from July 1, 2027).

title: Domestic and Sexual Violence Protections
bodyText: Virginia lets a tenant who is a victim of family abuse, sexual abuse or criminal sexual assault, stalking or human trafficking end the lease on 28 days' written notice with a copy of a protective order or of a conviction, warrant, summons, information or indictment; rent is owed through the effective date, no liquidated damages may be charged, co-tenants remain liable, and if the perpetrator is the only remaining tenant the landlord may terminate and pursue the perpetrator for damages. A lease may not terminate solely because of family abuse against the tenant where the perpetrator is barred by the landlord or by a court order. A tenant or authorized occupant with a family abuse protective order (Va. Code Ann. § 16.1-279.1) or a divorce or custody court order under Va. Code Ann. § 20-103(B), not issued ex parte, granting possession to the exclusion of a co-tenant or occupant may ask the landlord to install new exterior locks or security devices at the landlord's actual cost, or to let the tenant do so; an excluded person gets no keys; a non-tenant granted possession by such an order may apply to become a tenant within 10 days or must leave within 30. Landlords must consider evidence of family abuse to offset a low credit score in screening.

title: Servicemember Rights
bodyText: Virginia gives members of the Armed Forces and full-time National Guard members (and Guard civil service technicians) a statutory right to end a lease on permanent change of station orders, temporary duty over three months, discharge or release, orders to government quarters, or a qualifying stop movement order, effective at least 30 days after the next rent due date following written notice, with a copy of the orders; no liquidated damages may be charged. Since July 1, 2026 there is no rule that the termination date be within 60 days of departure. A lease may not require a waiver of Servicemembers Civil Relief Act rights before a dispute, and military status is a protected class under Virginia fair housing law. Virginia also extends the federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act's protections to Virginia National Guard members called to Title 32 or state active duty for 30 or more consecutive days. The federal SCRA provides additional protections.

title: When a Sole Tenant Dies
bodyText: If the sole tenant under a written lease who still lives in the unit dies and no one has court authority over the estate, the Virginia lease ends on the date of death without a court order, occupants and guests must leave within 10 days, and the landlord may dispose of the belongings after at least 10 days' written notice to the emergency contact named in the application or lease (or to the tenant at the unit if none), stating that unclaimed property will be treated as abandoned. The named contact may, with proof of identity, enter, see the records and claim the property. The estate remains liable for actual damages, which the landlord must mitigate.

title: Selling or Losing a Rented Property
bodyText: When a Virginia rental is sold, the landlord must tell the tenant and give the buyer's name, address and phone number, and must transfer security deposits and any accrued interest to the buyer; a seller who sells in good faith is released from later liability after notice to the tenant, and the new owner is bound to return deposits owed. A landlord of a single-family rental must tell the tenant within five business days of receiving a lender's default, acceleration or foreclosure-sale notice, or the tenant may end the lease on five business days' notice. After a foreclosure sale, a buyer who will live in the home gives the tenant at least 90 days' notice to vacate; any other buyer takes subject to the lease. A former owner who stays after a foreclosure sale becomes a tenant at sufferance who can be removed on three days' notice. When a rental building is converted to condominiums, the developer must give each tenant formal notice of the offering price of the tenant's unit, projected assessments and any relocation help, and the tenant then has 60 days' exclusive right to buy the unit; a lease cannot waive the conversion notice.

title: Landlord's Lien and Distress for Rent
bodyText: Virginia keeps the old remedy of distress for rent: within five years after rent becomes due, a landlord may petition a judge or magistrate for a distress warrant, post bond, and have the sheriff levy on the tenant's goods on the premises (or removed within the past 30 days), subject to the tenant's exemption claims and a hearing. For residential premises the landlord's priority over other liens is limited to six months' rent. It is a court process; a lease cannot authorize the landlord to seize property itself. For that six-month limit, a month-to-month or week-to-week tenancy counts as one continuing lease, not a new lease each period, until a new written lease is made. If a judge later finds the warrant should not have issued, the court may dismiss it and award the tenant actual damages and reasonable attorney fees, and a landlord who acts irregularly or unlawfully in a distress is liable for the special damage caused.

title: Tenant Records and Confidentiality
bodyText: A Virginia landlord may not release a tenant's or applicant's information to third parties except with written consent or in listed cases (public records, rent payment summaries, unremedied noncompliance or termination notices where the tenant left, law enforcement, subpoenas, the commissioner of revenue, a buyer or lender who agrees to keep it confidential, the tenant's commanding officer, the landlord's attorney or collection agency, emergencies, a new managing agent, and the census). Application information is confidential except by subpoena. A tenant may designate a third party to receive duplicate copies of notices and eviction summonses. Tenants may request copies of their records; from July 1, 2027, a written request must be answered within 10 business days with a statement of all charges and payments (landlords with fewer than four units receiving no rental or utility assistance for the tenant are exempt). A landlord owning more than 200 rental units attached to the same piece of real property must have key-control policies and a policy requiring a pre-employment criminal history check for job applicants who will have key access (financial institutions and real estate licensees are exempt).

title: Rules and Regulations
bodyText: Virginia enforces a landlord's rules only if they serve tenants' convenience, safety or welfare, protect the property or fairly distribute services; are reasonably related to that purpose; apply fairly to all tenants; are explicit; do not evade the landlord's duties; and were given to the tenant at signing or when adopted. A rule adopted or changed later binds the tenant on reasonable notice if it is not a substantial modification of the bargain; a substantial modification needs the tenant's written consent. Courts treat violations of reasonable rules as lease breaches.

title: Towing From Rental Property
bodyText: A Virginia owner, operator or lessee of a parking area may have a trespassing vehicle towed if signs at every entrance clearly disclose that unauthorized vehicles will be towed and give the phone number of the local police nonemergency line or the tow operator (unless the locality regulates towing by ordinance instead); the tow operator must report the tow to the police. Localities may regulate private towing by ordinance. In a multifamily lot you own and maintain, a resident's vehicle that you know belongs to a resident (by permit, registry or other identification) and that meets the lease's vehicle requirements may not be towed for an expired registration or inspection sticker until 48 hours after the towing operator posts a dated written notice on it; the operator must send you a copy, and if it skips the notice it repays the towing and storage charges and faces a civil penalty of up to $100. Every local towing ordinance must contain the same rule.

title: Lead-Based Paint
bodyText: Federal law requires the lead disclosure, records and pamphlet for pre-1978 housing. Virginia adds that an agent who complied with the federal disclosure law, gave the pamphlet and disclosure and got a signed acknowledgment before an initial lease is protected from personal injury damages for lead poisoning, if the property is maintained under the property maintenance code and new information is disclosed in writing during the tenancy. In pre-1978 housing where the disclosures were given and the lease says so, the tenant may not paint, disturb painted surfaces or make alterations without the landlord's prior written approval. The landlord must keep painted surfaces in line with the property maintenance code; if it does not, the tenant may end the lease. Terminating the lease or taking any other action to retaliate after the tenant reports in writing a lead hazard, or that the tenant's child living in the unit has an elevated blood lead level, is unlawful retaliation, and violating lead hazard control rules that endanger pregnant women or children under six is a misdemeanor with a fine of up to $2,500. Lead paint the landlord knows about is also a ground for a tenant's rent escrow case.

title: Renter's Insurance and Damage Insurance Rules
bodyText: A Virginia landlord may require renter's insurance or damage insurance as a condition of the tenancy and may provide it through its own program, recovering the actual cost plus administrative and opt-out fees; premiums paid to the landlord are rent, not a deposit. The landlord must tell the tenant in writing of the right to buy a separate policy, give a policy summary or certificate before signing (for renter's insurance, stating whether it waives subrogation), and make the policy available on request. If a tenant lets required renter's insurance lapse, the landlord may place coverage and charge the premiums until the tenant shows reinstated coverage. The security deposit plus any premiums paid before the tenancy begins may not exceed two months' rent, though the landlord may add monthly rent to recover later renter's insurance premiums. If the lease does not require renter's insurance, the landlord must give a written notice before signing that it is not responsible for the tenant's property, that its insurance does not cover it, and that renter's insurance does not cover floods.

title: Cable, Satellite and Internet Providers
bodyText: A Virginia landlord of a multifamily building may not take payment from a television or cable provider merely for access to its tenants, and may not charge tenants for such service unless the landlord is the provider, nor vary rent between tenants who do and do not take it. The landlord may require the provider and tenant to pay installation and removal costs and to give reasonable indemnity or security, and may be paid for real marketing services and the use of its property.

title: Squatters and Unauthorized Occupants
bodyText: Virginia has no sheriff-only squatter removal. The owner of a single-family home may get an emergency unlawful detainer hearing within 14 days of filing if the court finds there was never a lease with the occupant, the occupant is there without permission, and the owner gave written notice to vacate at least 72 hours before filing. A guest who stays beyond permission is not a tenant; the landlord may bar a tenant's guest by written notice and then use a trespass warrant. The writ of eviction binds the named tenants and their authorized occupants, guests and any trespassers.

title: Firearms in Rental Housing
bodyText: Virginia bars a public housing lease from prohibiting or restricting lawful firearm possession inside individual units unless federal law or regulation requires it. No Virginia statute limits a private landlord's lease rules on firearms.

title: The Tenant's Right of Redemption
bodyText: If you file an eviction case only for nonpayment of rent, the tenant (or someone for them) can have it dismissed by paying you, your attorney or the court all rent due as of the court date, other charges and fees, late charges, reasonable attorney fees and court costs at or before the first return date, or by presenting a written commitment from a local government or nonprofit to pay within 10 days (Va. Code Ann. 55.1-1250). After the first return date, the tenant can still cancel a scheduled eviction by paying everything claimed, including sheriff fees, at least 48 hours before it. On written request, give the tenant a written statement of all amounts owed; redemption payments come by cashier's check, certified check or money order. A landlord with four or fewer units may limit redemption to once per lease period with written notice (the lease's optional clause).

title: Tenants' Right to Plug-In Solar (From 2027)
bodyText: From January 1, 2027, a tenant may install a small portable solar device (up to 1,200 watts per unit, plugged into an outlet, meeting Virginia's safety and certification requirements) on the exterior of their premises, subject to your reasonable restrictions on size, place and manner (Va. Code Ann. 55.1-1212.1). The tenant gives you written notice at least seven days before, with documentation and the proposed location, and is responsible for any damage. You may prohibit or restrict installation elsewhere on the property; the right doesn't apply where utilities are billed by ratio billing, or to devices needing alterations to the building, wiring or panels without your written approval. A landlord with four or fewer units isn't bound and may require consent (the lease's optional clause).

title: Military Tenants: Right to End the Lease
bodyText: A member of the U.S. Armed Forces, or a National Guard member on full-time duty or serving as a civil service technician, may end the lease on receiving permanent change of station orders, temporary duty orders of more than three months, discharge or release, orders to government quarters forfeiting the housing allowance, or a stop-movement order of at least 30 days that prevents occupancy (Va. Code Ann. 55.1-1235). The tenant gives written notice effective at least 30 days after the next rent due date, and before then a copy of the orders or a commanding officer's letter. You may not charge liquidated damages; the tenant's maintenance duties continue to the termination date, and federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act rights still apply.

title: Fire or Casualty: The Tenant's Options
bodyText: If fire or casualty damages the property so that the tenant's use and enjoyment is substantially impaired, or repairs can be made only if the tenant leaves, the tenant may move out and give you written notice within 14 days after vacating (21 days under the version of the law in force from January 1, 2027) that they are ending the lease, which then ends on the date they moved out (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1240). This applies to every landlord under Virginia's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act; the Act has no exemption for small landlords or single-family homes. The tenant has this right even if the tenant's side caused the damage. From 2027, a tenant who receives your termination notice may ask in writing within seven days that you reevaluate the damage with them. If the lease ends, return the deposit as the law requires and any prepaid rent, with interest recoverable by law, unless you reasonably believe the tenant, an authorized occupant, or a guest or invitee caused the damage; in that case give the tenant a written statement accounting for the deposit and prepaid rent based on the damage, and you may recover your actual damages, including rent until the term ends or a new tenancy starts, whichever comes first, less what you mitigate. Rent is prorated as of the casualty date. If continued occupancy is lawful, rent is reasonably reduced until the home is restored, but only where the damage happened without the tenant's fault or negligence.

title: Disclosures Owed Before Signing: Meth, Drywall, Military Air Zones
bodyText: Before a lease is signed, Virginia requires written disclosure if you actually know the property was used to manufacture methamphetamine and hasn't been cleaned up under Department of Health guidelines (Va. Code Ann. 55.1-1219), or contains defective drywall that hasn't been remediated (55.1-1218), and if the property is in a noise zone or accident potential zone on the official zoning map of a locality with a military air installation (55.1-1217). Give the written disclosure before the tenant signs, not only inside the signed lease; the lease's optional clauses record that it was given.

title: No Just-Cause Eviction Rule
bodyText: Virginia has no just-cause or good-cause eviction rule. A landlord may decline to renew a fixed-term lease, or end a month-to-month or week-to-week tenancy with the required notice, without giving a reason; the Act says a landlord may terminate 'for any other reason not prohibited by law' unless a court finds the reason was retaliation. Limits that apply only in particular situations: no rent increase, cut in services, eviction or threat of eviction, or termination in retaliation for a housing-code complaint, a complaint or suit under the Act, organizing or joining a tenants' organization, or testifying against the landlord (from January 1, 2027 also media and fair housing complaints, and refusing to renew a voucher holder); a family-abuse victim's lease does not end solely because of the abuse where the abuser has been barred from the home by the landlord or by a court order the tenant has provided; an owner who declines to renew the greater of 20 or 50 percent of the month-to-month tenancies in a multifamily property within 30 days must give each of them 60 days' notice; ending leases to rehabilitate or change the use of a building with four or more units takes 120 days' notice in a separate writing (30 days for month-to-month), and a lease cannot waive that or a condominium or cooperative conversion notice; no suit for a lease violation until the tenant has the state's statement of tenant rights; and a public housing authority that gives notice that it will apply to demolish or dispose of a project may not evict, except for lease violations, for 12 months. Fair housing law applies everywhere.

title: Tenant's Belongings and Animals After an Eviction
bodyText: When the sheriff executes a writ of eviction, the sheriff oversees moving the tenant's belongings into the public way or, at your request, into a storage area you designate, which may be the unit itself. The tenant may take them from the public way during the 24 hours after the eviction, and from your storage area at reasonable times during those 24 hours and afterwards until you dispose of them; if you refuse reasonable access, the tenant can go to court. After 24 hours you must remove or dispose of anything left in the public way, and you may dispose of anything left in your storage area as you see fit. During the 24 hours and until you dispose of the belongings, neither you nor the sheriff is liable for the risk of loss. If you sell anything, pay the money to the tenant's account and apply it to what the tenant owes, including your reasonable eviction, storage and sale costs; treat any balance as a security deposit. The sheriff's 72-hour notice must explain these rights and attach the statute. The writ binds the named tenants, their authorized occupants, guests and invitees, and any trespassers. Virginia has no separate rule for animals left behind after an eviction.

title: A Landlord's Duties During and After an Eviction Case
bodyText: Duties a Virginia landlord has in an eviction case: tell the court of any payments by or for the tenant that reduce what is owed. To raise the amount at the hearing when the summons did not ask for all amounts due as of the hearing, give the tenant a separate written notice of the added amounts and of your intent to amend; once the amount is requested or amended that way, you may not file later suits for amounts that could have been included. If the case is continued to decide final rent and damages, mail the tenant notice of the continuance date and the amounts at least 15 days before it and file a copy with the court. If you get judgment for the whole month's rent and re-rent the home before the month ends, mark that part of the judgment satisfied. When a judgment is paid, have it marked satisfied within 30 days; failing to do so can bring a $100 fine and an order to pay the tenant's costs and attorney fees. When a tenant redeems by paying all amounts at least 48 hours before the scheduled eviction, promptly tell the sheriff to cancel it. A writ of eviction must be issued within 180 days of the judgment for possession and is void if not executed within 30 days of issue, and none may issue if you signed a new written lease with the tenant after the judgment. When the summons is served by posting, it must also be mailed at least 10 days before a default judgment. A business landlord may file eviction papers through an officer, an employee or its managing agent without a lawyer. On an appeal, the tenant (unless indigent) pays the amounts owed into court and then pays you the rent by the fifth of each month; if not, you may ask the court for judgment and possession without a hearing. An owner renting a one- to four-family home whose tenant is unpaid in a federal shutdown can get a 60-day stay of a foreclosure on it by asking the lender, with proof, within 90 days.

title: Virginia Consumer Protection Act and Rentals
bodyText: The Virginia Consumer Protection Act does not reach any part of a rental covered by the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act unless the landlord's act is a misrepresentation or fraudulent practice the Consumer Protection Act prohibits. One listed practice bears directly on leases: using in a lease a liquidated damages clause, penalty clause or waiver of defense that is void or unenforceable under Virginia or federal law, or trying to collect under one. A tenant who suffers a loss may recover actual damages or $500, whichever is greater (up to three times actual damages or $1,000 if the violation is willful), plus attorney fees and court costs. The Consumer Protection Act prescribes no lease wording, no statement of waivers and no readability standard.

title: No Plain-Language Lease Rule
bodyText: Virginia has no plain-language or readability law for residential leases and no required statement of waivers. The state's statement of tenant rights and responsibilities, which the landlord must give with the lease, is written in plain language in at least 14-point type by the Department of Housing and Community Development, but that rule governs the Department's form, not the lease.

title: Damage Caused by the Tenant
bodyText: If the tenant, an occupant or a guest damages the home, Virginia law gives you these remedies. The tenant must not deliberately or negligently damage the premises or let anyone else do so, and is responsible for guests' conduct. If the damage materially affects health and safety and can be fixed by repair, replacement or cleaning, you may give written notice, do the work and send an itemized bill for the actual and reasonable cost, which is due as rent on the next rent due date, or at once if the lease has ended. You may recover damages for the breach and apply the security deposit to damage from the tenant's breach of duties, less reasonable wear and tear. If fire or casualty makes the home unlivable, the tenant may still end the lease even if the tenant's side caused the damage; you then give a written statement accounting for the deposit and prepaid rent based on the damage and may recover your actual damages, including rent until the term ends or a new tenancy starts, whichever comes first, with a duty to mitigate and no accelerated rent. From January 1, 2027, you may end the lease on 21 days' notice without first meeting the tenant or offering another unit if you determine the tenant's breach of duties caused the damage. If the tenant stays, rent is reduced during repairs only where the damage happened without the tenant's fault or negligence. Because a lease cannot make the tenant give up a right under the Act, no clause can keep the lease and rent running after the tenant ends it for casualty damage.

title: No Rule on Algorithmic Rent-Setting
bodyText: Virginia has no statute on setting rents with algorithmic pricing software or on landlords sharing rent data, and no rent control. Federal law still applies.

title: Fees Count as Rent
bodyText: In Virginia, 'rent' means all money other than a security deposit owed or paid to the landlord under the lease, including rent paid more than one month ahead, so charges the lease imposes are rent unless a section says otherwise. The Act says so expressly for damage-insurance and renter's-insurance premiums the landlord charges, ratio-billed utility charges and allocated local government fees with their administrative charges, the utility late charge where ratio billing is used, and the bill for repairs the landlord makes after a tenant's breach. Every deposit and rent charge must appear in the first-page fee disclosure or in a later addendum.

title: Landlord's Right to Fix a Tenant's Breach
bodyText: If a tenant's breach of the lease or of the tenant's statutory duties materially affects health and safety and can be fixed by repair, replacement of a damaged item or cleaning, you may send a written notice specifying the breach and stating that you will enter, do the work in a workmanlike manner and send an itemized bill. The actual and reasonable cost is due as rent on the next rent due date, or at once if the lease has ended. In an emergency you may enter and do the work as promptly as conditions require. You may do the work yourself or hire someone. The right exists by law whatever the lease says.

title: No Statutory Rule on Blank Spaces in a Lease
bodyText: Virginia has no statute requiring every blank in a written lease to be completed or making an incomplete lease a breach. Completing every blank is still good practice, and the fee disclosure on the first page must list every deposit and rent charge.

title: Quiet Enjoyment in Virginia Law
bodyText: Virginia has no statute that writes a covenant of quiet enjoyment into every residential lease. If a lease uses the short phrase that the landlord covenants 'for the lessee's quiet enjoyment of his term', Virginia law gives it a set meaning: a tenant who pays the rent and keeps the lease may peaceably possess the home for the term without interruption or disturbance from anyone. The Residential Landlord and Tenant Act protects the same interest in other ways: it limits the landlord's entry, bars lockouts and cutting off essential services, and makes each tenant responsible for keeping guests from disturbing the neighbors' peaceful enjoyment.

title: Forms Virginia Law Supplies
bodyText: Virginia statutes supply or require several forms: a short lease form a lease may follow; the Department of Housing and Community Development's statement of tenant rights and responsibilities and the acknowledgment form the parties sign; the Department's sample termination notice with the language for accepting rent with reservation; the fixed sentence above the first-page fee list; the words a tenant uses to waive the homestead exemption; and the hearing-request form served with a distress warrant. From July 1, 2027, the Department also publishes a sample payment plan.

title: Tenant-Installed Security Systems and Cameras
bodyText: A Virginia tenant may install new security systems the tenant believes necessary for safety, including chain latches the landlord approves and fire detection devices, if the installation does no permanent damage, the tenant gives the landlord a duplicate of all keys and the operating instructions for every device, and the tenant pays the reasonable cost of removing the devices and repairing any damage when the tenancy ends. The statute does not mention cameras or video doorbells; a camera installed as a security system falls under the same conditions, and the lease's alteration and rules terms cannot take the right away.

title: Abandonment, Remaining Rent and the Duty to Mitigate
bodyText: In Virginia, a tenant who abandons the home ends the lease: the law treats the lease as terminated by you as of the date of abandonment. If you can't tell whether the tenant has left, serve a written notice (by the usual notice rules) requiring the tenant to tell you in writing within seven days that the tenant intends to stay. If the tenant answers, or you otherwise find the tenant is still living there, you may not treat the home as abandoned. If not, once the seven days pass the home is presumed abandoned (the tenant can rebut this) and the lease ends that day. Once the lease ends, by abandonment or for any other reason, you may claim possession and rent and, separately, actual damages for the breach. Those damages may include the rent that would have come due until the lease term ends or a new tenant's lease begins, whichever comes first, but you must mitigate your damages, and after you have possession you may not seek a judgment for accelerated rent for the rest of the term. So the lease does not keep the full remaining rent owing no matter what: a clause saying you need not try to re-rent, or that all remaining rent is due at once, will not hold (see Casualty Rights and Mitigation Cannot Be Waived). Virginia's statutes do not say what efforts mitigation takes; the cautious course is to advertise and show the home promptly at a market rent and keep a record of what you did. If you get a judgment for the whole month's rent and re-rent the home before that month ends, mark that part of the judgment satisfied. If the lease requires the tenant to tell you of an absence of more than seven days and the tenant doesn't, you may recover your actual damages (see Notice of Extended Absence), and during any absence of more than seven days you may enter when reasonably necessary to protect your property. When the tenant has left, credit the security deposit under the deposit rules. For belongings left behind, use the library's Abandonment and Property Left Behind clause.

title: Accessory Dwelling Units
bodyText: Until July 1, 2027, Virginia has no statewide accessory dwelling unit (ADU) rule: whether you may build or rent one depends on your locality's zoning ordinance. From July 1, 2027, single-family zoning districts are treated as allowing an ADU (an attached or detached unit on the same lot as the main home, with its own living, sleeping, eating, cooking and sanitation facilities) as a permitted accessory use. You need an ADU permit from the locality (fee up to $500), and the locality may require only what the statute lists, including: a lease term of 30 consecutive days or longer for renting the ADU; owner occupancy of the ADU or the main home, but not both, and only at the time you apply to build or convert it; parking; size limits of no less than 350 or 500 square feet depending on lot size; building, water, sewer, flood and historic-district compliance; no ADU on a lot with more than one dwelling unit; and no separate sale. A locality may not require that the ADU's occupants be related to the main home's occupants, or impose setbacks, height or other limits stricter than for the main home. The statute does not apply to a locality that adopted an ADU ordinance before January 1, 2026, to ADU permits approved before July 1, 2027, or to a substantially compliant ordinance adopted before then. Recorded covenants, condominium instruments and property owners' association declarations can still restrict ADUs. Renting an ADU is an ordinary residential tenancy under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, with all its rules; a rental for fewer than 30 days is a short-term rental that the locality may regulate and register. For rental inspection purposes, part of an owner-occupied home counts as a rental unit when the tenant's part has its own cooking and sleeping areas and a bathroom, unless the zoning ordinance provides otherwise.

title: Agreed Ways of Giving Notice
bodyText: Virginia's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act treats a person as having notice of a fact he actually knows, has been told orally, or has reason to know from the circumstances, but a notice that is not in writing puts the burden on the sender to prove it was given. The standard methods for a written notice are regular mail or hand delivery, with the sender keeping a certificate of service. The parties may agree on an additional method: if the lease provides for it, landlord and tenant may send notices in electronic form, and the tenant may at any time elect paper instead. The sender must keep sufficient proof of the electronic delivery, such as an electronic delivery receipt, a fax confirmation, or a certificate of service. The library's optional Electronic Notices clause sets this up by e-mail. The Act's electronic form is not limited to e-mail; if you want another electronic channel, such as a text message or a portal message, name it in the lease and keep a delivery record, but keep mail or hand delivery available for termination notices and any tenant who asks for paper. A notice reaching an organization, such as a management company, is effective from when it reaches the person handling that matter, or when it would have with reasonable diligence. The landlord's place for receiving notices is the place of business where the lease was made or any place held out for receipt of notices; the tenant's is the last known residence, which may be the unit.

title: Notice of Claims and Proceedings Against the Property
bodyText: Virginia has no statute requiring a tenant to tell you about a foreclosure, tax sale, ejectment suit or other claim against the property. Make it a lease duty with the library's Notice of Proceedings Against the Property clause. If someone else claims the property, a tenant's attornment to that stranger (agreeing to hold under the stranger or pay rent to the stranger) is void unless you consent or a court orders it. When you sell, the buyer takes the rent and reversion without the tenant's attornment, but a tenant who paid rent to you before learning of the sale is not harmed by having done so; tell the tenant of the sale and give the buyer's name, address and phone number. Your duties to tell the tenant about a proceeding: if you rent out a single-family home and receive a lender's notice of default, acceleration or foreclosure sale, you must tell the tenant in writing within five business days (see Telling Tenants About a Mortgage Default or Foreclosure). A trustee's foreclosure notice goes to the owner, lienholders and associations, not the tenant. In a condemnation, the condemning agency must serve its notice on a tenant entitled to take part (a lease of 12 months or longer) whose lease is recorded or whose tenancy it knows of (see When Rental Property Is Taken by Eminent Domain).

title: Charging for a Disabled Smoke or CO Alarm
bodyText: Virginia sets no fee for a tenant's removing or tampering with a smoke or carbon monoxide alarm, and no statute authorizes a fixed tampering charge. The tenant must not remove or tamper with a properly functioning smoke or carbon monoxide alarm you installed, including by removing working batteries, and must maintain the alarms as the fire and building codes require (see Tenant's Statutory Duties and Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Alarms). If the tenant disables an alarm, your remedies are cost-based: a disabled alarm is ordinarily read as a breach that materially affects health and safety and can be fixed by repair or replacement (no court decision reviewed), so you may give written notice, repair or replace the alarm, and send an itemized bill for the actual and reasonable cost, due as rent on the next rent due date; you may also give a notice to remedy the breach, and apply the deposit to the damage when the tenancy ends. The Act's ban on maintenance and repair fees does not apply when the tenant's violation made the repair necessary. A fixed fine unrelated to your cost is the risky course: Virginia has no statute approving liquidated damages for this, and the Consumer Protection Act lists using a void penalty clause in a lease, or trying to collect under one, as a prohibited practice (it reaches transactions governed by the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act only for acts that are a misrepresentation or fraudulent act or practice under § 59.1-200, which describes its list as fraudulent acts or practices) (see Liquidated Damages in Virginia Leases). The only alarm charges the law itself allows are a reasonable fee to install a carbon monoxide alarm the tenant asks for, and a refundable deposit, up to the greater of the original or replacement cost, for a smoke alarm for a tenant who is deaf or hard of hearing. The Statewide Fire Prevention Code also makes it unlawful, as a misdemeanor, to remove or tamper with a required fire detection and alarm system; whether that reaches a single smoke alarm in a home is unsettled. Never leave a disabled alarm unrepaired.

title: Substitute Housing and Temporary Relocation
bodyText: Virginia has no general duty to provide or pay for alternate housing whenever a rental becomes unfit. The rules are specific. Tenant-triggered: if, contrary to the lease or the Act, you willfully or negligently fail to supply an essential service (heat, running water, hot water, electricity, gas, or central air conditioning you supplied and that was operating when the lease took effect), the tenant may give you written notice and, after a reasonable time to correct it, procure reasonable substitute housing while the failure lasts; the tenant is then excused from rent for that period as the court determines, and may recover attorney fees. The statute does not make you pay for the substitute housing itself, and the remedy is lost if the tenant's side caused the condition. The tenant may choose damages for lost rental value instead. Landlord-initiated: for a nonemergency repair that can only be done with the unit empty, you may, on at least 30 days' written notice, require the tenant to move for up to 30 days to a comparable unit or hotel you select, at no cost to the tenant, while rent continues. Mold has its own rule: where mold materially affects a tenant's or occupant's health or safety, you may require the tenant to move for up to 30 days to a comparable unit or hotel you select, at no cost to the tenant, while rent continues; that statute sets no notice period, and you pay the relocation and remediation costs unless the mold results from the tenant's failure to meet the tenant's duties. Fire or casualty: no duty to rehouse, but from January 1, 2027, before you end a lease for casualty damage the tenant didn't cause, you must offer any substantially similar unit in the same complex available within a reasonable time, on the current lease terms. One local exception: a county under the county manager plan may by ordinance make the county and owner split a tenant's relocation costs when a building of four or more units is emptied by 120 days' notice for rehabilitation. Government projects that displace people carry their own relocation assistance, not a landlord duty.

title: Tenant's Animals Left Without Care
bodyText: Virginia has no rule that lets you enter a rental to feed, care for or remove a tenant's animal when the tenant is away, hospitalized or detained. Your access rights are limited to those the Act lists: entry with the tenant's consent for inspections, repairs, services and showings; entry without consent in an emergency; entry during an absence of more than seven days at times reasonably necessary to protect your own possessions and property; entry to do repair, replacement or cleaning work that a tenant's breach materially affecting health and safety requires, after written notice or at once in an emergency; entry under a court order; and entry after the tenant abandons or surrenders the unit. Whether an animal left without food or water is an emergency that justifies entry is unsettled. Animal welfare law works through officers instead: a humane investigator, law-enforcement officer or animal control officer may seize an animal that has been abandoned or is in direct and immediate danger, and then must petition the general district court for a hearing, to be held not more than 10 business days after the seizure. Leaving an animal without basic care for four consecutive days counts as abandoning it. Be careful acting on your own: dogs and cats are personal property, and anyone who keeps, harbors or has an animal in his care is an owner under the animal welfare law, with its duties of care. When the sole tenant under a written lease dies and no one has been appointed by the circuit court to handle the estate, the authorized contact named in the application, lease or other landlord document may, after giving reasonable proof of identification if you ask, enter, see the records and claim the tenant's property, which includes pets (see When a Sole Tenant Dies). What to do: ask in the application or lease for an emergency contact who can care for animals, keep a record of the animals the lease allows, and if an animal seems abandoned, try to reach the tenant and the contact, then call animal control rather than taking the animal yourself.

title: Asbestos in Rental Buildings
bodyText: Virginia has no statute requiring you to inspect a rental for asbestos, to disclose asbestos to a prospective or current tenant, or to post or give tenants an asbestos notice. Asbestos rules apply when work disturbs it. Renovation and demolition: for a building whose first building permit was issued before January 1, 1985, the local building department will not issue a renovation or demolition permit until you certify that a licensed asbestos inspector has inspected the affected parts and found no asbestos-containing material, or that the federal response actions and worker protections will be followed. Roofing, flooring or siding repair can instead be covered by a statement that the materials are assumed to contain friable asbestos and will be handled by a licensed asbestos contractor. This permit rule does not apply to single-family homes or residential buildings with four or fewer units unless the work is for commercial or public development, or to small amounts (under 260 linear feet on pipes, 160 square feet on other components, or 35 cubic feet). An abatement area may not be reoccupied until you certify that the work is done and final air clearances meet the state limits. The construction code also requires a permit to remove or disturb asbestos-containing materials during construction or demolition. Who may do the work: anyone contracting for compensation to do an asbestos project must hold an asbestos contractor's license, and workers and supervisors need licenses, except for roofing, flooring or siding work by trained workers. A landlord whose own employees do an asbestos project on property the landlord owns or leases is exempt from these licenses, but federal air-quality and worker-protection rules still apply. Condominium conversions: a declarant converting a building finished before July 1, 1978 must state in the public offering statement whether it was inspected for asbestos and whether response actions are needed. Practical point: before renovating an older building, get a licensed inspection, schedule work to limit tenant exposure, and keep the reports; disturbing asbestos carelessly can also breach your duty to keep the premises safe. See Repair Duties and Tenant Remedies.

title: Association Documents and the Tenant
bodyText: Virginia does not require a lease of a condominium unit, cooperative unit or lot in a property owners' association to disclose the association's obligations or documents to the tenant, or to include any statement by you or the tenant about them. Two rules still make giving the tenant the association's rules the safe course. First, the association may require you, as owner, to give it the names and contact information of your tenants and authorized occupants and of your authorized agent, the tenants' and occupants' vehicle information, and the tenant's acknowledgment of and consent to the association's rules.
