Second, under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act a rule binds a tenant only if, among other conditions, the tenant got a copy when signing the lease or when the rule was adopted, and a later rule that substantially changes the tenant's bargain binds only with the tenant's written consent; the statute speaks of rules a landlord adopts, and it is not settled whether it reaches association rules the lease incorporates. So give the tenant a copy of the association's rules before signing and get a signed acknowledgment (see Homeowner / Condominium Association Compliance). The association may not make you use its own lease or lease addendum unless the condominium instruments or declaration expressly allow it. When you buy a unit to rent out, the association's resale certificate must state any restriction on an owner's ability to rent the unit.

title: Attorney Fees Under a Virginia Lease
bodyText: A Virginia lease may make the tenant pay your attorney fees only as the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act provides (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1208); the guidance on prohibited lease terms states the basic limits. In more detail: When the tenant breaches the lease, you may recover reasonable attorney fees as the lease provides or as the law allows, whether or not you file suit; costs of the proceeding only once a court action has been filed; and in a lawsuit you win, the court awards reasonable attorney fees unless the tenant proves that the failure to pay rent or vacate was reasonable (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1245, subsections H and I now, J and K from July 1, 2027). After termination the fee claim travels with your claims for possession, rent and actual damages (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1251). The Act also allows fees, without depending on the lease, against a tenant who holds over (unless the failure to vacate was reasonable), fails to surrender, or refuses lawful access; and, if the lease says so, against a tenant who without reasonable justification refuses a showing (Va. Code Ann. §§ 55.1-1210, 55.1-1229, 55.1-1233, 55.1-1253). For a bounced check or rejected electronic payment, attorney fees under the bad-check statute are recoverable only if awarded by the court. To redeem the tenancy in an unlawful detainer for rent, the tenant must pay reasonable attorney fees as the lease provides and as the law allows. Virginia has no rule making a lease attorney-fee clause automatically two-way, and no required wording for it. But the Act gives tenants fee awards of their own in many cases, including your noncompliance (unless you prove your actions were reasonable), a willful deposit violation, unlawful exclusion or interruption of services, abuse of access, a willful, bad-faith failure to deliver possession, a willful or negligent failure to supply an essential service, and a suit to enforce a prohibited lease term; the court may also award the tenant fees in a rent escrow case or on a successful defense to a nonpayment case. The library's default clause uses a prevailing-party fee sentence limited to what applicable law permits.

title: Automatic Lease Renewal
bodyText: A Virginia lease may provide that it renews automatically; the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act lists automatic renewal among the terms the parties may agree on (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1204). Without such a term, a tenant who stays on with your consent after the lease ends becomes a month-to-month tenant on the old terms, and if you never offered a written lease, the 12-month tenancy the law creates does not renew automatically. If you own more than four rental units in Virginia (or more than a 10 percent interest in more than four), you must give a tenant whose lease renews automatically, or who has an option to renew, written notice of any rent increase for the next term at least 60 days before the lease ends, and must give any tenant written notice of nonrenewal at least 60 days before the lease ends. From July 1, 2027, the rent-increase notice must be given at least 90 days before the lease ends and must set a deadline, at least 30 days after the notice is delivered, for the tenant to say whether it will renew; the nonrenewal notice stays at 60 days. A landlord with four or fewer units has no statutory renewal-notice deadline but must follow the lease. The Act requires no separate reminder before an automatic renewal and does not limit how early you may ask a tenant to commit to renewing. Virginia's separate automatic renewal law for paid subscriptions and purchasing agreements requires clear and conspicuous terms, an easy cancellation method, and, for a renewal of more than 12 months, a reminder 30 to 60 days before the cancellation deadline. That law is not written for leases, and whether it reaches a residential lease is not settled, so the cautious course is to set the renewal clause off with a clear heading, keep each renewal term to 12 months or less, and remind the tenant in writing before the deadline to give notice. The optional Automatic Renewal clause does this. Manufactured home lot leases have their own renewal rules under a separate Act.

title: No Balcony Inspection Rule
bodyText: Virginia has no law requiring periodic inspection of balconies, decks, porches or other exterior elevated elements at rental properties, by an engineer or anyone else, and no report you must give tenants or file. Your duties are the general ones. You must keep the premises fit and habitable, keep common areas of a multifamily property structurally safe, and comply with building and housing codes affecting health and safety. The state Maintenance Code requires the exterior of a structure to be maintained in good repair and structurally sound, and handrails and guards that were required or provided when the building was built to be maintained under that code. Rebuilding: if you use the construction code to reconstruct a deck, balcony or porch 30 inches or more above grade on a one- or two-family home or townhouse, the rebuilt structure must meet current loading, connection and attachment rules (the handrail and guard height rules are not reset). An unsafe balcony can be declared an unsafe structure by the local code official, and after a tenant complaint the building department must enforce the unsafe-structure rules. A practical precaution is a periodic visual check of wood balconies, ledger connections, railings and stairs, with repairs by a licensed contractor, and a lease rule limiting heavy loads (such as hot tubs or large planters) on balconies. See Repair Duties and Tenant Remedies.

title: Pest Reporting and Treatment Cooperation
bodyText: Virginia has no bed bug statute, but its general pest rules set the tenant's duty to cooperate, and the library's Virginia clauses already put them in the lease. The tenant must keep the part of the unit and premises the tenant occupies free from insects and pests and promptly tell you about any; must prepare the unit for a pesticide treatment as your written instructions direct and, if pests are found, follow your written instructions after the treatment; and pays the added cost of treatment caused by unreasonable delay in reporting, and the cost of treatment caused by the tenant's fault in failing to prevent an infestation (see Tenant's Statutory Duties). You give 48 hours' written notice before applying pesticide in the unit unless the tenant asked for it or agrees to a shorter period, and the tenant may not unreasonably refuse entry to treat (see Landlord's Access and Pesticide Notices to Tenants). If the tenant doesn't cooperate and the breach materially affects health and safety and can be fixed by repair, replacement or cleaning, you may give a written notice that you will do the work, then do it and send an itemized bill for the actual and reasonable cost, due as rent on the next rent due date (in an emergency, do it first and bill after), or give a notice to remedy. Otherwise treatment is your cost: you must keep the premises fit and habitable and may not charge a maintenance or repair fee the tenant's violation did not make necessary. The Virginia Maintenance Code also requires every structure to be kept free from insect and rodent infestation, with prompt extermination by approved processes, and Virginia deleted the model code's sections dividing that duty between owner and occupant. A rodent infestation is one of the conditions behind the tenant's repair, escrow and move-in remedies. The library's multistate Pest Reporting and Treatment clauses are not used for Virginia, because they say you pay in every case the tenant did not cause, which would give up the added cost of a tenant's late report.

title: Arbitration Clauses in Virginia Leases
bodyText: Virginia allows binding arbitration of future disputes by a provision in a written contract: the agreement is valid, enforceable and irrevocable except on grounds that would allow revoking any contract, and a court must order arbitration when a party refuses (Va. Code Ann. §§ 8.01-581.01, 8.01-581.02). The Residential Landlord and Tenant Act says nothing about arbitration, and Virginia has no rule excluding residential leases. A lease arbitration clause in Virginia should keep these points. Possession cases (unlawful detainer) belong in court, where the Act's notices, hearing deadlines, redemption and appeal rules run; and court-based tenant remedies such as rent escrow and the petition for an unlawful lockout should be left out. The clause must not take away any right or remedy the Act gives (a lease may not make the tenant waive them), so the arbitrator must be able to award whatever a court could. Each side keeps the right to a lawyer; a waiver of that right made before the hearing is ineffective. Since 2026, for a pre-dispute arbitration agreement with a consumer, a business that drafted the clause and must pay fees for the arbitration to proceed is in material breach, in default, and treated as having waived arbitration if it does not pay within 30 days after they are due; the consumer may then go to court or compel arbitration at the drafter's expense for attorney fees and costs. High-volume arbitration providers must also use a fair arbitrator-selection process, and these requirements are treated as material terms of the agreement (Va. Code Ann. §§ 8.01-581.017 to 8.01-581.021). Whether a residential tenant counts as a consumer under those sections is not settled, so plan as if it does: pay the fees promptly and use a provider with a neutral selection process. Including a term the Act prohibits carries no penalty by itself, but if you bring an action to enforce a prohibited term the tenant may recover actual damages and attorney fees, so a clause that overreaches is a risk when you rely on it. Asking a court to send a tenant's claim to arbitration is such an action, and no Virginia statute says whether an arbitration clause is a waiver of the Act's remedies (Virginia case law was not reviewed). For that reason this library does not offer an arbitration clause for Virginia. If you want one anyway, have a Virginia lawyer draft it with the points above, and keep possession cases, rent escrow and lockout petitions in court. Federal law also makes written arbitration provisions in contracts involving commerce enforceable on the same terms as other contracts.

title: Marijuana in Virginia Rentals
bodyText: Virginia lets adults 21 and older possess marijuana and grow up to four plants per household at their main residence, but no Virginia statute protects a tenant's use or growing of marijuana, or a medical cannabis patient's use, against a lease that forbids it, and none limits a lease ban. You may ban smoking or vaping marijuana (the Smoking Policy clause already bans smoking of any kind), growing it, or possessing or using it on the property with the optional Marijuana Restrictions clause. Put the ban in the lease at signing: a rule you adopt later binds the tenant only after reasonable notice and, if it substantially changes the bargain, only with the tenant's written consent (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1228). A tenant who does grow at home must keep the plants out of public view, keep people under 21 away from them and tag each plant, and no one may make marijuana concentrate at home; an owner may not intentionally or knowingly allow that (Va. Code Ann. § 4.1-1101). A dwelling used for illegal drug activity with the owner's or lessor's knowledge is a common nuisance, and an owner who knowingly permits it commits a crime (Va. Code Ann. § 18.2-258). If a tenant with a medical cannabis certification asks for an exception as a disability accommodation, get advice first: marijuana remains illegal under federal law, and this library has not reviewed the case law.

title: Carpet Cleaning at Move-Out
bodyText: Virginia has no statute on carpet cleaning at move-out. No law lets you require professional carpet cleaning on a stated condition (such as having cleaned the carpets before the tenancy), and none sets an age or useful-life test for carpet or paint deductions; the only measure is reasonable wear and tear. The tenant must leave the unit in good and clean order, reasonable wear and tear excepted, and you may apply the deposit to damage from the tenant's breach of the tenant's duties (less reasonable wear and tear), to other charges the lease provides, and to actual damages, itemized in writing within 45 days. But you may not require a tenant to pay a fee for maintenance or repair of the unit unless the tenant's violation of the Act made it necessary, so a carpet-cleaning charge taken whatever the carpet's condition is the risky course. Charge for carpet cleaning only when the carpet is soiled or stained beyond reasonable wear and tear, use the actual reasonable cost, and record the carpet's condition in the move-in report. The library's Use of Security Deposit clause already limits cleaning charges to a unit left substantially less clean than at the start, and its multistate professional carpet-cleaning clause is not used for Virginia (see No Statutory Schedule of Deposit Charges).

title: Casualty Rights and Mitigation Cannot Be Waived
bodyText: Neither the tenant's fire-and-casualty rights nor your duty to mitigate can be waived in a Virginia lease. Both are in the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, and a lease may not make the tenant waive rights or remedies under the Act (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1208). Casualty: if fire or casualty substantially impairs the tenant's enjoyment (use and enjoyment, from January 1, 2027) or repairs require the tenant to leave, the tenant may move out and end the lease by written notice within 14 days after vacating (21 days from January 1, 2027), even if the tenant's side caused the damage; you must then account for the deposit and prepaid rent, and where you reasonably believe the tenant's side caused it you may recover actual damages (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1240). A lease cannot keep rent running after such a termination or release you from these rules, and a release of your liability for casualty losses is itself a prohibited exculpatory term. Mitigation: when a lease ends early, you may claim rent until the term ends or a new tenancy starts, whichever comes first, but nothing diminishes your duty to mitigate, and you may not seek accelerated rent after possession; the same duty applies after abandonment (Va. Code Ann. §§ 55.1-1249, 55.1-1251). A clause saying you need not try to re-rent, or that all remaining rent is due at once, does not hold. What you can put in the lease is your own right to end it after a casualty, on the statute's notice and, from 2027, its conditions; the library's casualty clause does that. See the guidance on the tenant's casualty options and on damage caused by the tenant.

title: No Certificate of Occupancy Disclosure
bodyText: Virginia has no rule that you tell a tenant whether the unit has a certificate of occupancy or give the tenant a copy. The certificate matters in other ways. Under the Building Code, a certificate of occupancy must be obtained before a new building, or a building whose occupancy classification changes, is occupied. If the building department has no certificate for an older building, the owner may ask for one, and it will be issued if there are no current maintenance or fire code violations and the use has not changed; such buildings may continue in use. A certificate can be suspended or revoked for repeated code violations or when a notice of unsafe structure is not complied with, and a locality fighting drug or other criminal blight may seek a court order revoking it. A unit with a certificate of occupancy issued within the last four years is exempt from a local rental inspection program for four years. If you repair or improve your own rental units yourself, you do not need a contractor's license for that work, but the work must meet the Building Code, and if you later sell the building you must first obtain a certificate of occupancy for the work unless the buyer acknowledges in writing that none was issued; violations are Class 1 misdemeanors, and a third conviction within 36 months is a Class 6 felony. Whatever the certificate's status, the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act requires you to comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety and to keep the unit fit and habitable.

title: Children and Occupancy Limits
bodyText: Familial status is protected by the Virginia Fair Housing Law: one or more children under 18 living with a parent, a legal custodian, or a custodian's written designee, and also anyone who is pregnant or is in the process of securing legal custody of a child (Va. Code Ann. § 36-96.1:1). You may not refuse to rent, set different terms or charges, steer families to particular buildings or floors, limit their use of facilities, advertise "adults only" or "no children", or evict because of familial status, including when a child is born or joins the household during the tenancy (Va. Code Ann. § 36-96.3; 18VAC135-50-80, 18VAC135-50-90, 18VAC135-50-100). You may set reasonable occupancy standards based on the number and size of bedrooms and the overall size of the unit, as long as they don't violate local, state or federal limits; a limit of two persons per bedroom is presumed reasonable, subject to fair housing law, and the building code requires at least 70 square feet per bedroom and 50 square feet per occupant where more than one person sleeps in a bedroom (Va. Code Ann. §§ 36-96.2, 36-105.4). An application may ask the number, ages, sex and family relationship of the applicants and intended occupants (Va. Code Ann. § 36-96.2). The familial-status protection doesn't apply to housing for older persons: housing under a program designed for the elderly, housing solely for people 62 or older, or housing intended for people 55 or older where at least 80 percent of occupied units have a person 55 or older and the owner publishes and follows policies showing that intent (Va. Code Ann. § 36-96.7). The small-landlord exemptions (up to three single-family houses rented without a broker, or an owner-occupied building of up to four units) don't cover discriminatory advertising. Virginia doesn't require the lease to address children. House rules for children's safety in common areas should be tied to real safety concerns and, where possible, apply to adults too; a rule that singles out children can itself be a discriminatory limit on facilities. The library's permitted-occupants clause lists occupants by name; list children there like any other occupant.

title: No Cold-Weather Notice Before Vacating
bodyText: Virginia has no rule requiring a tenant to warn you before moving out or leaving the home empty in cold weather, and no criminal penalty for failing to. What protects the pipes instead: The tenant must keep all utility services the tenant pays for on at all times during the lease, so a tenant who leaves early and shuts off heat or water before the lease ends breaks the lease and is responsible for the resulting damage. If the lease requires notice of an anticipated absence of more than seven days and the tenant does not give it, you may recover your actual damages; use the library's optional Notice of Extended Absence clause. During any absence of more than seven days you may enter at reasonable times to protect your property, for example to keep the heat on or drain the pipes. If you cannot tell whether the tenant has abandoned the home, give the seven-day written notice the abandonment rules require before treating it as abandoned. Electric and gas utilities do not cut off residential service for nonpayment when the forecast low is 32 degrees or below, but a tenant can still close an account, so act quickly if you learn a unit is empty in winter. Your own duty to supply heat in season continues where the lease has you furnish heat. The library has no separate cold-weather notice clause; the extended-absence clause and the tenant's utility duty cover the risk. See Notice of Extended Absence and Abandonment and Property Left Behind.

title: Collection Fees on Past-Due Rent
bodyText: Virginia has no statute that names or caps a "collection fee" on past-due rent. The Residential Landlord and Tenant Act controls what you can collect instead: rent, other charges and fees, and late charges as the lease provides; reasonable attorney fees as the lease provides or the law allows; costs of the proceeding only once a court action has been filed; and damages to the unit (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1245). The guidance on prohibited lease terms covers the attorney-fee and service-cost limits; here is what it does not say. First, a charge must be in the lease to be recoverable as a contracted fee, and a lease may not make the tenant pay your attorney fees except as the Act provides, so a percentage "collection fee" that is really an attorney or agency fee is not a way around those limits (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1208). Second, a fee for collecting or processing a payment is banned unless you offer a payment method with no added fee, and a card or electronic-payment fee may not exceed the actual third-party cost; the bad-check processing fee is whatever the lease specifies up to $50 (Va. Code Ann. §§ 55.1-1200, 55.1-1204). Third, every charge the tenant must pay counts as rent and the lease must itemize, beginning on its first page, the deposit, periodic rent and one-time charges, under a statutory sentence saying no additional deposits or rent will be charged unless listed or added by separate addendum; list any collection-related charge there or in an addendum (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1204.1). Fourth, a fixed charge larger than your actual cost risks being a penalty, and using a void penalty clause in a lease is a prohibited practice under the Consumer Protection Act. You may share a tenant's information with your attorney or collection agency. A third-party collector may also be subject to federal debt-collection law, which this guidance does not cover.

title: Lighting in Common Areas
bodyText: Virginia sets no specific lighting level for hallways, stairways, parking areas or other common areas of rental housing. Your duties are general: keep common areas shared by two or more units of a multifamily property clean and structurally safe, comply with building and housing codes affecting health and safety, and maintain the electrical facilities you supply. The state Maintenance Code requires every habitable space, hallway, stairway, bathroom and other space to be kept lit, naturally or artificially, to the extent the building code in force when the building was built required or to the extent you provided, and requires lighting circuits and fixtures to be maintained under that code. Virginia removed the model maintenance code's own minimum for common halls and stairways, so the construction code that applied to your building (including its exit-path lighting) sets the standard. A building that lacks illumination or other essential equipment to a dangerous degree can be declared unsafe, and a lack of light is one of the conditions that can support a tenant's rent escrow case, a defense to a nonpayment eviction, or repair by a licensed contractor after 14 days' written notice. No Virginia statute addresses common-area lights wired to a tenant's own electric meter. If a small building's hall or porch lights run on a tenant's service, say so plainly in the lease before signing; billing tenants a share of a building's utility bill is allowed only through the submetering, allocation or ratio billing rules stated clearly in the lease (see Utilities Billed by Landlord). Good lighting at entrances, stairs and parking areas also reduces your exposure if someone is hurt or a crime occurs. See Repair Duties and Tenant Remedies.

title: No Communal or Tribal Land Lease Approval Rule
bodyText: Virginia has no communal land system and no statute requiring a government officer or tribal body to approve a lease of tribal, reservation or communal land before it is valid. For an ordinary Virginia rental, no approval is needed. If the property is on an Indian reservation recognized by the Commonwealth, or is land held in trust for a tribe, different rules can apply: tribal law and federal law govern leasing of such land, federal approval may be required for land held in trust by the United States, and a state-recognized tribe that has adopted the Uniform Statewide Building Code by tribal ordinance may enforce it on its own reservation instead of the locality (Va. Code Ann. § 36-105.5). Whether Virginia's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act applies on a reservation is a question of tribal and federal law this library has not reviewed, so get advice before leasing such land. A community land trust's long-term ground lease is a different arrangement: Virginia defines community land trusts and gives their ground-leased homes special tax assessment, but requires no approval of the lease (Va. Code Ann. §§ 55.1-1200, 58.1-3295.2).

title: Condemned Units: Rent and Refunds
bodyText: Virginia has no general statute that bars you from collecting rent once a unit is condemned or ordered vacated, but its specific rules have the same effect in most cases. Condemnation after the tenant's warning: if the tenant gave you notice during the tenancy that the unit violated an applicable building code, the violation posed a substantial risk to the tenant's health, safety or welfare, and it led to the tenant being excluded because the unit was condemned, you are liable for the tenant's actual damages and must return prepaid rent not yet due on the condemnation date, the security deposit, and any rent paid to you after the unit was condemned. This does not apply if the condemnation was caused by the deliberate or negligent act or omission of the tenant, an authorized occupant or a guest, or by an act of God, or if the lease was properly ended for fire or casualty damage. Fire or casualty: if damage substantially impairs the tenant's enjoyment or the tenant must leave for repairs, either side may end the lease; rent is prorated as of the date of the casualty and you return the deposit and prepaid rent, less amounts for damage you reasonably believe the tenant's side caused (see Fire or Casualty: The Tenant's Options). Other protections: a condition at move-in that seriously threatens health or safety lets the tenant end the lease within seven days and get back all deposits and rent; a violation or condemnation notice from a government agency counts as notice to you for the tenant's rent escrow action and defense to a nonpayment eviction, where a court can abate rent; and once an unsafe structure is placarded, no one may occupy it until the code official allows.

title: No Confession of Judgment in a Lease
bodyText: A Virginia lease may not authorize anyone to confess judgment on a claim arising out of the lease (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1208). A cognovit or warrant-of-attorney clause letting you, or an attorney you name, enter a judgment against the tenant without a lawsuit is unenforceable in a residential lease, and if you bring an action to enforce it the tenant may recover actual damages and reasonable attorney fees. Virginia does allow confessed judgments in general: a debtor, or an attorney-in-fact under a power of attorney, may confess judgment in a circuit court clerk's office, and a note or bond with a confession provision must carry a boldface notice warning that it waives important rights; the debtor may move to set the judgment aside within 21 days after notice of it (Va. Code Ann. §§ 8.01-432, 8.01-433, 8.01-433.1). Those rules are for notes, bonds and other debt instruments. Because the ban covers any claim arising out of the rental agreement, do not route lease debts (rent, damages, fees) into a separate note or guaranty with a confession provision; collect them through an unlawful detainer or a warrant in debt. A defendant in a suit already pending may still choose to confess judgment for an amount the plaintiff will accept, which is a step in a lawsuit, not a lease term.

title: Habitability Rules Virginia Has and Lacks
bodyText: How Virginia compares on habitability features found in other states. Present: (1) a fitness duty and code-compliance duty that a lease cannot waive, though the tenant may agree in writing, in good faith, to take on common-area cleaning, trash, water, hot water, heat or air conditioning, or specified repairs; (2) written-notice termination for a material breach (21 days to remedy, termination at least 30 days after notice); (3) a seven-day right to end the lease if the unit is seriously unsafe or lacks heat, water, electricity or sewage disposal at the start of the tenancy; (4) essential-service remedies (damages or substitute housing) for heat, running and hot water, electricity, gas and central air conditioning you supply that is operating when the lease takes effect; (5) repair by a licensed contractor after 14 days' written notice, up to the greater of one month's rent or $1,500; (6) rent escrow through the general district court and a habitability defense to a nonpayment eviction, with a rebuttable presumption that more than 30 days is unreasonable delay; (7) locality habitability suits on tenants' behalf (since July 1, 2026); (8) a statewide heat standard where the lease has you furnish heat (68°F from October 15 to May 1) and a cooling standard where you furnish cooling in an apartment building (77°F from May 15 to October 1); (9) mold, smoke alarm and carbon monoxide alarm rules. Absent (no Virginia statute or held regulation): (1) a right to withhold rent outside court; rent reductions come through escrow, the court, or repair by a licensed contractor; (2) a water heater temperature rule; (3) a duty to supply a stove or refrigerator, or a presumption that appliances present are yours; (4) radiator cover, child window guard and balcony inspection rules; (5) a required lease statement of habitability, or a presumption that a code violation is itself a breach; (6) a statutory list of minor or cosmetic defects that do not count; (7) a tenant right to install a window or portable air conditioner; (8) a private well testing duty for rentals; (9) a sprinkler retrofit duty for ordinary rental housing or a sprinkler disclosure; (10) a state lead-safe certificate or lead notice beyond the federal disclosure (a licensee leasing for you must disclose known non-lead-free plumbing); (11) an asbestos disclosure duty. The state Maintenance Code is a regulation each locality chooses whether to enforce generally, but after a tenant complaint the building department must enforce its unsafe-structure rules. Each item has its own row in the library. Case law and local ordinances were not searched.

title: Other Rules Virginia Does Not Have
bodyText: Several rules found in other states do not exist in Virginia law. (1) False rental applications: no statute gives you a special right to end a lease because the application was false. Use the library's Accuracy of Rental Application clause, which makes a material falsehood a material breach handled through the ordinary breach notices (see Grounds to End a Lease and the Chance to Cure); do not rely on information you may not lawfully ask for or consider. (2) Smoke and carbon monoxide alarms: no statute makes your compliance or noncompliance with the alarm rules inadmissible in an injury case, or limits what an insurer may do because of it. The alarm duties themselves still apply, and the tenant must not remove or tamper with a working alarm (see Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Alarms). (3) Double letting: no statute on renting the same unit to two tenants at once; the failure-to-deliver-possession rules apply (see the double-letting row). Other rules some states lack do exist here: a payment-processing fee is allowed only if you also offer a fee-free way to pay and only up to the actual third-party cost (see Rent Payments, Receipts and Statements). Each of these is covered in its own row as well: no eviction defense for late benefit payments, no hardship stay, no possession bond, and federal law alone on a tenant's bankruptcy.

title: Whole-Code Checks: Squatters, Receipts, Registration and Out-of-State Parties
bodyText: Virginia's whole Code was checked, not only the landlord-tenant law, for questions landlords ask. (1) Squatters: there is no sheriff-only removal, but the owner of a single-family home can get an emergency eviction hearing within 14 days of filing (or, if it cannot be heard by then, within 30 days) if the court finds there never was a lease with the occupant, the occupant is there without permission, and the owner gave written notice to vacate at least 72 hours before filing (see Squatters and Unauthorized Occupants). (2) Cash receipts: you must give a written receipt whenever rent is paid in cash or by money order (see Rent Receipts). (3) Registration: there is no statewide landlord registration or rental license, and nothing makes registration a condition of filing or winning an eviction. General business filings can still stop a suit: an out-of-state LLC, corporation, nonstock corporation, business trust, limited partnership or registered limited liability partnership that transacts business in Virginia may not maintain a suit until it registers or gets authority from the State Corporation Commission (it can still defend one, and its leases stay valid); anyone doing business under an assumed or fictitious name may not maintain a suit until the assumed-name certificate is filed; and an individual owner living outside Virginia may not sue over the property until the Virginia agent designation is filed (see Business Landlords in Court and Before Suing and Virginia Agent of Nonresident Owner). (4) Suing someone who has left Virginia: a Virginia court can hear a claim against a person arising from having an interest in, using or possessing real property in Virginia, or from transacting business here, so a former tenant who moved away can still be sued for rent or damages. Process can then be served on the Secretary of the Commonwealth as the person's statutory agent: file an affidavit that the person is a nonresident (or cannot be found after diligent effort) giving the last known address, and the Secretary mails it by certified mail. In a general district court warrant case, service is void if the Secretary receives it within 10 days of the return date, so file early.

title: Contractors' Liens for a Tenant's Work
bodyText: Under Virginia's mechanics' lien law, a contractor or supplier who is not paid can claim a lien on the building and land it worked on. For work a tenant orders, two rules protect you. If the person who orders the work owns less than the full ownership of the land (a tenant owns only a leasehold), only that person's interest is subject to the lien. And for repairs or improvements to existing structures, no lien attaches to the property unless the owner or the owner's agent ordered or authorized the work. So the risk is that a consent you give to an alteration is treated as authorizing it. Virginia has no notice of nonresponsibility you can post or record to disclaim a tenant's work, and a lease term cannot cut off a contractor's lien rights: a contractor's own advance waiver in a contract is void, and a lease is not a contract with the contractor. What helps: do not order, pay for or direct a tenant's work; make any consent to an alteration a consent only between you and the tenant; and use the library's optional No Liens for Tenant Work clause, which makes the tenant pay everyone it hires, discharge any lien within a set time and tell contractors that the tenant, not you, is responsible.

title: Converting or Changing the Use of a Rental Building
bodyText: Converting a rental building, or changing its use, brings these Virginia notice rules. Change in use: in a multifamily residential building with at least four units, you may end a lease, whatever its terms, because of rehabilitation or a change in use of all or part of the building, on 120 days' written notice. Changes in use include conversion to hotel, motel, apartment hotel or other commercial use, a planned unit development, substantial rehabilitation, demolition, and sale to a buyer who requires an empty building. The notice must be a separate writing, not part of the lease. The 120 days cannot be waived, and a lease may not make the tenant give up this notice or the condominium and cooperative conversion notices below, except that a month-to-month tenancy may still be ended on 30 days' written notice before the next rent due date. Condominium conversion: the developer must give each tenant formal notice, by hand or first-class mail return receipt requested, of the offering price of the tenant's unit, the projected assessments for at least the first year, any relocation help it knows of, its measures to reduce displacement and any relocation plan. For the first 60 days the tenant has the exclusive right to buy the unit, if the unit's layout will not substantially change. The notice may double as the termination notice, but then a month-to-month tenancy needs 120 days. Until the 120 days run out, the developer may enter only under the usual access rules, or on 45 days' written notice to make repairs or improvements, with the tenant's consent or while the tenant is out, and without evicting the tenant in effect. Cooperative conversion: similar notice; no tenant may be made to leave on less than 120 days' notice except for nonpayment, waste or disturbing other tenants, the tenancy terms cannot change during that period, each tenant gets a 60-day offer to buy, the unit may not be offered to others on better terms for the next 180 days, and failure to give the notice is a defense to an eviction. Time-share conversion: at least 90 days' notice, with a 60-day exclusive right to buy a time-share in the tenant's unit; a month-to-month tenancy needs 120 days. Prospective tenants: once an application to register the building as a condominium or cooperative has been filed, or there is a plan within six months to displace tenants by demolition, substantial rehabilitation or conversion to office, hotel, motel or planned-unit use, tell prospective tenants in writing. Local role: a locality may not ban condominiums because of their form of ownership; it may require a special use permit for a conversion that does not conform to zoning, filing of the tenant notice, lease offers to elderly or disabled tenants for up to 20 percent of the units for up to three years, and, in counties with the urban county executive or county manager form of government and their adjoining cities and towns, reimbursement of displaced tenants' moving costs. Virginia does not forbid converting rental housing to hotel or other transient use; the 120-day notice is the protection. No lease clause is required. See Selling or Losing a Rented Property.

title: Criminal Activity: Your Remedies and Your Own Exposure
bodyText: Your remedy: when a breach of the tenant's duties under the Act or the lease involves a criminal or willful act that can't be remedied and poses a threat to health or safety, you may terminate immediately and go to court for possession; illegal drug activity, or any criminal or willful act threatening health and safety, by the tenant, an authorized occupant or a guest is an immediate nonremediable violation, no conviction is needed, you must prove it by a preponderance of the evidence, and the tenant is presumed to know of an occupant's or guest's activity unless the tenant rebuts it (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1245; edu-expedited-criminal-eviction-va for the hearing schedule). Other breaches that can't be remedied need 30 days' written notice. A lease clause on criminal activity (criminal-activity-va) isn't required, but it ties the conduct to the lease. The Act lets you terminate for criminal activity but doesn't require you to, and Virginia has no statute on crime-free leases, addenda or programs (edu-no-drug-free-addendum-rule-va). Your exposure: an owner, lessor or agent who knowingly permits a dwelling or apartment to be a place used for illegal possession, manufacture or distribution of controlled substances, or frequented by people under their influence, commits a misdemeanor (a felony for a repeat offense) (Va. Code Ann. § 18.2-258); a court may close such premises after a conviction, but no judgment goes against an owner or lessor unless the owner knew of the use and had the right to repossess because of it (Va. Code Ann. § 48-16), and prosecutors or citizens may sue to enjoin the nuisance (Va. Code Ann. § 18.2-258.01). An owner or lessee who knows or should know a place is used for illegal gambling and lets it continue without notifying police commits a misdemeanor (Va. Code Ann. § 18.2-329), and anyone who knowingly owns or leases a building used for prostitution or criminal street gang activity is guilty of a nuisance that can be enjoined and closed (Va. Code Ann. §§ 48-7, 48-8, 48-12). A locality may, by ordinance, require an owner to correct criminal blight; an owner who in good faith sues to remedy or end the tenancy of the tenant causing it is deemed in compliance (Va. Code Ann. § 15.2-907). So act promptly on credible reports, keep records, and use the termination remedy. Fair housing: you need not rent to someone whose record makes the person a clear and present threat (edu-tenant-screening-va), and don't penalize a victim of family abuse (edu-dv-eviction-protection-va).

title: Grounds to End a Lease and the Chance to Cure
bodyText: Virginia lets you end a lease for a tenant's breach on these tracks (Termination Notices for Tenant Default has the details): unpaid rent, a 14-day written notice to pay (from July 1, 2027, a landlord with more than four Virginia rental units, or more than a 10 percent interest in more than four, must instead give a notice offering a payment plan when the amount owed is no more than one month's rent plus late charges); a breach that can be fixed, a written notice giving the tenant 21 days to fix it and ending the lease on a date at least 30 days after the tenant receives it (the lease does not end if the tenant fixes it in time); a breach that can't be fixed, a notice ending the lease at least 30 days after receipt; a breach of the same kind as one the tenant already fixed after your notice, committed on purpose, a 30-day notice that refers to the earlier breach; and a criminal or willful act that can't be fixed and threatens health or safety (including illegal drug activity by the tenant, an occupant or a guest), immediate termination. The ground for the non-rent tracks is a material breach of the lease, or a breach of the tenant's statutory duties that materially affects health and safety. Virginia's Code does not define material or let the lease decide which terms are material; a court decides, so labeling every rule as material in the lease may not settle it. The cure and notice periods come from the statute, not the lease. You may give the tenant more time, but a lease cannot shorten the periods or take away the chance to cure, because a lease may not make the tenant waive rights or remedies under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act (see Lease Terms Virginia Prohibits). Notices must be in writing and go to the tenant's last known address, which may be the home, by regular mail or hand delivery, keeping your own certificate of service. Electronic notices are allowed only if the lease provides for them, and the tenant may ask for paper instead (see Electronic Notices). On your request, the sheriff may deliver a breach or nonpayment notice for you for a fee of up to $12. For a breach materially affecting health and safety that a repair, replacement or cleaning can fix, you may instead give written notice, do the work and bill the tenant, with the bill due as rent (see Landlord's Right to Fix a Tenant's Breach). The court will not grant possession without a proper termination notice in evidence, and from July 1, 2027 you may not file an eviction case for a lease violation until you have given one.

title: No Statutory Schedule of Deposit Charges
bodyText: Virginia has no statute that lists pre-set deposit charges, allows or forbids a fixed carpet-cleaning or cleaning charge in the lease, or requires a special notice for one. The deposit may be applied only to unpaid rent (including late charges the lease sets), damage from the tenant's failure to meet the tenant's statutory duties less reasonable wear and tear, other damages or charges the lease provides, and actual damages for breach (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1226). So a lease may list charges, such as a cleaning or rekeying charge, but keep each one tied to something the tenant did or failed to do: the tenant must leave the unit in good and clean order, reasonable wear and tear excepted (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1233), and you may not require a fee for maintenance or repair of the unit unless the tenant's violation of the Act made it necessary (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1208). A flat turnover or carpet charge taken from every deposit whatever the unit's condition is the risky course. Set any listed charge close to the real cost, charge it only when the work is needed and done, and itemize it in the written disposition within 45 days. The library's Use of Security Deposit clause already limits cleaning charges to a unit left substantially less clean than at the start; the library does not offer a separate schedule of fixed move-out charges.

title: Unclaimed Security Deposits and Rent Credits
bodyText: A deposit refund you can't deliver never becomes yours. If no tenant gives a forwarding address, you still make the disposition within 45 days, may keep holding the refund, and after one year from the end of that 45-day period may send it to the State Treasurer as unclaimed property on the Treasurer's form, with each tenant's name, Social Security number if known and last known address (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1226). Virginia's Unclaimed Property Act lists security deposits, refunds, credits and customer overpayments as unclaimed property, and property held in the ordinary course of business and unclaimed for more than five years after it became payable is presumed abandoned (Va. Code Ann. §§ 55.1-2500, 55.1-2501). A holder of such property must report and remit it before November 1 each year for the period ending June 30, and for an item of $100 or more with an address on file must first mail a letter to the owner's last known address at least 60 days before the report. Late or missing reports cost interest and daily civil penalties. Once you remit, you are relieved of liability for that amount. The same applies to a rent overpayment or credit balance owed after move-out, and to money left from the sale of abandoned property, which Virginia law treats as a security deposit (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1254). A lease clause saying an unclaimed deposit is forfeited to you would be unenforceable, because a lease cannot waive the tenant's rights under the Act (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1208).

title: No Right to Pay the Deposit in Installments
bodyText: Virginia gives a tenant no right to pay the security deposit in installments, and no statute stops you from agreeing to it. If you agree, put the schedule in the written lease and list the deposit on the first-page fee disclosure, because no security deposit may be charged that isn't listed there or added by a later addendum (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1204.1). All installments together still count toward the two-month cap on the deposit plus any damage or renter's insurance premiums paid before the tenancy begins (Va. Code Ann. §§ 55.1-1206, 55.1-1208, 55.1-1226). An unpaid deposit installment is not rent, since Virginia's definition of rent excludes the security deposit, so treat a missed installment as a breach of the lease rather than unpaid rent. Money paid toward the deposit before the lease commencement date is treated as an application deposit until then (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1200).

title: Last Month's Rent and the Security Deposit
bodyText: Virginia has no rule written for last month's rent, but two rules decide how it works. First, money collected now for a month more than one month ahead is prepaid rent. It is rent, not a security deposit, and you must place it in an escrow account at a federally insured depository authorized to do business in Virginia by the end of the fifth business day after you receive it, and leave it there until it comes due; you may not remove it without the tenant's written consent unless you have otherwise become entitled to it (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1205). It must be returned if the tenant ends the lease because you willfully fail to deliver possession; if the lease ends after a fire or casualty, unless you reasonably believe the tenant, an occupant or a guest caused it, in which case you give a written statement for the deposit and prepaid rent and may recover actual damages; and if the tenant is excluded because the unit is condemned as a result of a building code violation, posing a substantial risk to health, safety or welfare, that the tenant had reported to you during the tenancy, unless the tenant's side or an act of God caused it or the lease was properly ended under the casualty rule (Va. Code Ann. §§ 55.1-1238, 55.1-1240, 55.1-1243.2). Label it as rent for a named month and list it on the first-page fee disclosure; money held to secure the tenant's performance is a security deposit whatever it is called, and counts toward the two-month cap (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1226). Second, a tenant can't use the security deposit as the last month's rent. The deposit is applied only after the tenancy ends or the tenant vacates, the tenant is not entitled to an immediate credit for it against unpaid rent, and the court may give you judgment for rent and possession without crediting the deposit; the deposit is then credited when the tenant vacates (Va. Code Ann. §§ 55.1-1226, 55.1-1251).

title: Who May Do Repairs at Your Expense
bodyText: Virginia law, not the lease, decides who may do repairs a tenant has made at your expense. Under the repair remedy, if you don't take reasonable steps within 14 days after the tenant's written notice of a serious condition, the tenant may hire a third-party contractor licensed by the Board for Contractors or, for a rodent infestation, a licensed pesticide business; a local government or nonprofit may hire one for the tenant. The tenant recovers or deducts the actual invoiced cost, up to the greater of one month's rent or $1,500, after giving you an itemized statement with receipts. No Virginia law lets a lease name the contractor a tenant must use for that work, and a lease cannot make a tenant give up a remedy under the Act, so a term requiring your contractor, or your approval before the tenant uses the remedy, would be unenforceable. What you can control: the lease may name your repair contact and where repair requests go, and you choose who does the repairs you make yourself. In a rent escrow case the court may release escrowed money to a contractor you choose, and will make sure it is spent on the repair. If you and the tenant agree in writing, in good faith, that the tenant will do specified repairs or maintenance, that written agreement can say how the work is done (see Tenant-Performed Duties and Repairs by Written Agreement).

title: Disability Accommodations and Modifications
bodyText: Under the Virginia Fair Housing Law you must grant a reasonable accommodation in rules, policies, practices or services when it may be necessary to give a person with a disability an equal opportunity to use and enjoy the home, and you must permit reasonable modifications of the premises at the tenant's expense when they may be necessary for full enjoyment (Va. Code Ann. § 36-96.3). A request that is necessary and imposes neither an undue financial and administrative burden nor a fundamental alteration of your operations must be granted; requests are decided case by case; if a request may impose such a burden or alteration, you must offer a good-faith interactive process to find an effective alternative, and the tenant need not accept an alternative if the original request is also reasonable; a request for accessible parking is an accommodation request (Va. Code Ann. § 36-96.3:2). For modifications, you may, where reasonable, condition permission on the tenant agreeing to restore the interior at the end of the tenancy (reasonable wear and tear excepted), and on a reasonable description of the work with reasonable assurances that it will be done in a workmanlike manner with any required permits. You may not raise the usual security deposit for a tenant with a disability; where necessary to be reasonably sure restoration will be paid for, you may negotiate, as part of the restoration agreement, payments over a reasonable period into an interest-bearing escrow account of a reasonable amount not exceeding the restoration cost, with the interest belonging to the tenant (18VAC135-50-200). The library's optional modification clause (disability-modification-restoration-mn) takes the restoration promise but not the escrow; if you want the escrow, agree it in writing when you approve the request. Don't ask whether an applicant has a disability or about its nature or severity (edu-protected-class-inquiry-va). No Virginia statute requires the lease to state any of these rules. Assistance animals have their own rules (edu-assistance-animals-va, assistance-animal-accommodation-va). Covered multifamily buildings first occupied after March 13, 1991 must also meet accessible design and construction requirements.

title: Guests Displaced by a Disaster
bodyText: Virginia has no rule that lets a tenant house people displaced by a hurricane, flood or other disaster despite the lease's guest or occupancy limits, that bars you from enforcing those limits after a disaster, or that places evacuees in private rentals. Your lease's guest and occupancy terms still apply (see the Guest Policy clauses). The Act's own terms frame it: a guest or invitee is someone the tenant has allowed to visit but not to occupy the home, and an authorized occupant is someone who lives there with your consent without signing the lease. The tenant is responsible for guests' conduct. Two cautions. During a declared emergency the Governor's executive orders can control the occupancy of premises in the emergency area and have the force of law, so check them before acting. And fair housing law, including familial status, applies to how you set and enforce occupancy limits. Cautious course: be flexible after a disaster. Agree in writing to any temporary extra occupants (who they are and for how long), so it is clear they are guests or authorized occupants and not tenants, and do not use their stay to raise the rent at an unconscionable level while the emergency price-gouging rules apply (see Declared Disasters and Emergencies).

title: Declared Disasters and Emergencies
bodyText: Virginia has no rule that ends a tenancy, suspends rent or stops evictions because a disaster or state of emergency has been declared, and none on what rent is owed while an undamaged home can't be reached, for example during an evacuation. What applies instead: Damage: if fire or casualty (storm or flood damage included) substantially impairs the home, the casualty rules decide whether the lease ends, with rent prorated as of the casualty date and deposits and prepaid rent returned, or rent reasonably reduced if the tenant stays (see Fire or Casualty: The Tenant's Options). Price gouging: during a declared state of emergency, and for at least 30 days after the disaster, you may not rent or offer to rent housing or lodging in the emergency area at an unconscionable price. Courts compare your price with what you charged in the 10 days before; an increase that only covers your added costs, or a regular seasonal change, is evidence it is not unconscionable. A violation is also a Consumer Protection Act violation. Governor's orders: in an emergency the Governor may order evacuations and control movement in the emergency area and the occupancy of premises there, and those executive orders have the force of law, so check the orders for the particular emergency. Disease emergencies: during a Governor-declared emergency for a communicable disease, a tenant may ask in writing that nonemergency repairs wait (and then gives up claims for not making them); you may still enter for nonemergency work on seven days' written notice at a time the tenant agrees to, no more than once every six months, with protective equipment. A tenant's written health concern also justifies refusing in-person showings if the tenant offers a video tour. Federal shutdowns: a federal employee or contractor tenant who is furloughed or unpaid during a federal government closure and brings written proof to the first court date gets a 60-day continuance of your nonpayment case, unless you have served a notice for a non-rent breach. If you rent a one-to-four-family home and your tenant is affected, you can get a 60-day stay of foreclosure. Cautious course: if the home can't be reached but isn't damaged, agree in writing with the tenant on rent for that period.

title: No Double-Letting Statute
bodyText: Virginia has no statute on double letting, that is, renting the same dwelling unit, or parts of the same room, to two tenants or households at once, and no rule like some states' that the first tenant takes the whole room. The Residential Landlord and Tenant Act handles the problem through possession: if you willfully fail to deliver possession of the unit to the tenant, for example because you rented it to someone else who is living there, rent abates until you deliver it, and the tenant may either end the lease on at least five days' written notice (you must then return all prepaid rent and security deposits) or demand performance. The tenant may also sue for possession against you or any person wrongfully in possession and recover damages, and if the failure is willful and not in good faith, actual damages and reasonable attorney fees. So do not sign a second lease for a unit until the first is ended, and if you rent rooms in a shared unit to separate people, give each a separate lease that identifies the room and the shared spaces. A roomer, who rents a unit without its own full bathroom or kitchen and shares those facilities with other units, is a tenant under the Act. If a delay in possession is not your fault, the library's Possession Delay clause governs.

title: No Virginia Rule on Drug-Free or Crime-Free Addenda
bodyText: Virginia has no statute on drug-free or crime-free lease addenda: none requires one, none prescribes its wording, and none limits it. You don't need one to act on drug activity, because the Act itself makes illegal drug activity involving a controlled substance by the tenant, an authorized occupant or a guest an immediate nonremediable violation, so you may terminate and seek possession without waiting for a conviction (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1245). The library's criminal-activity clause (criminal-activity-va) states that rule in the lease; use it instead of a separate addendum. If you use an addendum anyway, it may not take away any tenant right under the Act, and it may not reach beyond the statute in ways that penalize a victim of family abuse whose abuser has been barred (edu-dv-eviction-protection-va). Federally assisted housing may require its own lease language under federal program rules, which this row doesn't cover. Related: edu-criminal-activity-va.

title: Keeping a Victim's Information Confidential
bodyText: Virginia has no confidentiality rule written for what a victim of family abuse, sexual abuse, stalking or trafficking tells you, but the general tenant-records rule covers it. You may not release information about a tenant or applicant to a third party unless the person has given prior written consent or a listed exception applies, such as a matter of public record, a request by a law-enforcement or public safety official in the performance of duties, a civil subpoena, your attorney or collection agency, an emergency, or a new managing agent (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1209). Anything an applicant gives you with the application, including a letter, police report or court order offered as evidence of family abuse to offset a low credit score, is a confidential tenant record that may be released only in response to a subpoena (Va. Code Ann. §§ 55.1-1203, 55.1-1209). The protective order, conviction, warrant or other papers a tenant gives you to end the lease early, to change the locks, or to keep the lease from being terminated are tenant information under the same rule. Even where a court order is a public record, the cautious course is not to share it. Because the excluded or accused person may be a co-tenant or the person asking, keep these papers apart from the general file, let only staff who need them see them, and never tell the other person where the victim has moved. Virginia's Address Confidentiality Program, which lets enrolled victims use a substitute address, binds state and local agencies, not landlords. In federally assisted housing covered by the Violence Against Women Act, anything a tenant or applicant submits about the abuse, including the fact of being a victim, must be kept in confidence and kept out of shared databases unless the person asks or consents in writing, it is needed in an eviction or termination proceeding, or other law requires disclosure. Related rows: edu-tenant-records-va, edu-dv-tenancy-protections-va, edu-dv-qualifying-documents-va.

title: Security Deposits When a Victim Ends the Lease Early
bodyText: Virginia sets no special deposit timetable when a victim of family abuse, sexual abuse or criminal sexual assault, stalking or trafficking ends the lease early under the statutory termination right, so the ordinary deposit rule applies: within 45 days after the tenancy ends or the tenant vacates, whichever is later, give the tenant a written itemization of the deposit and any deductions, with any amount due (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1226). On an early termination the victim owes rent only through the effective date of the 28-day notice, you may not charge liquidated damages, and the victim's duties to keep up the unit continue through that date (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1236). So don't deduct an early-termination fee, or rent for any period after the effective date, from the victim's deposit; deductions remain limited to accrued rent and lease-provided late charges, damage beyond reasonable wear and tear, other charges the lease provides for, and actual damages for breach. The statutes don't settle one point. If co-tenants stay, they remain liable for the rent for the rest of the term and the tenancy goes on, and neither section says whether the victim's share of the deposit is due 45 days after the victim's termination date or only when the whole tenancy ends; with more than one tenant, the refund goes in one check payable to all tenants unless each tenant agrees otherwise in writing. No Virginia case on this was looked at here. The cautious course: within 45 days after the victim's termination date, give the victim a written statement of the deposit; refund the victim's share only under a written agreement signed by every tenant; otherwise tell the victim in writing that the deposit stays with the continuing tenancy and will be accounted for to all tenants when it ends. Don't send the victim's forwarding address to the remaining tenants. Related rows: edu-security-deposit-rules-va, edu-dv-tenancy-protections-va, edu-dv-confidentiality-va.

title: Eviction Protection for Victims of Family Abuse
bodyText: Virginia protects a victim from losing the lease in one situation. If a tenant is a victim of family abuse that occurred in the unit or on the premises, and the abuser has been barred from the unit either by you (a written bar notice to a guest or invitee, based on information the tenant gave you) or by a court (a family abuse protective order, a divorce or custody court exclusion order, or an order in a criminal case), the lease may not terminate solely because of an act of family abuse against the tenant. The protection applies only if the tenant gives you a copy of the protective order or the abuser has been barred by you or by a court (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1245). You may still end the tenancy for other breaches. Family abuse means an act of violence, force or threat that causes bodily injury or reasonable fear of death, sexual assault or bodily injury, committed by a family or household member: a spouse or former spouse, a parent, child, sibling, grandparent or grandchild, an in-law living in the home, a person with a child in common, a person who lives or lived with the tenant in the past 12 months, a legal custodian, or an intimate partner from the past 12 months (Va. Code Ann. § 16.1-228). The protection therefore doesn't reach abuse, assault or stalking by someone outside that circle. If a victim ends the lease early and the abuser is the remaining sole tenant, you may terminate and recover actual damages from the abuser (edu-dv-tenancy-protections-va). Virginia has no statute that otherwise bars refusing to rent to, refusing to renew, or retaliating against someone because the person is a victim, or that limits a victim's liability for damage the abuser caused; victim status isn't a protected class under the Virginia Fair Housing Law, and no Virginia case on whether a policy against victims can be sex discrimination was looked at here, so the cautious course is to judge a victim's tenancy by the same lease standards as anyone else's. In screening you must consider evidence of family abuse to offset an otherwise qualified applicant's low credit score (edu-application-fees-va). In federally assisted housing covered by the Violence Against Women Act, you may not deny admission to or evict a tenant because the tenant is a victim; an incident of actual or threatened domestic violence, dating violence, sexual assault or stalking is not a serious or repeated lease violation or good cause to terminate; criminal activity directly relating to the abuse, by a household member or guest, is not a ground against the victim; you may divide the lease to remove the abuser; and you may still evict for unrelated violations, using the same standard as for other tenants, or on an actual and imminent threat to others.

title: Lock Changes After a Court Order Excluding a Household Member
bodyText: Virginia gives a lock-change right in one situation. A tenant or authorized occupant who has a court order granting the tenant possession of the home to the exclusion of a co-tenant or other occupant (a full family abuse protective order, or an exclusion order from a divorce or custody court) may give you a copy of the order and ask you either to install a new lock or other security devices on the exterior doors at your actual cost, or to let the tenant install them. The tenant's own installation must do no permanent damage, and you must receive duplicate keys and operating instructions. When the tenancy ends, the tenant pays the reasonable cost of removing the devices and repairing damaged areas. Once you have such an order, don't give a key to anyone it excludes. The right doesn't arise from an order entered ex parte, from a preliminary or emergency protective order, from a protective order under the general law for acts of violence, force or threat, or without a court order (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1230). The section doesn't say plainly whether the actual cost is yours to bear or the tenant's to pay; the cautious course is to act promptly and charge, if anything, only your documented out-of-pocket cost, with no fee or markup, and not to hold up the change for payment. Virginia sets no deadline and no statutory damages for this right, but a lease term that takes it away is unenforceable. Where a victim has no qualifying order and asks to rekey, the law leaves the decision to you; agreeing, at no more than cost, is the safer course. In federally assisted housing covered by the Violence Against Women Act, nothing stops you from complying with a court order on access to or control of the property. Early termination, the excluded person's right to apply, and the eviction protection are in edu-dv-tenancy-protections-va.

title: Domestic Violence Law Citations Current in Virginia
bodyText: The Virginia landlord-tenant rules for victims point to laws that are still in force under the same numbers. The early-termination right (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1236) relies on the family abuse definition in the juvenile and domestic relations court law (§ 16.1-228), the sexual abuse definition and the criminal sexual assault article in the crimes title (§§ 18.2-67.10, 18.2-61 and following), the stalking crime (§ 18.2-60.3), the preliminary and full family abuse protective orders (§§ 16.1-253.1, 16.1-279.1) and the preliminary and full protective orders for any act of violence, force or threat (§§ 19.2-152.9, 19.2-152.10). The lock-change rule and the protection against termination (§§ 55.1-1230, 55.1-1245) also point to the divorce or custody court exclusion order (§ 20-103) and the guest-barring section (§ 55.1-1246). Three details. First, the trafficking reference begins at § 18.2-344, a section since repealed; another Code section cites the same article as beginning at § 18.2-346 (§ 15.2-907), and the commercial sex trafficking crime (§ 18.2-357.1) sits in that chapter of the crimes title, so read the reference as that article. Second, emergency protective orders (§§ 16.1-253.4, 19.2-152.8), which expire at the end of the third day after issue unless a short extension is granted, are not among the orders that support early termination, a lock change or the termination protection; ask for the later preliminary or full order. Third, from July 1, 2027, the screening rule on family-abuse evidence moves from subsection D to subsection E of § 55.1-1203, and the fair housing cross-reference (§ 36-96.2) changes to match. The federal Violence Against Women Act housing section is now 34 U.S.C. § 12491; it was formerly classified as 42 U.S.C. § 14043e-11, so update older forms that cite the old number. Related rows: edu-dv-tenancy-protections-va, edu-dv-qualifying-documents-va.

title: Documents Victims Give Landlords in Virginia
bodyText: Each Virginia protection for victims names its own documents, and the lists differ. To end a lease early, the tenant serves a written termination notice effective 28 days after service, with a copy of either the protective order (a family abuse preliminary or full protective order, or a preliminary or permanent protective order for an act of violence, force or threat) or the conviction order, warrant, summons, information or indictment for a covered crime against the tenant (family abuse, sexual abuse or criminal sexual assault, stalking or trafficking). A protective order must have been obtained during a current lease, and the notice given while the order or an extension is in effect; a conviction, warrant, summons, information or indictment must have been entered or issued during a current lease, and no other time limit applies; a conviction supports ending the lease in effect when it was entered and one later lease (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1236). For screening, an applicant may show family abuse with a letter from a sexual and domestic violence program, a HUD-certified housing counselor or the applicant's attorney, a law-enforcement incident report, or a court order (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1203). For a lock change, the tenant gives you a copy of a non-ex parte family abuse protective order or divorce or custody court exclusion order granting possession (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1230). For protection against termination, the tenant gives you a copy of the protective order, unless you or a court barred the abuser (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1245). The statutes don't authorize you to demand other proof or details of the abuse, and the landlord-tenant and fair housing laws set no penalty for a false notice or document; accept what the statute lists, and if a document looks doubtful, confirm it with the court or agency that issued it rather than asking the tenant for more. Keep what you receive confidential (edu-dv-confidentiality-va). In federally assisted housing covered by the Violence Against Women Act, you may ask in writing for documentation and must allow 14 business days (you may extend); the tenant chooses among the HUD certification form, a statement signed by a victim service provider, attorney, or medical or mental health professional under penalty of perjury, a record of a law enforcement agency, court or administrative agency, or, if you accept it, the tenant's own statement; you may require third-party documentation only when submissions conflict.

title: Submetered Electricity and Gas: Lease Statement and Utility Rules
bodyText: Virginia has no separate submetering disclosure form, but the lease itself must say certain things. By statute you may bill tenants through submeters, energy allocation equipment or a ratio utility billing system only if the lease clearly says so (use the library's Utilities Billed by Landlord clause). For electricity or natural gas measured by submeters or energy allocation equipment in an apartment building of three or more units (the buildings those rules cover), the State Corporation Commission's rules add that every lease must also clearly state that the unit uses that equipment, that your bills will be based on its readings, and that any dispute over the amount of a bill or the accuracy of the equipment is between the tenant and you (use the library's Submetered Electricity or Gas Statement clause). Billing tenants for electricity or gas does not make you a public utility. That holds if you buy the service from a utility or licensed supplier, charge each tenant only the part of your bill that comes from that tenant's use plus the billing service charges the lease allows, and keep three years of billing records. In those buildings the Commission's submetering rules also apply: you may not charge more than the utility's own rate per kilowatt hour, cubic foot or therm plus its demand and customer charges and taxes (agreed third-party billing costs aside); you may submeter one apartment only if every apartment in the building is submetered as far as the building allows; you must tell the Commission and the utility in writing within 90 days after installing the equipment; bills must cover the utility's billing period, go out no later than 15 days after you receive the utility's bill, show the readings, units, average unit cost and charges, and say plainly that they are not from the utility; initial and final bills must use actual readings taken on the move-in and move-out dates; you must test the equipment free on a tenant's request once every 24 months; and you must keep billing records three years and let a tenant inspect the utility's bills, your cost calculations and the tenant's own readings for the past 36 months. For enforcing those rules only, the Commission treats you like a public service corporation and can fine violations, and the tenant can also sue for breach of the lease. You may still recover in the rent the tenants' fair share of electricity or gas for owner-paid areas (halls, laundry rooms, offices, vacant units) and your cost of installing and keeping up the equipment. From July 1, 2027, a nonpayment termination notice must list the tenant's utility debits and credits, and the statement of charges you must give a tenant on written request must disclose the allocation method (landlords with fewer than four Virginia rental units are exempt from that statement rule unless they receive rental or utility assistance for the tenant). See Utilities Billed by Landlord (Submetering, Allocation or Ratio Billing).

title: Emergency Contacts
bodyText: Virginia has no statute requiring you to give tenants an emergency or 24-hour telephone number, to post one, or to keep an after-hours line, and none requiring the lease to carry a management website or a social-services hotline notice. Nothing requires a tenant to name an emergency contact either. Two related rules apply. First, at or before the start of the tenancy you must disclose in writing the name and address of the person authorized to manage the premises and of an owner or a person authorized to act for the owner, keep that information current, and give the tenant the purchaser's name, address and telephone number if you sell; a person who fails to make the disclosure becomes an agent of each landlord for service of process and notices (see Owner and Manager Disclosure). Second, a contact the tenant names in the rental application, lease or another landlord document as the authorized person to contact on the tenant's death or emergency has a defined role: if the sole tenant under a written lease dies while still living in the unit and no one has been authorized by the circuit court to handle the tenant's probate matters, that person receives your 10-day notice about the tenant's belongings and may, on reasonable proof of identity, have access to the unit and the tenant's records and claim the property. The library's Authorized Contact on Tenant's Death or Emergency clause collects that contact. Giving tenants a way to report emergencies is still good practice: you may enter without consent in an emergency, and a tenant's right to end the lease for your breach runs from the tenant's written notice to you (see Repair Requests and Notice).

title: When Rental Property Is Taken by Eminent Domain
bodyText: Virginia has no statute saying what happens to a residential lease, or to the rent, when the property is taken by eminent domain: no rule ending the rent, letting the court cancel the lease, or deferring to the lease. The lease decides, so use the library's optional Condemnation clause, which ends the lease on a total or untenantable taking, reduces rent on a partial one, and keeps the award for you apart from the tenant's own relocation and moving payments. In the condemnation case, a tenant whose lease runs 12 months or longer (counting renewal options the tenant can enforce in writing) may join the proceeding to set just compensation by filing a petition at least 10 days before trial, with a sworn copy of the lease and an affidavit, and the condemnor must serve such a tenant with notice if the lease is recorded or the tenancy is known.
