The tenant may offer evidence of the property's value but not of the value of the leasehold itself. A tenant displaced by a state agency's project gets relocation help: moving costs, and, after at least 90 days' occupancy, a payment to rent a comparable replacement dwelling for up to 42 months, capped at $7,200, which the tenant may instead put toward buying a home. To the greatest extent practicable, no one occupying the property must move without at least 90 days' written notice from the agency. These payments belong to the tenant, not to you.

title: Background Checks for Employees With Key Access
bodyText: A landlord who owns more than 200 rental units attached to the same piece of real property in Virginia must have a policy requiring every applicant for a job with access to unit keys (any physical or electronic means of entry) to undergo a pre-employment criminal history records check, and written policies on the storage, issuance, return and security of keys and key codes, access to them, and their use and deactivation where applicable. Financial institutions and real estate licensees are exempt (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1209.1). Smaller landlords have no statutory duty to screen staff, but doing so for anyone with key access is the safer course. When you screen job applicants, private employers not subject to federal hiring rules may not require disclosure of sealed arrests, charges or convictions (Va. Code Ann. § 19.2-392.15), and no employer may require disclosure of expunged records (Va. Code Ann. § 19.2-392.4). Related: edu-tenant-records-va, keys.

title: No Energy Benchmarking or Usage-Data Release Rule
bodyText: Virginia has no energy benchmarking law for private rental buildings, and no statute that lets or requires a lease clause to authorize a utility to release a tenant's energy usage data to you. Whether a utility will share a tenant's account data with you is a matter of the utility's terms and the State Corporation Commission's rules; if you need the data, get the tenant's own written consent and give it to the utility. The only usage-data consent rule in the statutes is for shared solar programs, which must get a customer's written or electronic consent before billing and usage data goes to a subscriber organization. If you bill utilities yourself through submeters, allocation equipment or ratio billing, the readings are already in your records, and the tenant may inspect and copy those records. Going the other way, information about a tenant that you hold may be released to a third party only with the tenant's prior written consent or under a listed exception, so get a signed consent before passing a tenant's usage data to an outside service. See Submetered Electricity and Gas: Lease Statement and Utility Rules, and Tenant Records and Confidentiality.

title: Business Landlords in Court and Before Suing
bodyText: In general district court, a corporation, LLC, partnership or business trust landlord may, without a lawyer, prepare, sign, file and have served a summons for unlawful detainer, a warrant in debt, a distress warrant, an order of possession, a writ of eviction, garnishment papers and a civil appeal notice, within that court's limits (which do not cap rent and damages in an eviction case). The papers may be signed by an officer, an LLC manager, a general partner or a trustee, or, with written authority, by an employee, a licensed property manager or your managing agent under a written management agreement. A licensed property manager, a managing agent or an authorized employee may also get the judgment for possession, rent or damages. Court rules let you, your attorney or your regular and bona fide employee ask in person for a default judgment and note an appeal. What a nonlawyer may not do: file a bill of particulars or grounds of defense, argue motions, issue subpoenas or show-cause rules, or conduct debtor interrogatories. Plan on a lawyer for a contested trial, an appeal to circuit court and any circuit court case; practicing law without a license is a crime. In small claims court (claims of $5,000 or less) a business may appear through an owner, officer, member or employee. Before you sue: a foreign LLC or corporation that transacts business in Virginia may not maintain a suit until it has registered with the State Corporation Commission (it may still defend one, and its leases stay valid); owning property alone is not transacting business, but renting it out may be, so register if you lease Virginia property through an out-of-state entity. If you do business under an assumed or fictitious name, file the assumed-name certificate with the Commission first: until you do, you cannot maintain a suit, and doing business without it is a misdemeanor. An individual owner who lives outside Virginia must name a Virginia agent in every lease and file the designation before suing (see Virginia Agent of Nonresident Owner).

title: Environmental Events and Ending the Lease
bodyText: Virginia has no rule that lets you, or the tenant, end a residential lease because of an environmental event as such, for example contamination, a chemical or fuel spill, a sewage backup or a government order to vacate, and no statutory opt-in termination right for one. The rules that do touch it: fire or casualty damage that substantially impairs the home or requires the tenant to leave for repairs lets either side end the lease, though from January 1, 2027 you may end it only after meeting or trying to meet with the tenant and offering any substantially similar unit in the same complex available within a reasonable time, unless the tenant's violation caused the damage (see Fire or Casualty: The Tenant's Options and the casualty clause); whether a contamination event with no physical damage counts as a casualty is unsettled. A tenant may end the lease if, at move-in, the unit has a condition that is a fire hazard or a serious threat to life, health or safety, or if your move-in report discloses visible mold. A tenant you didn't warn about an uncleaned former meth lab or defective drywall may end the lease within 60 days after discovering it. For mold remediation you may move the tenant temporarily at your cost, and once the mold is properly remediated the tenant cannot end the lease over it. If a unit is condemned after the tenant reported the code violation, you owe damages and refunds (see Condemned Units: Rent and Refunds). The library offers no separate environmental-event termination clause. Cautious course: don't charge rent for a period the home can't lawfully or safely be occupied, and if both of you want to end the lease after such an event, sign a written early-termination agreement.

title: No Rule on Chargers When the Tenancy Ends
bodyText: Virginia has no rule about electric vehicle charging equipment at the end of a tenancy: nothing says who owns a charger the tenant paid for, whether the tenant may or must remove it, or whether you must buy it. Settle it in the lease. The library's optional charger installation clause makes you choose, when you approve the charger, whether the tenant removes it and repairs any damage or leaves it in place as yours. Without a lease term, general rules decide. Whether an attached charger has become part of the property is a question of real estate law that no Virginia statute answers for chargers. A tenant must not deliberately or negligently damage or remove any part of the premises, so damage from pulling out a hard-wired unit is chargeable to the tenant, including from the security deposit, less reasonable wear and tear. A charger left behind as personal property after the lease ends and you have possession may be treated as abandoned and disposed of only after the notice the abandoned-property rules require, with any sale proceeds applied to what the tenant owes. If the unit is in a condominium or cooperative, the association may require the owner to pay to remove the charger and restore the area, so make the tenant's removal duty match. See Abandonment and Property Left Behind, and Electric Vehicle Chargers: Utility, Billing and Parking Rules.

title: Electric Vehicle Chargers: Utility, Billing and Parking Rules
bodyText: Virginia gives tenants no right to install or demand electric vehicle charging, so whether a charger goes in is your decision; if you allow one, use the library's optional charger installation clause. Rules that reach you once a charger is in: Selling charging does not make you a utility. A person who sells electric vehicle charging service at retail is not a public utility for that reason, the State Corporation Commission does not regulate the price you charge, and furnishing the electricity is not a retail sale of electricity if it is used only for charging vehicles and you buy it from the utility that serves your area. Measuring and billing: Virginia makes the federal NIST Handbook 44 the standard for commercial weighing and measuring devices. Whether a charger or separate meter you bill from is such a device, and what the Handbook requires of it, is set in the Handbook and in Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services rules that this library has not reviewed. The submetering law's exemption from that department covers submetering of the unit, not chargers. Cautious course: charge a flat fee that does not depend on a measured amount, or use equipment certified for commercial billing and ask the department. Whatever you bill for charging under the lease is rent under the Virginia Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, so say in the lease how it is figured. Reserved spaces: parking a vehicle that is not a plug-in electric vehicle, or one that is not charging, in a space next to a charging station clearly marked as reserved for charging is a traffic infraction with a civil penalty of up to $25, but no penalty can be imposed unless the sign includes the words "PENALTY, UP TO $25." Localities may adopt matching ordinances. If the property is in a condominium, cooperative or homeowners' association, the association's charging rules bind you as the owner. Using a vehicle to power a home must follow the vehicle maker's instructions and the electrical code. See No Tenant Electric Vehicle Charging Right.

title: No Rule on Chargers in Shared Parking Areas
bodyText: Virginia has no statute on electric vehicle charging in a shared parking area of a rental property. Tenants have no right to install a charger anywhere on the premises, so whether a charger goes in a shared lot or garage, who may use it, whether a space is reserved for it, and what you charge are yours to set. Put the terms in the lease or in written rules. A rule about shared parking or chargers binds a tenant only if it serves the tenants' convenience, safety or welfare, protects the property or fairly distributes facilities, is reasonably related to that purpose, applies fairly to all tenants, is explicit, is not meant to evade your own obligations, and was given to the tenant at signing or when adopted; a rule adopted later that substantially changes the tenant's bargain needs the tenant's written consent. A fee to reserve or use a charging space is rent under the Virginia Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, so list it in the lease. Enforcement: if a space next to a charging station is clearly marked as reserved for charging plug-in electric vehicles, parking a vehicle there that is not a plug-in electric vehicle, or one that is not charging, is a traffic infraction with a penalty of up to $25, but only if the sign includes the words "PENALTY, UP TO $25." Towing from that space follows the ordinary towing rules. If the property is in a homeowners' association, the association may prohibit or restrict chargers on the common area; in a condominium or cooperative, the association's charging conditions bind you as the owner. If you sell charging from shared chargers, the utility and billing rules in Electric Vehicle Chargers: Utility, Billing and Parking Rules apply. The library has no separate Virginia shared-area clause: to let a tenant install a charger at a shared space, use the optional charger installation clause and name the space. See also Rules and Regulations and Towing From Rental Property.

title: No Hardship Stay of Eviction
bodyText: Virginia has no rule letting a court postpone an eviction because moving would be hard on the tenant, for example because of age, illness, disability, children, the weather or the season. The delays that do exist are specific. Appeal: the tenant has 10 days to appeal, and the sheriff may not evict before that period ends; an appeal stops the eviction (an indigent tenant posts no appeal bond; others pay the amounts owed into court). Execution: the sheriff must give at least 72 hours' notice of the eviction date and time, and should carry out the writ within 15 days of receiving it, and in no case later than 30 days after it issues; an unexecuted writ is void after 30 days. Continuances: if the tenant asks for a continuance or a contested trial, the court must, at your request, order the rent due into court first, unless it finds the tenant has a good-faith defense. A tenant who presents a written commitment from a local government or nonprofit to pay the full amount gets a 10-day continuance, and a tenant who pays everything at least 48 hours before the scheduled eviction cancels it. Where the general district court runs the Eviction Diversion Program, an eligible tenant who pays at least 10 percent at the first hearing gets a three-month court payment plan. A federal employee or contractor tenant who is furloughed or unpaid during a federal government closure and brings written proof to the first court date gets a 60-day continuance of your nonpayment case, unless you have served a notice for a non-rent breach (see Federal Government Shutdowns and Rent). Under federal law, a court may on its own, and must on the request of a servicemember whose ability to pay is materially affected by service, stay an eviction for 90 days (or adjust the lease) where the rent is within the federal cap (see Servicemember Rights). A court's ordinary handling of its docket is outside this row.

title: No Statute on Eviction Fees
bodyText: Virginia has no statute that names an "eviction fee" and bans or allows it. What a lease can make the tenant pay because of an eviction is set by the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act: rent, other charges and fees, and late charges as the lease provides; reasonable attorney fees as the lease provides or the law allows, which the court will not award if the tenant proves the failure to pay or vacate was reasonable; costs of the proceeding only once a court action has been filed; the cost of serving notices and process, up to $12; and actual damages (Va. Code Ann. §§ 55.1-1245, 55.1-1251). A lease may not make the tenant pay your attorney fees except as the Act provides (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1208). So a flat "eviction fee" or "legal processing fee" on top of those amounts is, at best, a disguised attorney fee or cost the Act limits, and at worst a penalty. Virginia's statutes have no general rule on penalty clauses outside sales and leases of goods; whether a fixed charge is an unenforceable penalty is a question of case law. The Consumer Protection Act makes it a prohibited practice to use a void penalty clause in a lease or to try to collect under one (it reaches transactions governed by the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act only for acts that are a misrepresentation or fraudulent act or practice under § 59.1-200, which describes its list as fraudulent acts or practices). The cautious course is to recover what the Act lists, in the amounts actually incurred, and nothing labelled as an eviction fee. To redeem at or before the first return date in a nonpayment case, the tenant pays rent due, late charges, attorney fees and court costs; a payment under the general redemption rule, of rent due as of the court date, also includes other charges and fees the lease contracts for, and after the return date the tenant may stop the eviction by paying everything claimed on the summons, including sheriff fees, no less than 48 hours before the scheduled eviction (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1250). So the redemption rules don't settle whether a charge labelled as an eviction fee is owed; the limits above do.

title: Who Receives Eviction Court Papers
bodyText: Serving the tenant: Virginia has no rule letting a lease name someone to accept eviction court papers for the tenant. The summons is served by the sheriff or by a private process server (an adult who is not a party), and must reach the tenant in one of the ways the law sets: handed to the tenant; if the tenant is not found at home, given to a family member at least 16 years old who lives there (not a guest); or, failing that, posted on the main door, in which case you or your attorney or agent must mail the tenant a copy at least 10 days before a default judgment and file a certificate of mailing (mailing the eviction application or summons with the court date satisfies this). Serve the summons at least 10 days before the court date. A business tenant is served through its officers or registered agent. Virginia's Address Confidentiality Program, for victims of domestic violence, stalking and similar crimes, makes the Attorney General's office the participant's agent for receiving mail only; it sets no special rule for serving court papers, so serve a participant at the rental home in the usual way. Papers served on you: at or before the start of the tenancy you must give the tenant, in writing, the name and address of the person managing the property and of an owner or someone authorized to act for the owner, for service of process and notices, and keep it current; anyone who fails to do so becomes your agent for service. If an owner is an individual who lives outside Virginia, every lease must name a Virginia agent for service (see Virginia Agent of Nonresident Owner and Owner and Manager Disclosure).

title: No Releases of the Landlord's Liability
bodyText: A Virginia lease may not make the tenant agree to release or limit any liability you have to the tenant arising under law, or to indemnify you for that liability or its costs (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1208). That reaches general releases ("Landlord is not liable for any injury or loss"), releases of negligence, casualty, water, mold or pest claims, caps on your liability (such as limiting recovery to your interest in the property), and clauses making the tenant pay your defense costs for your own liability. Such a term is unenforceable. Including it carries no penalty by itself, but if you bring an action to enforce it, the tenant may recover actual damages and reasonable attorney fees. The law itself already limits your liability in some ways, and these apply without any clause: for the repair and maintenance duties you are liable only for actual damages proximately caused by your failure to use ordinary care; a landlord who sells in a good faith sale to a bona fide purchaser is released for events after notice of the sale to the tenant, and a managing agent for events after written notice that its management has ended, unless otherwise agreed; and a landlord who uses a third-party records service is not liable under the records section for that provider's data breach, except for gross negligence or an intentional act (Va. Code Ann. §§ 55.1-1209, 55.1-1220, 55.1-1224). A lease may still make the tenant responsible for damage the tenant, occupants and guests cause, require renter's insurance, and tell the tenant that your insurance does not cover the tenant's belongings; those allocate the tenant's own responsibility rather than excuse yours.

title: Fast-Track Eviction for Criminal or Drug Activity
bodyText: Virginia has an expedited eviction for criminal and drug activity. When the tenant's breach involves a criminal or willful act that can't be remedied and poses a threat to health or safety, or illegal drug activity, by the tenant, an authorized occupant or a guest, you may terminate immediately and file for possession without waiting for a criminal conviction. You must prove the violation by a preponderance of the evidence, and the tenant is presumed to know of an occupant's or guest's activity unless the tenant rebuts the presumption. The initial hearing on your action for immediate possession must be held within 15 calendar days after service on the tenant, or earlier if you allege emergency conditions on the premises that immediately threaten other tenants' health or safety; any later hearing or contested trial gets docket priority where practicable and must be heard within 30 calendar days after service; in between, the court may grant relief needed to protect the parties or other tenants; and a court's failure to meet these deadlines is not a ground to dismiss the case (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1245). The eviction itself is your action. Separately, a prosecutor or any local citizen may sue to enjoin a drug nuisance at a property, and the injunction can bind owners and tenants (Va. Code Ann. §§ 18.2-258.01, 48-17); after a drug-nuisance conviction a court may close the premises, in addition to your right of immediate termination (Va. Code Ann. § 48-16). Related: edu-criminal-activity-va, criminal-activity-va, edu-eviction-process-va.

title: Family Child Care in a Rental
bodyText: Virginia does not require you to let a tenant run child care in a rental. Unless the lease says otherwise the tenant must use the unit only as a residence, and a Virginia lease may expressly allow a tenant of an apartment building to provide child care services that meet state and local law; the library's optional Child Care clause does this with conditions. If you allow it, the tenant's operation must meet state child care law: home-based child care (care in the provider's home for one through 12 children under 13, not counting the provider's own or resident children, with at least one paid) must be licensed when five through 12 children are served, unless all are related to the provider, and no more than four children under two, counting the provider's own children and any children who live in the home, may be served without a license or voluntary registration. A licensed, system-approved or voluntarily registered home-based provider must tell each parent in writing whether liability insurance covers the operation, and get a signed acknowledgment. Except in a city or county covered by the separate local child care licensing statutes, zoning must treat home-based child care for one through four children as a residential use by a single family, with no stricter conditions than for families; for five through 12 children a locality may use an administrative permit with notice to neighbors. Some cities and urban counties license child care themselves. In a property owners' association, home-based child care that the locality treats as a residential use counts as a residential use unless the declaration prohibits or restricts it or the association restricts it by rule. Whatever you agree, a lease may not make the tenant release you from, or indemnify you for, your own liability to the tenant arising under law.

title: Hunting and Fishing on Rented Land
bodyText: No Virginia statute says whether a tenant who rents a house with farmland or other acreage gets the right to hunt, fish or trap on it, or whether that right stays with you; the lease decides. Several statutes treat a lessee as able to control the land: an owner or lessee may post land against hunting, fishing and trapping, and a hunter must show his license on the demand of the owner or lessee (Va. Code Ann. §§ 18.2-134.1, 29.1-337). It is a crime to go on another's land to hunt, fish or trap without the consent of the landowner or his agent, and on posted land without written consent or the owner's presence (Va. Code Ann. §§ 18.2-132, 18.2-134). The statutes don't say whether a tenant in possession counts as the landowner for that consent, so if you want to keep control, say so in the lease: the optional Hunting, Fishing and Trapping clause bars the tenant from hunting, fishing or trapping, or letting others do so, without your separate written consent. Your written consent also matters to the tenant: a bona fide tenant may hunt, trap and fish without a license on the land where he lives only if he carries the landlord's written consent (Va. Code Ann. § 29.1-301). Anyone who owns, leases or occupies land owes no duty to keep it safe for people who hunt or fish there and does not answer for their acts merely by giving permission, unless a fee is charged or the conduct is grossly negligent or willful (Va. Code Ann. § 29.1-509). An owner or tenant may kill beaver damaging crops or lands (Va. Code Ann. § 29.1-518). Crops are separate: a farm tenant's right to emblements (crops planted before the tenancy ends) follows the common law, and a crop planted under a lease of a year or less survives a later foreclosure sale (Va. Code Ann. §§ 55.1-1700 to 55.1-1702).

title: Fees for Services Not Provided
bodyText: Virginia has no statute that says, in so many words, that you may not charge a tenant a fee for a service you don't provide. Related rules point the same way. A misrepresentation or false promise about a charge is a prohibited practice under the Consumer Protection Act, which reaches a landlord's misrepresentations and fraudulent practices even though it otherwise leaves Virginia Residential Landlord and Tenant Act tenancies alone (Va. Code Ann. §§ 59.1-199, 59.1-200). Pass-through charges are tied to real costs: payment-processing fees may not exceed the actual third-party cost, utility billing service charges cover actual third-party costs, and insurance programs recover actual premium costs with administrative fees (Va. Code Ann. §§ 55.1-1204, 55.1-1206, 55.1-1212). If you fail to supply an essential service the lease promises, the tenant may, after written notice and a reasonable time to fix it, recover the drop in rental value or get substitute housing and owe no rent for that period (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1239). Cautious course: charge a recurring fee only for something you actually provide (for example an amenity that is open and working), say in the lease what it covers, and stop or credit it while the service isn't available.

title: Fire Code and Building Code Standards
bodyText: Virginia has one statewide fire code and one statewide building code, and both are based on the 2021 editions of the International Code Council's model codes. The Statewide Fire Prevention Code is a state regulation adopted by the Board of Housing and Community Development with the Fire Services Board; it incorporates the 2021 International Fire Code with Virginia's own changes and supersedes earlier local fire prevention regulations. It is chiefly a maintenance and operations code: it requires the fire protection equipment, systems and safeguards that were provided and approved when a building was built to be kept up, and it does not require you to install a system the building code did not require. A building built before the Building Code took effect in 1973 must also be maintained under the state fire and public building regulations in effect before March 31, 1986, if those applied to it. Enforcement is local and optional: a city, county or town may enforce the whole Fire Prevention Code or only its rules on open burning, fire lanes, fireworks and hazardous materials, and the State Fire Marshal enforces it where the locality does not. A locality may also adopt fire prevention rules stricter or broader than the state code, as long as they do not change how buildings are constructed. The Uniform Statewide Building Code governs construction (based on the 2021 International Building and Residential Codes), rehabilitation of existing buildings, and maintenance (the Virginia Maintenance Code, based on the 2021 International Property Maintenance Code, which includes fire-safety maintenance such as exits, fire-rated construction and alarms). It supersedes local building codes. For a landlord, these codes matter in two ways: a fire official or building official can order you to correct a violation, and your duty under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act to comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety makes a serious violation a repair problem the tenant can enforce. See Fire Sprinklers in Rental Buildings, Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Alarms, Fire Safety & Grilling and Model Code Editions Virginia Adopts.

title: Fire Sprinklers in Rental Buildings
bodyText: Virginia does not require you to add sprinklers to an existing apartment building or rental home. Sprinkler duties come from the Building Code and depend on when and how the building was built. New construction: a residential building of the apartment or other Group R type built under the current construction code must have an automatic sprinkler system throughout, except that two kinds of smaller apartment buildings (two stories or less with no more than 16 units per fire area and exterior exit access for every unit, or units no more than two stories above the exit level separated by two-hour fire barriers) are excused only when the water pressure or volume the system needs is not available. Attics must also be sprinklered in certain wood-frame or similar apartment buildings marketed to people 55 or older. One- and two-family homes and townhouses need sprinklers only where the builder chose to install them; if installed, they must meet the code's design standards, and adding to or altering a home without sprinklers does not trigger them. Existing buildings: the code's retrofit list reaches hotels and motels, high-rise college dormitories, nursing homes, hospitals and assisted living facilities, not ordinary rental housing, and retroactive sprinkler rules in the model fire code are not enforced unless that list requires them. Maintenance: a sprinkler system that the building has, whether required or not, must be kept operable at all times and maintained under the Building Code and the Statewide Fire Prevention Code; a required system taken out of service must follow the Fire Prevention Code, with immediate notice to the fire department and fire official. You may install sprinklers voluntarily with a permit; a nonrequired system may be reduced or discontinued only with the building official's approval and with visible heads removed so it does not give a false sense of protection. Tenants must not deliberately or negligently damage or impair the system, which is part of the premises. See Fire Code and Building Code Standards.

title: Foreclosure of a Rented Home
bodyText: Before a sale: if you rent out a single-family home and receive a lender's notice of mortgage default, acceleration or a foreclosure sale, you must tell the tenant (and any prospective tenant) in writing within five business days, unless the tenant gave you the lender's notice; if you don't, the tenant may end the lease on five business days' written notice, and you handle the deposit as usual. The trustee's notice of a foreclosure sale goes to the owner, lienholders and associations, not to the tenant, so your notice may be the tenant's only warning. If your tenant is a federal employee or contractor unpaid in a federal government closure and the home has one to four units, you can get a 60-day stay of the foreclosure by asking your lender, with the tenant's written proof, within 90 days of the closure or of its end, whichever is later. After a sale: a buyer who will live in the home must give the tenant written notice ending the lease at least 90 days ahead; any other buyer takes the home subject to the lease for the rest of its term, though it may still end the lease for the tenant's breach or under the lease's own terms. The tenant then pays rent to the new owner as it directs in writing, to the managing agent, or into court escrow, and, if the lease names no managing agent, is not late or charged a late fee until the new owner says in writing whom to pay. Whoever holds the landlord's interest when the tenancy ends must return the deposit, whether or not it was handed over. A written property management agreement with a real estate licensee in place at the sale becomes month-to-month with the new owner, and the licensee may collect rent but must put it in escrow. A former owner who stays after the sale becomes a tenant at sufferance and can be removed on three days' written notice. Federal law (the Protecting Tenants at Foreclosure Act) gives a bona fide tenant the same 90-day notice and keeps a lease running to its end unless the buyer will occupy; it does not displace longer state protections. Foreclosure-rescue sellers: a person who offers to help a homeowner avoid foreclosure may not collect fees before performing, may not take the home and then skip the mortgage payments while keeping the rents, and may not promise the seller a right to buy back unless a written contract states the terms and price. Virginia has no rule requiring a sale-leaseback contract to recite the lease or giving the homeowner a cancellation period. See Selling or Losing a Rented Property.

title: Telling Tenants About a Mortgage Default or Foreclosure
bodyText: Virginia's one foreclosure disclosure applies to a home used as a single-family residence. If you receive a lender's written notice of mortgage default, mortgage acceleration or a foreclosure sale on the loan, you must tell the tenant and any prospective tenant in writing within five business days. You need not do so if the tenant or prospective tenant gave you the lender's notice, and a managing agent who never received a copy of it is not bound. If you fail to give the notice, the tenant may end the lease on at least five business days' written notice, and you handle the deposit as usual. The statute counts the five days from your receipt of the lender's notice; for an applicant who comes along later while the default or sale is still pending, the cautious course is to give the same written notice before the lease is signed. Virginia has no foreclosure disclosure for other kinds of rentals, and no lease form or clause wording is required (the notice is a separate written notice, not a lease term). A related pre-signing disclosure applies to multifamily buildings: if an application to register the building as a condominium or cooperative has been filed, or there is a plan within six months to displace tenants by demolition, substantial rehabilitation or conversion to office, hotel, motel or planned-unit use, you must tell prospective tenants in writing. A real estate licensee you hire to lease the property must also disclose known material adverse facts about the property's physical condition. See Selling or Losing a Rented Property and Foreclosure of a Rented Home.

title: Foreign Adversaries and Agricultural Land
bodyText: Any alien who is not an enemy may buy and hold real estate in Virginia, and Virginia has no general rule against renting a home to a foreign national, no rule requiring you to ask about citizenship, and no recording or approval step for a lease to a foreign person or a corporation. National origin is protected by fair housing law, so do not screen applicants by nationality (see the immigration-status row). One restriction can reach a rental: since July 1, 2023, no foreign adversary may acquire any interest in agricultural land in Virginia, and an acquisition in violation is void, with title passing to the Commonwealth. A foreign adversary is a foreign government or other person that the U.S. Secretary of Commerce has determined to be one under a federal regulation; the statute does not on its face reach a person merely because of the person's nationality. Agricultural land is real estate used for farming or forestry, or zoned so that it could be, which can include a house on rural or agriculturally zoned land. An interest counts only if it gives the holder the ability to possess or occupy the land or direct the farm operation, so a lease appears to count, and the statute has no exception for short leases. It puts no duty on you to investigate an applicant, and it names no penalty on the landlord beyond voiding the transaction; the locality's attorney, the Attorney General or a non-adversary party to the void transaction may sue in circuit court to eject the foreign adversary or clear title. Cautious course: for land zoned to permit agriculture, do not lease to a foreign government or an entity you know to be on the federal list, and get legal advice if an applicant may be one.

title: Undoing a Termination for Unpaid Rent
bodyText: In a Virginia residential lease, unpaid rent ends the tenancy only through the 14-day notice, and the tenant can undo the termination at several points. Before the notice runs out: paying the rent within the 14 days keeps the lease in force. After you file: the tenant, or anyone for the tenant, may pay you, your attorney or the court all rent due as of the court date, other lease charges and fees, late charges, reasonable attorney fees and court costs, and the case is dismissed unless you also sued on grounds other than nonpayment; a written commitment from a local government or nonprofit to pay within 10 days gets a 10-day continuance for that purpose. After judgment: the tenant may still cancel the eviction by paying everything claimed on the summons, including sheriff fees, at least 48 hours before the scheduled eviction, and you must then tell the sheriff promptly to cancel it. On written request, give the tenant a statement of the exact amount owed; payments are by cashier's check, certified check or money order. A landlord with four or fewer Virginia units may limit the right to once per lease period by written notice (see Right of Redemption Limited to Once per Lease Period). Two related rules: if you accept full payment you cannot go on to evict for nonpayment alone, and accepting partial payment keeps your right to evict only if you gave the written reservation notice; and signing a new written lease with the tenant makes an earlier possession order unenforceable (see Accepting Rent With Reservation, and the Right of Redemption). The older forfeiture and re-entry procedures in Virginia's law (ejectment for rent in arrears, relief by paying before trial, and restoration within a year after a recorded re-entry) are in the nonresidential tenancy chapter and do not govern a dwelling lease. A lease clause saying you may re-enter for default never lets you lock the tenant out without a court order (see No Self-Help Eviction).

title: Model Code Editions Virginia Adopts
bodyText: Virginia's statutes do not freeze a building or fire code at a named edition for rental housing. They direct the Board of Housing and Community Development to adopt the codes by regulation, with due regard for the standards of the International Code Council and the National Fire Protection Association, and to amend them after public hearing. The regulations then fix the editions. The Uniform Statewide Building Code now in force uses the 2021 editions: the 2021 International Building Code (which brings in the 2021 International Residential, Plumbing, Mechanical, Fuel Gas and Energy Conservation Codes and the 2020 National Electrical Code), the 2021 International Existing Building Code for rehabilitation, and the 2021 International Property Maintenance Code for maintenance, each with Virginia's printed amendments. The Statewide Fire Prevention Code incorporates the 2021 International Fire Code. A newer national edition has no effect in Virginia until the Board adopts it. Which edition governs your building depends on the question. New construction follows the edition in effect when the permit application was submitted, with a one-year window after a new edition takes effect in which the applicant may choose the prior edition, and a properly issued permit is not reopened by a later edition. Maintenance follows the code under which the building was built: equipment and safeguards approved at construction must be kept up, and buildings built before 1973 must also be maintained under the fire and public building regulations in effect before March 31, 1986, where those applied. Some retrofit rules name a past edition directly (for example, hotel and motel smoke alarms and sprinklers as required by the code in effect March 1, 1990). A few statutes point to a standard without freezing it: the lead-paint immunity statute measures maintenance against the International Property Maintenance Code as adopted in the Building Code, and from January 1, 2027 a tenant's plug-in solar device must meet the most recent version of the National Electrical Code. Ask the local building official which edition applied when your building was built or last permitted. See Fire Code and Building Code Standards.

title: No Good-Cause Eviction Notice
bodyText: Virginia has no good-cause eviction law, so there is no notice telling tenants whether such a law covers their unit, and you need not state a reason when you decline to renew a lease or end a month-to-month or week-to-week tenancy with the required notice. The Act lets you terminate for any reason not prohibited by law unless a court finds the reason was retaliation. One good-cause rule arrives on January 1, 2027: if you know that a tenant receiving rental assistance through a Housing Choice Voucher or another government program has made a protected complaint, joined a tenants' organization or testified against you, refusing to renew that tenancy counts as retaliation unless, among the statute's exceptions, you fail to renew for good cause. The statute does not define good cause, so keep a written record of the lease-based reason for any such nonrenewal. Notices that must state grounds are the default notices: a notice ending the lease for a tenant's breach must specify the acts and omissions, and a nonpayment notice must tell the tenant of the nonpayment and that the lease will end if rent is not paid within 14 days. Local governments cannot add a good-cause or notice rule, because the Act supersedes local landlord-tenant ordinances. See No Just-Cause Eviction Rule and Retaliation.

title: Passing Local Government Fees to Tenants
bodyText: Virginia lets you pass local government fees through to tenants only in a set way. In place of raising the rent, you may use a formula to allocate among the tenants of a residential building the actual or anticipated local government fees billed to you, if the lease clearly says so. Local government fees are charges or fees assessed against a residential building, such as stormwater, recycling, trash collection, elevator testing, fire or life safety testing, or residential rental inspection program fees. The allocation method may be based on square footage, occupancy, number of bedrooms or another method you and the tenant agree to in the lease, and you may also charge agreed service fees covering the actual cost of running the program. The allocated fees and service charges are rent. The library's Utilities Billed by Landlord clause has the wording. Because these amounts are rent, list them in the first-page fee disclosure (or add them later only by an addendum the tenant signs), and remember that a new charge in the middle of a lease needs the tenant's written consent. Fees that are not assessed against the residential building, such as building permit fees for your own work, and any fine or penalty, are outside this allocation. There is no local landlord registration fee to pass on: a rental inspection ordinance may not charge any fee for an owner's notice that a unit is rented (see Landlord Registration and Rental Licensing).

title: Government Fines and Tenants
bodyText: Virginia has no statute that bars, or expressly allows, passing a government fine or abatement charge on to a tenant, and none that makes a tenant liable to you for a fine you paid. Who is cited depends on the law involved. Building Code violations are unlawful for any owner or other person, and an enforcement officer may issue a summons or ticket to the lessor or sublessor of a residential unit if a copy goes to the owner; maintenance code notices may be issued to the owner, the tenant or whoever is responsible for maintenance, and the code treats a lessee in control of a building as an owner. A locality that abates a nuisance may charge the cost to the owners or occupants, and a person convicted of causing a nuisance may be ordered to reimburse the locality. No zoning fine for overcrowding a single-family home accrues against you while your court action against the tenant to end the overcrowding is pending. Between you and the tenant: the tenant must comply with the building and housing code obligations primarily imposed on tenants, and you may recover damages for the tenant's breach of the lease or those duties. Three limits shape any reimbursement term: you may not charge a tenant a fee for maintenance or repair unless the tenant's violation of the Act made it necessary; a lease may not make the tenant release or indemnify you for your own liability to the tenant arising under law; and money owed under a Virginia lease other than a deposit is rent, which must be listed in the first-page fee disclosure or a later signed addendum. The cautious course is to recover a fine caused by the tenant's breach as damages for that breach, documented with the citation, and never to bill a tenant for a fine on a condition that is your responsibility. The library does not use its general tenant-caused fines clause in Virginia.

title: Guarantors and Lease Renewals
bodyText: Virginia has no statute saying whether a lease guarantor stays liable through a renewal, extension or month-to-month continuation, and none requiring a guaranty to state a maximum amount or an end date. How far a guaranty reaches depends on its words and on court decisions, so say it expressly: if you want the guaranty to cover renewals, extensions, holdover and month-to-month periods and rent changes made under the lease, write that into the guaranty. The library's optional Guaranty clause offers both choices. Three statutes do apply. A promise to answer for another person's debt or default cannot be enforced unless it, or a memorandum of it, is in writing and signed by the guarantor or the guarantor's agent, so have the guarantor sign. Once a right of action has accrued, a guarantor may give you written notice requiring you to sue; if you do not sue every party who lives in Virginia and is not insolvent within 30 days, and pursue the case diligently, you lose your claim against the guarantor (your claim against the tenant is unaffected). A guarantor who pays may recover the amount from the tenant with interest and 5 percent damages. A guarantor who has no right to live in the home is not a tenant under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act. Any security deposit, however named, counts toward the two-month cap; the cautious course is to count money a guarantor puts up as security toward that cap.

title: Guests and Barring a Guest
bodyText: Virginia gives residential tenants no statutory right to have guests or service providers visit, and sets no rule against guest fees or registration for dwelling leases. A guest or invitee is a person, other than the tenant or an authorized occupant, who has the tenant's permission to visit but not to live in the unit. The lease may set reasonable guest rules, such as a limit on how long a guest may stay before becoming an occupant who needs your consent (see the Guest Policy clause). The tenant is responsible for the conduct of anyone on the premises with the tenant's consent, so that neighbors' peaceful enjoyment is not disturbed, and for damage those persons cause. You may bar a particular guest or invitee from the premises for conduct on your property that violates the lease, a local ordinance, or state or federal law. Serve the guest personally with a written notice describing the conduct, and serve a copy on the tenant; once the guest has been served, you may seek a trespass warrant from a magistrate if the guest returns. The tenant may ask the general district court to review the bar by filing a tenant's assertion. Fair housing law applies to guest rules as to everything else: apply them equally, and consider reasonable accommodations a tenant with a disability asks for (see Disability Accommodations and Modifications). A free-access rule for guests exists only for manufactured home parks, where a tenant's guest or invitee must have free access to the home site without charge or registration.

title: How Serious a Repair Problem Must Be
bodyText: Virginia measures most tenant repair remedies by how serious the problem is. Your duty itself is broad: comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety, make all repairs and do whatever is necessary to keep the premises fit and habitable, and maintain the facilities and appliances you supply. But the tenant's remedies turn on seriousness. Ending the lease for your breach requires a material noncompliance with the lease, or a noncompliance with the Act materially affecting health and safety, that you fail to remedy within 21 days of written notice. Rent escrow, repair by a licensed contractor, the defense to a nonpayment eviction and a locality's habitability suit require a condition that is a material noncompliance or that is, or if not promptly corrected will be, a fire hazard or serious threat to the life, health or safety of occupants; the statutes give as examples a lack of heat, hot or cold running water, light, electricity or adequate sewage disposal, a rodent infestation, and (for rent escrow) lead paint you have notice of. Ending the lease at move-in requires a fire hazard or serious threat at the start of the tenancy. Essential services (heat, running water, hot water, electricity, gas, and central air conditioning you supply that is operating when the lease takes effect) have their own remedy if you willfully or negligently fail to supply them. Virginia has no statutory list of minor or cosmetic defects that do not count; whether a condition is material is decided case by case, and your liability for damages is limited to a failure to use ordinary care. None of these remedies is available for a condition the tenant's household or guests caused. The same seriousness test applies to tenants: your own repair-and-bill remedy and your noncompliance termination rest on a tenant breach materially affecting health and safety. See Repair Duties and Tenant Remedies.

title: Habitability Duties Cannot Be Modified
bodyText: None of a Virginia landlord's habitability duties can be modified by the lease. The duty section has no "unless otherwise agreed" wording, which the Act uses elsewhere when it means to let the parties change a rule (for example, on the use of the home only as a residence). The only limits on the duties are built into the duties themselves and turn on facts, not on what the lease says: hot water, heat and air conditioning need not be supplied where the unit is built so that they are generated by an installation within the tenant's exclusive control or supplied by a direct public utility connection, and air conditioning is owed only if provided. Running water has no exception: the duty to supply running water applies to every unit, whatever its water source. Where a building or housing code sets a higher standard than the other duties, the code standard governs. A written agreement may move some of the work to the tenant (common areas, waste, water, heat and air conditioning, and specified repairs), but that is a change in who performs, not a change in the standard; see the guidance on the duty to keep the home fit and the optional tenant-repair agreement (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1220).

title: Presumptions in Repair Disputes
bodyText: Virginia has one statutory presumption that works against a landlord in a repair dispute, and it concerns delay: in a tenant's rent escrow case, and when a tenant raises your noncompliance as a defense to an action for unpaid rent or possession, there is a rebuttable presumption that letting more than 30 days pass after you received the tenant's written notice, or a violation or condemnation notice from a state or local agency, without fixing the condition is an unreasonable delay. Shorter periods are left to the court. In a rent escrow case where the court finds the tenant entitled to relief, the burden is on you to show why the rent should not be abated. No Virginia statute presumes that a code violation or a missing facility is itself a breach of your duty to keep the unit fit and habitable, or presumes that you had notice of a problem; the tenant must show the condition and the notice, and you may answer that the condition does not exist, has been fixed, was caused by the tenant's household or guests, or that the tenant unreasonably refused you entry. Two move-in rules help you: your written move-in inspection report is deemed correct unless the tenant objects in writing within five days, and if that report shows no visible mold and the tenant does not object, there is a rebuttable presumption that no mold existed at move-in. Answer repair notices promptly and in writing, and keep records of when you received each notice and when the work was done. See Repair Duties and Tenant Remedies and Move-In Inspection Report.

title: No Required Habitability Statement in the Lease
bodyText: Virginia does not require the lease to state that you will deliver or keep the unit fit for habitation. The duty exists whether or not the lease mentions it: the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act requires you to make all repairs and do whatever is necessary to put and keep the premises in a fit and habitable condition, to comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety, and to meet the other maintenance duties the Act lists. If you do not offer a written lease, the Act still applies to the tenancy by operation of law. If you do offer one, you must give the tenant the state's Statement of Tenant Rights and Responsibilities with it and have both parties sign the state acknowledgment form, and you may not sue on a lease violation until the statement has been provided; that statement, not the lease, is the state-required summary of the parties' rights. A lease may not take the duty away: a term by which the tenant waives rights or remedies under the Act, or agrees to limit your liability arising under law, is unenforceable, and if you sue to enforce one the tenant may recover actual damages and attorney fees. The library's maintenance clause (Maintenance & Repairs) states your repair undertaking in general terms; it does not narrow the statute. See Repair Duties and Tenant Remedies and Statement of Tenant Rights and Responsibilities.

title: No Waiver of the Duty to Keep the Home Fit
bodyText: A Virginia lease cannot remove or water down your duty to keep the home fit. You must comply with building and housing codes materially affecting health and safety; make all repairs and do whatever is necessary to keep the premises fit and habitable; keep shared common areas clean and structurally safe; maintain the facilities and appliances you supply; prevent moisture and mold; provide waste receptacles and removal; and supply running water, reasonable hot water, heat in season and reasonable air conditioning if provided (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1220). Those duties are the tenant's rights under the Act, and a lease may not make the tenant waive rights or remedies under the Act or release or limit your liability to the tenant arising under law (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1208). So an "as is" clause, a release of repair claims, or a promise not to use the tenant's remedies (the 21-day notice to cure, rent escrow, repair by a licensed contractor, damages and injunction) does not hold. Virginia has no rule letting a tenant accept a listed defect in return for lower rent; rent for an unremedied condition is reduced by a court in a rent escrow case, not by the lease. What a written agreement can do is move the work, not the duty: the tenant may agree in writing to keep shared common areas clean and safe, handle waste, or supply water, hot water, heat or air conditioning, and to do specified repairs, maintenance, alterations or remodeling, if the agreement is made in good faith, not to evade your obligations, and does not affect your obligations to other tenants. The library's optional tenant-repair agreement does this. Your code-compliance and fit-and-habitable duties stay with you either way. By law your liability for these duties is limited to the tenant's actual damages caused by your failure to use ordinary care; the lease cannot narrow it further.

title: Contamination, Brownfields and Environmental Covenants
bodyText: Virginia has no statute that requires you to tell a residential tenant that the property is or was contaminated with hazardous substances, is a brownfield, is on a federal Superfund (National Priorities List) site or is listed on the state's Hazardous Waste Site Inventory, and none that requires a lease to repeat recorded environmental use limits. Two narrower rules have their own rows: written disclosure before signing if you know the unit was used to make methamphetamine and was not cleaned up (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1219), and the federal lead-based paint disclosure for housing built before 1978. Environmental covenants are the exception to watch. A cleanup approved by the Department of Environmental Quality or another agency can leave a covenant recorded in the land records under the Uniform Environmental Covenants Act, with limits such as no use of groundwater, no digging, or keeping a cap or barrier in place. The covenant runs with the land, can forbid uses that zoning allows, and can be enforced in court by the agency, the parties, the locality and anyone whose interest or liability is affected (Va. Code Ann. §§ 10.1-1241, 10.1-1242, 10.1-1247). A lease made after the covenant is recorded generally takes subject to it under the recording laws; a lease already in place when a covenant is created is not affected unless the tenant agrees to subordinate it, and the agency's process sends a copy of a new covenant to each person in possession, tenants included (Va. Code Ann. §§ 10.1-1239, 10.1-1243, 10.1-1244). If your property has one, give the tenant a copy and use the optional Environmental Covenant clause so the lease's use rules match it. If you lease a one-to-four-unit home with an option to buy, the Residential Property Disclosure Act applies: give the Real Estate Board's residential property disclosure statement before the contract is signed. That statement says the owner makes no representations about the property's condition or recorded covenants; it has no contamination item (Va. Code Ann. §§ 55.1-701, 55.1-703, 55.1-709). Whatever the history, you must keep the dwelling fit and habitable (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1220), and you should never misstate what you know about contamination.

title: No Health-District Rental Rules
bodyText: Virginia has no health-district rental regulations and no rule that you give a tenant health-department rental rules on request or refer tenants to a health district. Every county and city has a local health department, and several may be combined into a district health department under the State Board of Health; local health ordinances may not be less protective than state law, but no statute gives them a rental-housing code. Housing conditions in a rental are instead set by the Building Code's maintenance part (the Virginia Maintenance Code), enforced by the locality's building or maintenance code official, and by your duty under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act to keep the unit fit and habitable. A tenant with a condition problem can complain to the local building department, which must enforce the unsafe-structure provisions if it finds there may be a violation; the tenant also has the Act's rent escrow remedy, and from July 1, 2026 a locality may sue on a tenant's behalf over serious habitability failures you have not fixed after its notice. Housing for migrant farmworkers is a separate regime: the Board of Health may regulate migrant labor camps, including their sleeping quarters and sanitation; those regulations are not covered here. One Board of Health regulation does reach rentals with a shared pool: the owner of an apartment or condominium pool must test the water daily and post the results (see Pools at Rental Properties). See also Local Rental Inspections and Local Landlord-Tenant Rules and Rent Control.

title: Heat: Season, Temperature and Remedies
bodyText: You must supply heat in season unless the unit is built so that its heat comes from equipment under the tenant's exclusive control or from a direct public utility connection, and you must keep any heating system you supply in good and safe working order. Where the lease, in writing or by implication, has you furnish heat, the state Maintenance Code (Part III of the Uniform Statewide Building Code) requires you to supply heat from October 15 to May 1 that keeps every habitable room, bathroom and toilet room at 68°F or warmer; on days colder than the locality's winter design temperature it is enough that the system runs at full design capacity. Unvented room heaters may not be the only source of heat in such a unit. A unit in a building built under the current construction code's building provisions and rented with heat must have heating able to hold 65°F from 6:30 a.m. to 10:30 p.m. and 60°F at other hours over the same season; a one- or two-family home or townhouse built under the residential code and rented with heat must have the heating facilities that code requires from October 15 to May 1. If you furnish cooling in an apartment building, the Maintenance Code also requires cooling from May 15 to October 1 that keeps habitable rooms at 77°F or cooler. Heat is an essential service: if you willfully or negligently fail to supply it, the tenant may give written notice and, after a reasonable time to correct, recover the lost rental value or move to substitute housing and owe no rent for that period. A lack of heat at the start of the tenancy lets the tenant end the lease by written notice within seven days and get a full refund; a lack of heat later can support a rent escrow case, a defense to a nonpayment eviction, and repair by a licensed contractor if you take no reasonable steps within 14 days of written notice. Rent escrow is not available where the tenant pays for the heating utility and the loss of heat is the direct result of the tenant's failure to pay it. A tenant may agree in writing to supply heat in your place, in good faith and not to evade your duties (see Tenant-Performed Duties and Repairs by Written Agreement). Your locality decides whether to inspect existing buildings for the Maintenance Code, but after a tenant's complaint it must enforce the unsafe-structure rules, and your duty under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act to comply with applicable building and housing codes applies either way. See Repair Duties and Tenant Remedies.

title: Renting in a Homeowners or Condominium Association
bodyText: If you rent out a lot in a property owners' association or a condominium unit, Virginia limits what the association can do about the rental. Unless the association law, the declaration (condominium instruments) or other law expressly allows it, the association may not: condition or prohibit the rental; charge a rental, application or processing fee of more than $50 during the term of a lease; charge an annual or monthly rental fee or another fee the law does not authorize; make you use its own lease or lease addendum; take a deposit from you or your tenant; evict your tenant or make you give it a power of attorney to do so; or refuse to recognize your authorized representative. It may require you to give it your tenants' and authorized occupants' names, contact and vehicle information, your agent's name and contact information, and the tenant's acknowledgment of and consent to its rules. Violations by your tenant are charged to you: where the instruments or rules expressly allow it, the association may, after written notice, a chance to fix the problem and a hearing, assess charges against you for violations your tenants, guests or family cause, capped at $50 for a single offense or $10 a day for a continuing one for no more than 90 days, and those charges are a lien on your unit or lot. Where the instruments or rules expressly allow it, and after the same notice, chance to fix and hearing, the association may also suspend services it provides directly for assessments more than 60 days overdue, but not in a way that blocks access or endangers an owner, tenant or occupant. Pass those charges on through the lease (see Homeowner / Condominium Association Compliance). Virginia has no rule letting an association collect rent from your tenant when you fall behind on assessments, or a court order for the tenant to pay rent to the association, and no statute deciding whether a rental restriction added to the declaration binds owners who bought before it; that is a question of the declaration's amendment terms and case law. In a property owners' association, home-based child care that the locality's zoning treats as a residential use counts as a residential use unless the declaration prohibits or restricts it or the association restricts it by rule; the landlord is separately free to allow or refuse it in the lease. When you buy, the resale certificate must disclose any restriction on renting.

title: Holding Deposits Before the Lease
bodyText: Virginia has no separate holding-deposit rule because its application-deposit rule covers one. Any refundable money an applicant pays to be considered as a tenant, including money meant to become the security deposit, is an application deposit, and a security deposit paid at signing stays an application deposit until the lease commencement date (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1200). So a holding deposit can't be made nonrefundable. If the applicant doesn't rent, you may keep only your actual expenses and damages (for example rent actually lost while you held the unit off the market) and must refund the rest with an itemized list within 20 days, or within 10 days if you rejected the applicant and the deposit was paid by cash, certified check, cashier's check or postal money order; otherwise the applicant recovers the amount wrongly kept and attorney fees (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1203). The only nonrefundable charge an applicant may pay is the application fee of up to $50 plus actual third-party screening costs. Virginia has no rule doubling a deposit if the landlord backs out. Put the amount, how long you will hold the unit and what happens to the money in writing when you take it. A real estate licensee taking it for you must escrow it by the fifth business banking day after you approve the application (Va. Code Ann. § 54.1-2108.1). Once it becomes the security deposit it counts toward the two-month cap.

title: Home Businesses in a Rental
bodyText: Virginia has no statute that makes a home-based business a permitted use of a rented home or that stops a landlord from restricting one. Under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, unless you agree otherwise the tenant must occupy the unit only as a residence, so the lease decides: the library's Residential Use Only clause bars commercial use, and you may allow a home business by written agreement, with conditions you choose. Whatever the lease says, the business must also meet local zoning: localities may require a special use or conditional use permit for home businesses and home occupations, and may license and tax businesses. In a property owners' association, the association may not prohibit a lot owner's home-based business in the owner's residence unless the declaration provides otherwise, but it may set reasonable time, place, manner and sign rules; that protection is written for lot owners, and your tenant must follow the association's rules through your lease. Child care is a special case: a lease may allow a tenant of an apartment building to provide child care services that meet state and local law (see Family Child Care in a Rental).

title: No Virginia Rule on Immigration Status in Renting
bodyText: Virginia has no statute on a tenant's or applicant's immigration status: none bars you from asking, none requires you to check, and none makes it unlawful to rent to a person who lacks lawful status. You may require each applicant to give a Social Security number or an IRS individual taxpayer identification number, so an applicant without a Social Security number can qualify with a taxpayer identification number, and you may copy a driver's license or similar photo identification (but not a U.S. government-issued identification where copying it would violate federal law) (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1203). The Virginia Fair Housing Law doesn't list immigration or citizenship status, but it protects national origin, and the Fair Housing Board treats words and statements indicating a national-origin preference as evidence of discrimination. Asking only some applicants about status, demanding extra documents from applicants who seem foreign, or turning down a taxpayer identification number you would accept in place of a Social Security number from others risks a national-origin claim. The cautious course: use one identity and income-verification standard for every applicant, accept either number, and don't ask about immigration status. Related rows: edu-tenant-screening-va, edu-fair-housing-va.

title: Ending a Lease for Illness, Age or a Move to Care
bodyText: Virginia has no rule that lets a tenant end a lease early because of age, illness or disability, or because the tenant must move into a nursing home, assisted living or other care facility, and no rule that ends a month-to-month tenancy when a party loses the capacity to contract. Unless the lease gives that right, a tenant who leaves early for those reasons is treated like any other tenant who leaves before the term ends: you must mitigate, and the tenant owes rent until the term ends or you re-rent, whichever comes first. A month-to-month tenant may end the tenancy on 30 days' written notice before the next rent due date, unless the lease sets a different notice period. Related rules: when the sole tenant under a written lease who still lives in the unit dies, the lease ends on the date of death (see When a Sole Tenant Dies). Living in a nursing home, hospital or similar institution incidental to medical or geriatric care is not a tenancy under the Act. Federal law lets a servicemember who suffers a catastrophic injury or illness in service end the lease, or the spouse or a dependent do so if the servicemember lacks the capacity to manage his or her affairs. Caution: a tenant with a disability who asks to be released early, or to give shorter notice, may be asking for a reasonable accommodation in your rules or policies, which fair housing law requires when it may be necessary and not an undue burden; decide such requests case by case (see Disability Accommodations and Modifications). If you want to offer a medical or care-facility release, put it in the lease or a written addendum with the notice and proof you will accept, and apply it to every tenant alike.

title: No Duty to Disclose Code Orders or Condemnation
bodyText: Virginia does not require you to tell a tenant or prospective tenant about outstanding code inspection orders, notices of violation or a condemnation of the building. The disclosure duties that come closest: for a multifamily unit, you must tell prospective tenants in writing if an application to register the property as a condominium or cooperative has been filed, or if within six months there is an existing plan to displace tenants by demolition or substantial rehabilitation or by conversion to office, hotel or motel use or a planned unit development; and for a single-family residence, you must tell the tenant or prospective tenant in writing within five business days after you receive a notice of mortgage default, acceleration or foreclosure sale (see Selling or Losing a Rented Property). Code officials, not landlords, carry the notice duties for code orders: a maintenance code notice of violation may go to the owner, the tenant or whoever is responsible for maintenance, with a copy to the owner; officials should give a notice of unsafe structure to tenants whenever possible; a structure ordered vacated is placarded at each entrance; and in a manufactured home park the locality must notify affected tenants if a health and safety violation is not fixed within seven days. Not disclosing does not protect you. If a tenant told you during the tenancy of a building code violation that posed a substantial risk to health or safety and the unit is then condemned, you are liable for the tenant's actual damages and must return prepaid rent not yet due, the security deposit and any rent paid after the condemnation, unless the tenant's side or an act of God caused it or the lease was properly ended for casualty damage. A violation or condemnation notice from a state or local agency also counts as notice to you for the tenant's rent escrow remedy and defense to eviction (see Condemned Units: Rent and Refunds).

title: Inspection Notices and the Deposit Penalty
bodyText: Virginia ties a real penalty to the move-out inspection notice, not to the move-in report. Move-out: when you ask the tenant to vacate, or within five days after you receive the tenant's notice of intent to vacate, you must give the tenant written notice of the right to be present at your inspection for the security deposit. If the tenant asks in writing to attend, you must tell the tenant the date and time, and the inspection must be made within 72 hours after the tenant delivers possession. The deposit section's penalty applies to these steps: if you willfully fail to comply with it, the court must order the whole security deposit returned with actual damages and reasonable attorney fees, unless the tenant owes you rent, in which case the court credits an amount equal to the deposit against the rent due. Move-in: within five days after the tenant moves in you must give a written report itemizing existing damage, with the mold disclosure; it is treated as correct unless the tenant objects in writing within five days. The move-in section states no penalty of its own, but without a timely report you lose the evidence the report gives you about the unit's starting condition when you later deduct for damage. See Move-In Inspection Report and Virginia Security Deposit Rules.

title: Jury Trials and Lease Jury Waivers
bodyText: Virginia's Constitution says that in controversies about property and suits between persons, trial by jury is preferable to any other and ought to be held sacred, and the Code preserves the right inviolate (Va. Const. art. I, § 11; Va. Code Ann. § 8.01-336). But a jury is never the default in a Virginia civil case: in an action at law the court decides the whole case unless a party demands a jury, and under the court rules failing to make a timely demand waives one. Most evictions start in general district court, where the judge hears the unlawful detainer without a jury. A jury becomes available if the case is filed in circuit court, or on appeal to circuit court, where trial by jury is had on any party's application (Va. Code Ann. §§ 8.01-125, 8.01-126, 8.01-129). No Virginia statute authorizes or bans a jury waiver in a residential lease, and the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act does not mention juries. The Act's non-waiver rule covers rights under the Act, and the jury right comes from the Constitution and Title 8.01, so whether a pre-dispute lease waiver would be enforced is a question of case law, not settled by statute. Because a waiver would matter only in the less common circuit court case, and its enforceability is uncertain against a right the Constitution calls sacred, the library does not offer a jury waiver clause for Virginia.

title: Key-Control Policies for Large Properties
bodyText: If you own more than 200 rental units attached to the same piece of real property in Virginia, you must have two things in place. First, a policy that every applicant for a job that will have access to the units' keys must undergo a pre-employment criminal history records check. Second, written policies and procedures on the storage, issuance, return and security of unit keys and electronic key codes, on who may have access to them, and, where it applies, on their use and deactivation. "Key" here means any physical or electronic mechanism used to get into a rental unit, so fobs, key cards, codes and app-based smart-lock credentials are covered. The rule does not apply to a financial institution or to a person who is a licensed real estate agent or broker. Owners below the threshold have no statutory key-control duty, but the same written practices protect you: keep a key log, limit who can issue or copy keys, and deactivate codes and credentials when a tenant or employee leaves. The statute says nothing about giving tenants a copy of the policy, so it need not go in the lease. See Locks, Peepholes and Security Devices and Smart Locks and App-Based Entry.

title: Using a Prohibited Lease Term: What It Costs
bodyText: Virginia's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act has no penalty for knowingly using a lease that contains a prohibited term, of the kind some states have. A prohibited term is unenforceable, and the tenant's remedy of actual damages and reasonable attorney fees arises only if you bring an action to enforce it (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1208). A second statute covers part of the same ground and does not depend on knowledge: the Virginia Consumer Protection Act makes it a prohibited practice to use in any lease a liquidated damage clause, penalty clause or waiver of defense that is void or unenforceable under Virginia or federal law, or to try to collect under one, and that practice stays within the Consumer Protection Act for landlords. A tenant who suffers a loss from it may recover actual damages or $500, whichever is greater, up to three times actual damages or $1,000 if the violation was willful, plus reasonable attorney fees and court costs (Va. Code Ann. §§ 59.1-199, 59.1-200, 59.1-204). So a void penalty or waiver-of-defense clause is a real exposure even if you never sue on it, and a prohibited term of any kind fails when you need it. Keep the lease to terms Virginia allows; the guidance on rights a lease cannot waive and on prohibited lease terms lists them.

title: Tenant's Remedies When You Breach
bodyText: When you breach the lease or the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, a Virginia tenant's remedies are set by the Act, and the lease cannot take them away. (1) Termination: for a material breach the tenant may give written notice ending the lease at least 30 days after you receive it unless you remedy within 21 days; for a breach that can't be remedied, the notice simply ends it in at least 30 days; and an intentional repeat of a remedied breach of the same kind allows a 30-day notice with no chance to cure. A tenant can't terminate over a condition the tenant's side caused.
