(2) Damages and an injunction for any breach of the lease or the Act, with attorney fees unless you prove you acted reasonably, and return of the deposit if the lease ends. (3) Unfit at move-in: written notice within seven days ends the lease, with a full refund within 15 business days unless you object in writing. (4) Willful failure to deliver possession: rent abates, and the tenant may end the lease on five days' written notice or demand possession; willful failure not in good faith adds damages and attorney fees. (5) Essential services you willfully or negligently fail to supply: after written notice and a reasonable time, damages for lost rental value or substitute housing with rent excused, plus attorney fees. (6) Repairs: rent escrow, the habitability defense to a nonpayment case, and repair by a licensed contractor after 14 days (see Repair Duties and Tenant Remedies and Rent Escrow). (7) Lockout, cutting services or making the unit unsafe: a court hearing within five days, possession or service restored, and actual damages plus $5,000 or four months' rent, whichever is greater, and attorney fees. (8) Unlawful or harassing entry: an injunction or termination, with damages and attorney fees. (9) Fire or casualty and condemnation: termination, refunds, and for a condemnation after the tenant reported the code violation, actual damages. (10) Missing pre-signing disclosures (military air zones, defective drywall, meth labs): termination within the stated period, the only remedy for that failure. (11) Retaliation: a defense to possession and actual damages. A tenant may also sue in circuit court for an injunction and damages over any act the Act prohibits, and from July 1, 2026 a locality may sue on tenants' behalf over serious habitability failures after notice to you.

title: No Landlord Liability Insurance Requirement
bodyText: Virginia has no rule that requires a residential landlord to carry liability insurance, to register proof of insurance with a locality or the state, or to tell tenants whether you are insured, and no locality may add such a requirement through a landlord-tenant ordinance, because the Act supersedes those. The Act touches your insurance in a few places: you must tell the tenant that your insurance does not cover the tenant's belongings when the lease does not require renter's insurance (see Renter's Insurance and Flood Notice); you may recover the tenant's prorated share of insurance you carry on the premises as rent if you provide it; and during a declared communicable-disease emergency the tenant must still allow maintenance or inspections your loan or insurance policy requires. A lease cannot make the tenant release or limit your liability under law, so your own coverage, not a lease clause, is what protects you from claims. What to do: carry landlord liability and property coverage anyway, check any lender or association insurance requirement, and keep your policy current when you change managers or sell.

title: Landlord Registration and Rental Licensing
bodyText: Apart from the Fair Housing certification described at the end, Virginia has no statewide registration or licensing requirement for landlords of long-term residential rentals, and the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act supersedes local ordinances on landlord and tenant relations and the leasing of residential property. What a locality can still require: (1) Rental inspection notice. Inside a rental inspection district, or for an individual unit the governing body finds blighted, deteriorating or in violation of the Building Code, a rental inspection ordinance may require you to tell the building department in writing that the unit is rented. The ordinance may not turn this into a registration requirement or charge any fee for the notice, may not make it due sooner than 60 days after the ordinance is adopted, and carries no penalty until the department gives you personal or written notice; the only penalty for a willful failure is a civil penalty of up to $50. Inspection fees under the ordinance are separate. (2) Short-term rentals. A locality may require operators of rentals for fewer than 30 consecutive days to register annually for a reasonable fee, with penalties of up to $500 per violation; real estate licensees and owners represented by one are among those exempt. (3) Tenant lists and license taxes. On the commissioner of the revenue's request, an owner or operator of an apartment house must file by February 1 each year a list of the names and addresses of its tenants as of January 1 (failure is a Class 4 misdemeanor), and some counties next to densely populated counties may require the same list from owners leasing houses. Localities generally may not levy a business license tax on an owner for renting residential real property, other than hotels, motels, lodging, rooming and boarding houses and similar lodging; a locality that imposed such a tax on January 1, 1974 may keep it. State filings that can apply: an individual owner who lives outside Virginia must appoint a Virginia agent, file the agent's name and office address with the State Corporation Commission, and name the agent in every lease (see Virginia Agent of Nonresident Owner); a nonresident individual, a nonresident estate or trust, a corporation not organized under Virginia law, or a partnership or S corporation with nonresident partners or shareholders that receives $600 or more in a calendar year in rent from Virginia real property must register with the Department of Taxation; the owner of an apartment house of more than two units who installs electric or gas submetering or energy allocation equipment must notify the State Corporation Commission and the utility in writing within 90 days of installation; and at or before the tenancy begins you must disclose to the tenant in writing the names and addresses of the manager and of an owner or the owner's agent (see Owner and Manager Disclosure). Fair Housing certification: the Fair Housing Board's certification regulations apply to anyone in the business of renting dwellings, which they define as owning any combination of residential units occupied by five or more families, unless the person holds a license from the Virginia Real Estate Board. To be certified you complete two hours of fair housing training approved by either Board, taken within two years before you apply; disclose any final finding by a court or agency in the last five years that you violated a fair housing law; give an address and email address; and pay a $25 nonrefundable fee. The certificate lasts two years. To renew you complete two more hours of approved training within the two years, disclose any such finding in the last two years, and pay $25; a renewal finished more than 30 days late costs a further $25, and after six months you must apply as new. The regulations do not say in so many words that an owner must hold the certificate or what happens if one does not, so the cautious course for an owner of five or more occupied units without a real estate license is to get certified and keep it renewed. See also Local Landlord-Tenant Rules and Rent Control.

title: Landlord's Remedies: Possession, Rent and Damages
bodyText: Before the lease ends: for any breach of the lease or of the tenant's statutory duties, you may recover damages and ask a court to order the tenant to stop. You are entitled to the rent, other fees and late charges the lease provides, reasonable attorney fees as the lease or the law provides, court costs once a case is filed, and damage to the home, whether or not you sue. When you win a case for a breach, the court enters a money judgment for those amounts, but not attorney fees if the tenant proves its failure to pay or leave was reasonable. After the lease ends: you may have a claim for possession and rent and a separate claim for actual damages, reasonable attorney fees and the cost of serving notices or process (no more than $12 per service), and you may enforce them in an unlawful detainer (eviction) case. Damages may include rent until the term would have ended or a new tenant's lease begins, whichever comes first, subject to your duty to mitigate; after you have possession you may not seek accelerated rent for the rest of the term (see Abandonment, Remaining Rent and the Duty to Mitigate). The court can give you possession and money together without first crediting the security deposit; you credit the deposit under the deposit rules once the tenant leaves. Courts: eviction cases are usually filed in general district court (a circuit court case is also possible), and in an eviction case that court's money limits do not apply to rent and damages claimed against anyone on the lease or its guaranty. At the first hearing you may ask for possession now and a second date, within 120 days, for final rent and damages, unless the tenant contests the amount at that hearing. If the summons asked for all amounts due as of the hearing, you may not sue later for amounts that could have been included; otherwise a possession judgment does not bar a later suit for rent or damages you did not claim. A claim for money alone goes to general district court on a warrant in debt (only that court for $4,500 or less; that court or circuit court for more than $4,500 up to $50,000), or to the small claims division for $5,000 or less, where each side represents itself, a business may appear through an owner, officer, member or employee, and the tenant may move the case to the regular district court. You may also use distress for rent (see Landlord's Lien and Distress for Rent), and holdover remedies apply if the tenant stays (see Holdover Remedies).

title: Late Fee Limit
bodyText: Virginia's late-fee limit applies to every residential lease under the Act: no late charge unless the written lease provides for it, and never more than the lesser of 10 percent of the periodic rent or 10 percent of the remaining balance due and owed by the tenant (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1204). Two other caps apply in their own settings: a late charge on a submetered or ratio-billed utility bill is capped at $5 and can't be due sooner than 15 days after the bill is mailed or delivered (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1212), and manufactured home lot rentals carry the same 10 percent cap in their own Act (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1302). After a foreclosure sale, a tenant with no managing agent named in the lease can't be charged a late fee until the new owner says in writing where to pay (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1237). A late charge within the lease and the law can be recovered from the deposit and claimed in an eviction case. The full rules are in Late Fees in Virginia, and the lease clause is the library's Virginia Late Fee clause.

title: Police, Investigators and Reporting Duties
bodyText: Virginia has no crime-free lease or crime-free housing statute, and no rule requiring you, as a landlord, to answer police or child-protection investigators' questions about tenants or to let them into a unit without a warrant, a court order or the tenant's consent. A lease can still make criminal activity a breach (see Criminal and Drug Activity), and a criminal or willful act that threatens health or safety allows immediate termination. What the law does say: you may release information about a tenant to a law-enforcement or public safety official acting in the line of duty (it is one of the listed exceptions to tenant-record confidentiality, so it is allowed, not required; see Tenant Records and Confidentiality). A court order for a wiretap, pen register or trap-and-trace device can direct a landlord to give police the information, facilities and technical help needed, and the state pays your reasonable costs. Where your locality has adopted a criminal-blight ordinance, it can require you, after an affidavit and written notice, to take corrective action against regular drug activity, commercial sex or illegal gunfire at the property. Your interest in property used in a tenant's crime cannot be forfeited if you did not know and had no reason to know of the tenant's conduct. Reporting duties that bind everyone, landlords included: if you find a tenant who died from violence, injury, accident or suicide, suddenly while in apparent good health, or without a physician in attendance, the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner must be notified, and any person with knowledge of the death may need to make that call; anyone who knows of an animal suspected to be rabid that may have exposed a person or animal must report it immediately to the local health department. Landlords are not on the lists of people who must report suspected child or adult abuse (unless they also serve in a listed role, such as paid child care), but anyone may report. Virginia also has no rule protecting a tenant who calls the police (see No Right-to-Call-Police Statute); for barring an unwelcome guest, see Trespass Warnings and Barring Persons.

title: No Lead-Safe Certificate
bodyText: Virginia has no lead-safe or lead-free certificate for rental units: no certificate you must obtain, attach to the lease as an exhibit or file with a registry, and no state inspection program that issues one. What exists instead: lead inspections, lead risk assessments, abatement and abatement clearance testing must be done by people licensed by the Virginia Board for Asbestos, Lead, and Home Inspectors, and a licensed inspector's or risk assessor's written report records what was tested and found. An owner may do lead inspection, risk assessment or abatement work in a home the owner owns without a license only when no one other than the owner's immediate family occupies it during the work and no child with an elevated blood lead level lives there, so that exemption does not cover a unit occupied by tenants. Federally assisted housing that complies with HUD's Lead-Safe Housing Rule is treated as meeting Virginia's lead licensing regulations. If you have a lead inspection, risk assessment or clearance report, the federal disclosure requires you to list it and give it to the tenant before the lease is signed. See Virginia Lead Notices Beyond the Federal Disclosure and Lead-Based Paint Disclosure.

title: Virginia Lead Notices Beyond the Federal Disclosure
bodyText: Virginia has no state lead notice, pamphlet or packet of its own that you must hand a tenant with the lease. For housing built before 1978, the federal lead disclosure is the required lease paperwork: a Lead Warning Statement, your disclosure of known lead-based paint and hazards, a list of available records and reports, the tenant's acknowledgment of the information and the federal pamphlet, and signatures, kept for at least three years (see Lead-Based Paint Disclosure). Virginia adds four things. First, if a real estate licensee is leasing the property for you, the licensee must tell prospective tenants in writing about any pipe, plumbing fitting, fixture, solder or flux the licensee actually knows does not meet the federal Safe Drinking Water Act definition of lead free, along with other known material adverse facts about the property's physical condition. Second, owners and agents who give the federal pamphlet and disclosure and get the tenant's signed acknowledgment before an initial lease, keep painted surfaces maintained under the Maintenance Code, and keep disclosing new lead information during the tenancy (an agent must do so in writing, with a summary and an offer to let the tenant inspect and copy the full reports) are protected from personal injury and wrongful death damages for lead poisoning. Third, the Maintenance Code requires painted surfaces with lead at or above the regulated level to be kept free of peeling, chipping and flaking paint, or removed or covered in an approved way, and a surface that is covered must first be marked with an approved warning about its lead content. Fourth, if you fail to maintain painted surfaces as that code requires the tenant may end the lease, and terminating or retaliating after a tenant's written notice of a lead hazard or of a child's elevated blood lead level is unlawful retaliation. Lead paint you have notice of is also a ground for a tenant's rent escrow case. See Lead-Based Paint.

title: What a Virginia Lease Must Contain
bodyText: Virginia requires few specific items in the lease document itself. You must offer a written lease containing the terms of the rental, and give with it the state Statement of Tenant Rights and Responsibilities and its signed acknowledgment form (separate documents); the lease takes effect on the date the parties sign it, and the tenant must get a copy of the signed lease within 10 business days (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1204). Required in the lease text: the fee itemization, beginning on the first page, of the security deposit, the rent for each payment period and any one-time charges due before or with the first payment, under the statutory sentence that no additional deposits or rent will be charged unless listed or added by separate addendum (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1204.1); and, for a nonresident individual owner, the name and Virginia office address of the owner's agent for service (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1211). Required in the lease if you want the term: late charges (up to the lesser of 10 percent of the periodic rent or of the remaining balance), electronic notices, submetering or ratio utility billing, a showing-refusal remedy, copy charges for extra tenant records, expedited deposit disposition, a holdover liquidated amount, the lead-paint rule that the tenant must get your written approval before painting or alterations in pre-1978 housing, and notice of extended absences. Virginia does not require the start and end dates, or anything other than the fee itemization, on the first page, and prescribes no form of lease. Other disclosures (owner and manager, renter's insurance and flood, military air zones, drywall, methamphetamine, lead paint) must be given in writing but need not be lease clauses; see the guidance on required disclosures. A lease for more than a year must be in writing and signed to be enforced (Va. Code Ann. § 11-2).

title: Giving the Tenant a Copy of the Lease
bodyText: Give the tenant a copy of the signed lease, together with the state Statement of Tenant Rights and Responsibilities, within 10 business days after the lease takes effect (the date both parties sign it). Missing that deadline does not make the lease invalid, but you may not file or keep up any court action against the tenant for a lease violation, including an eviction (unlawful detainer) case, until you have given the tenant the Statement. After that, on the tenant's request you must give one additional paper copy of the lease a year, or keep the lease in an electronic form the tenant can easily reach or share on request; an additional electronic copy is free. If a real estate licensee handles the rental, the licensee must also promptly deliver complete, legible copies of the lease to each principal to the transaction. The library's Statement of Tenant Rights and Responsibilities clause carries the copy promise into the lease. Copies of the tenant's other records are a separate rule (see Tenant Records and Confidentiality).

title: No Lease Initials Requirement
bodyText: No Virginia statute requires a tenant to initial particular lease clauses, or makes a clause enforceable only if it is initialed or separately signed. The tenant's signature on the lease is enough, and even an unsigned lease takes effect if the tenant accepts possession or pays rent without reservation (or, for your signature, if you accept rent without reservation), though only for one year if it states a longer term. The separate signatures and writings Virginia does require are these: both parties sign the state's form acknowledging that the tenant received the Statement of Tenant Rights and Responsibilities (if the tenant will not sign it, record the dates you gave it and that the tenant did not sign); a tenant who wants expedited security deposit processing under a lease that provides for it asks in a separate written document; and a notice ending tenancies to rehabilitate or change the use of a multifamily building with at least four units must be a separate writing, not part of the lease. Initials never rescue a term the Act forbids: a lease term waiving the tenant's rights or remedies under the Act is unenforceable however it is signed. Initials beside key terms (late fees, a longer notice period, automatic renewal) are optional evidence that the tenant saw them, not a Virginia requirement.

title: Recording a Lease
bodyText: Virginia does not require a residential lease to be registered or recorded, and recording does not change the tenant's rights or your duties under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act. Recording does matter against later buyers and lenders. A written contract, or a deed conveying any estate or term, is void as to purchasers for value without notice and lien creditors until it is recorded in the land records of the county or city where the property lies, and the tenant's mere possession is not, by itself, notice to a buyer. Instead of recording the whole lease, you and the tenant may record a memorandum of lease signed as a deed would be, giving the parties' names and addresses, the date, the property, and the term and any renewal or extension rights. Recording a lease or memorandum carries a recordation tax based on the rent over the term (or the property's value if that is lower). For an ordinary residential tenancy the Act gives the tenant protections that do not depend on recording: a buyer of the property is bound to return the security deposit, you must tell the tenant of a sale and the new owner's name, address and telephone number, and a buyer at a foreclosure sale of a single-family residence must either honor the lease or, if moving in, give at least 90 days' written notice (see Selling or Losing a Rented Property). Recording mainly matters for a long lease or one with an option to purchase, where the tenant's interest needs protection against a later buyer or lender; a lease option or rent-to-own contract for a home the buyer lives in may be recorded in the land records of the circuit court clerk where the property lies. A lease for more than one year must be in writing and signed to be enforced, and an unwritten contract for a term of more than five years is void as to purchasers for value without notice and creditors.

title: Lease Length and Signing Formalities
bodyText: Virginia sets no maximum term for a private residential lease, and no statute requires a spouse's consent or signature, a seal, a notary's acknowledgment or a deed for a lease to be valid. A written lease that conveys a leasehold is not invalid because it is not in the form of a deed. The length of the lease does change three things. A lease for more than one year cannot be enforced in court unless it, or a memorandum of it, is in writing and signed by the person it is enforced against. An unwritten contract for a term of more than five years is void as to later buyers for value without notice and creditors. And if one side never signs and delivers the written lease but the lease takes effect anyway because rent or possession was accepted without reservation, a lease written for longer than one year is effective for only one year. If you offer no written lease at all, the law creates a 12-month tenancy that does not renew automatically. A recorded lease or memorandum protects a long lease against later buyers and lenders; recording is optional (see Recording a Lease). Public bodies leasing their own property have their own term limits; those do not apply to private landlords.

title: No Rule Equalizing Month-to-Month and Fixed-Term Leases
bodyText: Virginia has no rule requiring a month-to-month or week-to-week tenancy to carry the same terms as a fixed-term lease, and no cap on the difference in rent between lease types. You may price and structure a month-to-month lease differently from a one-year lease, subject to the rules that apply to every lease: no term the Act prohibits, every rent and deposit charge in the first-page fee list, and fair housing law. What the Act does set for periodic tenancies is notice: either side may end a week-to-week tenancy with written notice at least seven days before the next rent due date, and a month-to-month tenancy with written notice at least 30 days before the next rent due date unless the lease sets a different period; a holdover or month-to-month tenancy that follows a lease keeps the old lease terms except for a new rent set by written notice. A same-terms rule does exist for manufactured home lot rentals: the landlord must offer year-round residents a lease of at least one year on the same terms as shorter leases, except for discounts for the longer lease. That rule is in the Manufactured Home Lot Rental Act and does not apply to dwelling leases.

title: No Minimum Type Size for Leases
bodyText: Virginia sets no minimum type size for a residential lease, and no rule makes a lease, or a clause in it, unenforceable or inadmissible because of small print. The type and placement rules that do touch a lease are narrow: the itemized list of the security deposit, rent per period and one-time charges must begin on the first page, under the statutory sentence; the state's Statement of Tenant Rights and Responsibilities you give with the lease is printed by the state in at least 14-point type; and a termination notice to a public housing tenant, or from a private landlord to a tenant with a housing voucher or other tenant-based rental assistance, must show legal aid contact information on its first page in type no smaller or less legible than the rest of the notice. Older type-size rules for printed sales contracts for goods, consumer credit and time-shares do not reach a dwelling lease, and the bold-type flood statement for manufactured home lot leases applies only to lot rentals. Readable type remains good practice (see No Font-Size or Single-Family Occupancy Disclosure Rule for the full list of layout rules).

title: Time Limits for Rent and Damage Claims
bodyText: Virginia's general time limits apply to landlord-tenant claims; the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act sets none of its own for suits over rent or damages. A claim on a written lease signed by the party you sue (for unpaid rent, damages or fees) must be filed within five years after the breach; on an oral lease, or a written one that person did not sign, within three years. A claim for damage to the property is also five years. A distress for rent must be brought within five years after the rent came due. An unlawful detainer (eviction) filed in circuit court by motion for judgment must be brought within three years after the unlawful entry or detainer. A judgment dated on or after July 1, 2021 can be enforced for 10 years (20 for older judgments), and the period can be extended by recording a certificate before it runs out. The time runs from the breach, not from when you discover the loss. A written, signed promise to pay, or a written acknowledgment from which a promise to pay can be implied, starts a new period for the amount promised. Virginia's limitation statutes say nothing about partial payments of rent, so do not count on a payment alone to restart the clock; get a signed written acknowledgment of the balance. A promise by one co-tenant does not extend the time against another co-tenant who would otherwise be protected. A written promise not to plead the time limit binds only if it is signed, made to put off a suit pending settlement, and the suit is filed within the limit counted from that promise (or any shorter time it sets); separately, if refusing to enforce a promise not to plead, written or not, would be a fraud on the person it was made to, the person who made it cannot plead the time limit. The tenant's claims against you on the lease fall under the same contract periods. Whether a tenant's claim under the Act itself, such as a security deposit claim, is a contract claim or a personal action with a two-year limit is not settled; the cautious course is to keep deposit records for at least five years after the tenancy ends.

title: Liquidated Damages in Virginia Leases
bodyText: Virginia has no general statute on liquidated damages in a residential lease. The Residential Landlord and Tenant Act deals with them in three places. Holdover: the lease may include a reasonable liquidated amount, not more than 150 percent of the per diem of the monthly rent (the per diem itself for public housing or other HUD-regulated housing), for each day the tenant stays after the termination date in your notice; the library's optional holdover clause does this (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1253). Statutory early terminations: when a servicemember, or a victim of family abuse, sexual abuse, stalking or trafficking, ends the lease under the Act, you may not charge any liquidated damages (Va. Code Ann. §§ 55.1-1235, 55.1-1236). Everything else: after the lease ends for the tenant's breach you recover actual damages, which may include rent until the term ends or a new tenancy starts, whichever is first, with your duty to mitigate and no accelerated rent (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1251). Outside the Act, Virginia's only statutory tests for agreed damages are in the Uniform Commercial Code for sales and leases of goods and in the computer-information statute; they do not govern a lease of a home. Whether any other fixed charge for a tenant's breach is a valid liquidated amount or an unenforceable penalty is a question of case law. The risk is real: the Consumer Protection Act makes it a prohibited practice to use in a lease a liquidated damage or penalty clause that is void or unenforceable, or to try to collect under one, and a tenant who suffers a loss may recover actual damages or $500, whichever is greater (up to three times actual damages or $1,000, whichever is greater, if willful), plus attorney fees (Va. Code Ann. §§ 59.1-200, 59.1-204). Apart from the holdover amount, charge actual, documented losses rather than a fixed sum for breach.

title: No Lockout for Unpaid Rent
bodyText: Virginia gives landlords no right to lock out a tenant for unpaid rent, and a lease can't create one. You may not take possession by cutting off an essential service or by refusing the tenant access to the unit unless a court has ordered possession (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1252). A tenant who is willfully removed or excluded without court authority can get a court order restoring possession within days and, at a full hearing, recovers actual damages, statutory damages of $5,000 or four months' rent, whichever is greater, and attorney fees; the court may also end the lease and order the whole deposit returned (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1243.1). For unpaid rent, use the 14-day nonpayment notice and an unlawful detainer case. Self-help is allowed only outside the Act: for a guest in transient lodging who has lived there as a primary residence for 90 consecutive days or less, after a five-day written nonpayment notice, and in commercial tenancies without a breach of the peace (Va. Code Ann. §§ 55.1-1201, 55.1-1400). The full rule is in No Self-Help Eviction.

title: Shifting Maintenance Work to the Tenant
bodyText: You and the tenant may agree in writing that the tenant will perform some of your duties: keeping common areas shared by two or more units clean and structurally safe, providing waste receptacles and arranging waste removal, and supplying running water, hot water, heat or air conditioning, plus specified repairs, maintenance tasks, alterations and remodeling. The agreement is valid only if made in good faith, not for the purpose of evading your obligations, and only if it does not diminish or affect your obligations to other tenants (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1220). It must be in writing, but the Act does not require a document separate from the lease or any particular consideration (rent credit or otherwise), and it does not let the agreement reach your duties to comply with health and safety codes or to keep the home fit and habitable; those stay with you. List the work specifically. Shifting the work is different from charging for it: unless the tenant's violation of the Act made it necessary, you may not require the tenant to pay any fee for maintenance or repair (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1208). The tenant's own statutory duties (cleanliness, waste, plumbing fixtures, reasonable use of facilities, no damage, smoke and carbon monoxide alarms, moisture and mold, pests) apply without any agreement. Use the library's optional tenant-repair agreement for the shift.

title: Energy Savings Charges on the Bill, and Submetered Water
bodyText: Energy savings charges. Virginia lets an electric cooperative run an on-bill program: energy efficiency work (heating and cooling systems, water heaters, insulation, windows, appliances) is installed with no upfront payment and repaid through an energy savings charge shown as a separate line on the electric bill. The charge can stay with the meter: the cooperative may bill it to later customers at the same premises, and the participating customer must notify the next customer of the agreement and the charge. Unpaid energy savings charges count as unpaid electric service and can lead to disconnection. So if you signed up and a tenant will be the cooperative's customer, tell the tenant in writing before the lease is signed (the library's optional Energy Savings Charge clause does this). If a tenant signed up and is moving out, the charge may pass to the next customer, so ask about it at move-out. Virginia has no rent-deduction remedy or other penalty in its statutes for a missed notice; complaints go to the State Corporation Commission. The statute covers cooperatives only; other utilities' efficiency programs are set by Commission orders and tariffs this library has not reviewed. Submetered water. You may submeter or ratio-bill water and sewer only if the lease clearly says so. To stay outside utility regulation you may charge each tenant only the part of your water and sewer bill that comes from that tenant's use, plus the billing service charges the lease allows (actual third-party billing costs) and a late charge of up to $5, and you must keep three years of billing records. Bill for the same period the utility bills you unless the lease says otherwise. For water, Virginia does not require a monthly statement showing both meter readings (the Commission's rules require beginning and ending readings on bills only for submetered electricity and gas), but the tenant may inspect and copy your billing records, and from July 1, 2027 a statement of charges you give on written request must disclose the allocation method and itemize utility debits and credits (landlords with fewer than four Virginia rental units are exempt from that statement rule unless they receive state or local rental or utility assistance funds on the tenant's behalf). No statute lets you add a separate surcharge for a water submeter to the usage bill; recover equipment costs through the rent. See Utilities Billed by Landlord (Submetering, Allocation or Ratio Billing).

title: Minors as Tenants and in Eviction Cases
bodyText: In Virginia a person becomes an adult at 18. The Residential Landlord and Tenant Act has no rule about minors as tenants or as eviction defendants, and no statute lets a person under 18 make a binding lease, with one exception: a minor emancipated by court order may make binding contracts, set up his or her own residence, and sue and be sued in his or her own name. Otherwise a lease signed by a minor is open to a defense of infancy, and a promise made after turning 18 to pay a debt contracted as a minor, or a ratification of a minor's contract, can be enforced only if it is in a signed writing. If you sue a minor, including in an unlawful detainer (eviction) case, the case is not stayed, but the court must appoint a guardian ad litem for the minor unless an attorney has appeared for the minor and the court does not require one. A minor who sues you does so through a next friend, usually a parent. The practical course: have an adult sign the lease as tenant (or, for an emancipated minor, keep a copy of the court order), treat minor children in the household as authorized occupants rather than tenants, and do not refuse or limit rentals to families with children, which fair housing law protects (see Children and Occupancy Limits).

title: Local Utility Liens for a Tenant's Unpaid Bills
bodyText: Water and sewer from a locality or water and sewer authority. The provider serves your tenant directly once you give it a written or electronic authorization (a short letter naming the tenant and the property) or a copy of the lease. It may then not require the service to be in your name (unless one meter serves more than one unit) or require a deposit or guarantee from you. To keep lien rights against your property it must collect a deposit from the tenant of three to five months of charges; if it takes no deposit, it waives its lien rights against you (but a tenant with need-based rental assistance who brings your authorization letter owes no deposit and the lien rights remain). Before it contacts you or liens your property it must use reasonable collection efforts against the tenant: apply the tenant's deposit, and refer the debt to the state setoff program or a collection agency. Any lien is limited to three months of the tenant's delinquent charges, requires at least 30 days' written notice to you with a copy of the bill before it is recorded, and ranks with real estate taxes; it does not bind a buyer without notice until it is recorded. If you pay a recorded lien you step into the provider's shoes against the former tenant. Unless a lien has been recorded, a new tenant may not be refused service because a former tenant left a balance. On request the provider must give you information about a current or former tenant, and if you ask and give an email address it must tell you when the tenant's bill is 15 days delinquent. Before shutting off service it gives the tenant 10 business days' written notice, with a copy to you. Older lien ordinances in some listed counties, cities and towns may not attach a lien to residential rental property unless you were the user or you arranged the service. Municipal gas: the same rental exception applies, and if the lease says the tenant contracts for the gas service, the locality may not require it to be in your name. Other local charges: charges for a locality's revenue-producing services (which include garbage and refuse collection) become a lien on the property ahead of the owner, with no rental exception in that statute, and a county may put its solid waste disposal fee on your real estate tax bill. Plan for this in the lease: use the optional Tenant Utility Accounts clause, and see Utility Deposits and Final Utility Bills for holding back part of the deposit for a final water bill.

title: The Notice for Unpaid Rent
bodyText: To end a Virginia lease for unpaid rent, serve a written notice telling the tenant the rent is unpaid and that you will end the lease if it is not paid within 14 days. If the tenant does not pay within the 14 days, you may end the lease and file for possession. For a bounced check, a rejected electronic payment or a bad-faith stop-payment, the notice says the rent must be paid by cash, cashier's check, certified check or a completed electronic transfer within the 14 days; to claim bad-check costs and fees in the eviction case, give that notice too, and it may go in the 14-day notice. Wording you must use or include: if you may accept partial payments and still evict, give written notice that all payments will be accepted with reservation, using the exact paragraph the statute supplies (it begins: Any partial payment of rent made before or after a judgment of possession is ordered will not prevent your landlord from taking action to evict you); it may go in the 14-day notice, and you give the court a copy to serve with the summons. The state housing department posts a sample termination notice with that language. A notice to a tenant using a housing voucher or other rental assistance has no effect unless its first page shows the statewide legal aid phone number and website; a public housing authority's notice must show the local legal aid program on page one and come with income-recertification information on pink or orange paper. From July 1, 2027, a nonpayment notice has no effect unless it includes a written statement of the charges and payments over the tenancy or the past 12 months, whichever is shorter, and the late charges, attorney fees, costs and other charges owed (with utility debits and credits if you bill utilities by submeter, allocation or ratio). Also from that date, a landlord with more than four Virginia rental units (or more than a 10 percent interest in more than four) whose tenant owes no more than one month's rent plus late charges must give a notice of the exact amount owed and offer a payment plan in equal monthly installments over six months or the rest of the lease, whichever is less, before ending the lease; the offer is owed once per lease term. The lease cannot serve as the notice, waive it or shorten the 14 days, and Virginia has no shorter period for small landlords or particular property types. Deliver the notice by regular mail or hand delivery, keeping a certificate of service, or electronically if the lease provides for it. The notice statutes add no days for mailing (the court rules that add three days cover court papers), so the cautious course is to count the 14 days from when the tenant will receive it. After you file, the tenant can still redeem by paying everything owed (see The Tenant's Right of Redemption). If the property has a federally backed mortgage or is in a covered federal program, federal law also requires a 30-day notice to vacate (see Federal 30-Day Notice to Vacate for Federally Backed Properties). For the other default notices, see Termination Notices for Tenant Default; for fees for serving notices, see Charging for Serving Notices.

title: Nonrefundable Fees and Deposits
bodyText: In Virginia a security deposit is by definition refundable, and the two-month cap reaches a deposit however it is labelled, so money that secures the tenant's performance or covers damage can't be made nonrefundable by calling it a fee (Va. Code Ann. §§ 55.1-1200, 55.1-1226). A true nonrefundable fee, such as a pet fee or amenity fee, is allowed: Virginia sets no cap on it (the application fee is capped at $50 plus third-party screening costs, and late charges and the bad-check fee have their own caps; see edu-statutory-caps-va) and requires no special notice. But three rules shape it. It is rent, because rent means all money other than a security deposit owed under the lease, so it must be listed on the first-page fee disclosure or added by a later addendum (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1204.1). You may not require a fee for maintenance or repair of the unit unless the tenant's violation of the Act made it necessary, so a flat nonrefundable cleaning, carpet, painting or turnover fee is the risky course (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1208). And no pet fee, deposit or extra rent may be charged for an assistance animal (Va. Code Ann. § 36-96.3:1). The library's Nonrefundable Fees clause lets you list the fees you charge.

title: No Separate Notice for Nonrefundable Fees
bodyText: Virginia does not require a separate written notice, signed acknowledgment or special type size for a nonrefundable fee. What it does require is that every deposit and every charge that counts as rent, including any nonrefundable fee, appear in the itemized fee disclosure that begins on the first page of the lease, under the statutory sentence that nothing else will be charged unless listed there or added by a later addendum (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1204.1). The only separate written document the deposit law asks for is the tenant's own request for expedited deposit processing, which lets you charge an administrative fee if the lease provides for it (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1226). From July 1, 2027, applicants must also be told in writing or by posting, before you take any payment, which application fees and deposits are refundable (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1203). See Nonrefundable Fees and Deposits for what such a fee may cover.

title: Charging for Serving Notices
bodyText: Virginia caps what you can recover from a tenant for serving notices and process. The sheriff may deliver a termination or noncompliance notice for you, for a fee of up to $12 (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1247). After the lease ends, you may claim the cost of serving any such notice, or process, by a sheriff or private process server, but that cost may not exceed the same $12 (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1251). Costs of the court proceeding (filing fees and the like) are recoverable as the lease provides or the law allows, but only once a court action has been filed (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1245). No Virginia statute authorizes a separate flat "notice fee" or "posting fee" for preparing or delivering a notice. Because the Act sets the service cost and limits attorney fees and costs to what it allows, and because a fixed charge above your actual cost risks being treated as a penalty, the cautious course is to charge only the actual cost of service, up to $12 per service, and to recover any attorney's charge for preparing a notice only as reasonable attorney fees under the lease. See the guidance on attorney fees and on collection fees.

title: Termination Notices a Lease Cannot Waive
bodyText: A Virginia lease cannot waive or shorten the notices the Act requires before you end a tenancy for the tenant's breach: 14 days to pay unpaid rent; 21 days to cure a remediable breach, with termination at least 30 days after receipt; 30 days for a breach that cannot be remedied or a repeat of a cured breach; and the immediate route only for a criminal or willful act that cannot be remedied and threatens health or safety (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1245). Those notices are tenant rights under the Act, and a lease may not make the tenant waive them (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1208). The court will not enter an order of possession unless a proper termination notice is in evidence. The one notice the lease may change is the notice to end a month-to-month tenancy: the 30-day period applies unless the lease provides a different notice period (Va. Code Ann. §§ 55.1-1204, 55.1-1253). The library's periodic-tenancy clause lets you state a different period that applies to both sides; keep the week-to-week seven-day period unless you have legal advice, since the Act ties the different-period wording to month-to-month tenancies in one section and to terminations generally in the other. Notices that cannot be shortened include the 60-day notice for a multifamily owner declining to renew a large share of month-to-month tenancies, the 120-day conversion or rehabilitation notice (except for a month-to-month tenancy, which may be ended on 30 days' notice), and, for a landlord with more than four units, the renewal and rent-increase notices. Rows on termination notices and periodic tenancies give the details.

title: Move-Out Forms and the Notice Period
bodyText: Virginia has no rule on a move-out or notice-to-vacate form you ask a tenant to sign, no required warning when such a form adds terms the lease does not contain, and no general ban on alterations or renovation while a notice to vacate is running. The lease stays in force until the tenancy ends, so the usual rules govern the notice period. A form that adds terms is a change to the lease, and no one-sided change is valid unless notice is given as the lease or the law requires and both parties consent in writing; a term in it waiving the tenant's rights or remedies under the Act is unenforceable. Keep a move-out form to the move-out date, the return of keys and a forwarding address. Within five days after the tenant tells you he intends to vacate, give written notice of the tenant's right to be present at the move-out inspection; a notice confirming the vacating date can also tell the tenant you may hold back part of the deposit for an unpaid utility account. During the notice period your duty to keep the unit fit continues, entry needs notice and must be at reasonable times, and you may not retaliate. Willfully interrupting an essential service or doing anything to make the premises unsafe for habitation lets the tenant get a court order within days, plus actual damages, statutory damages of $5,000 or four months' rent (whichever is greater) and attorney fees. Renovations that need the unit empty belong after move-out; a nonemergency repair that requires the tenant to leave temporarily needs at least 30 days' written notice and a comparable unit or hotel at your cost. One special rule: when a building is converted to a cooperative, no tenant may be required to vacate on less than 120 days' notice (except for nonpayment, waste or disturbing other tenants), the terms of the tenancy may not be altered during that period, and the declarant's access is limited.

title: Nuisance Laws and Tenant Crime
bodyText: Virginia's nuisance laws can reach you as the owner when a tenant uses the property for crime. Drug premises: a dwelling house, apartment or other building that, with the knowledge of the owner, lessor, lessor's agent, manager or tenant, is frequented by people under the influence of illegal drugs or used to obtain, make, possess or sell them is a common nuisance; an owner, lessor, agent or tenant who knowingly permits or maintains it commits a Class 1 misdemeanor, and a Class 6 felony on a second offense. (Until July 1, 2027 the section also covers marijuana.) The Commonwealth's attorney or any citizen of the locality may sue to enjoin the nuisance, and a temporary injunction can bind owners and tenants. After a conviction, a court may order the premises closed, but only after notice and a hearing for an owner or lessor not involved in the offense, and no judgment may be entered against an owner or lessor unless it is proved that they knew of the unlawful use and had the right, because of it, to enter and repossess; an owner may get the premises back by posting bond that they will not be used unlawfully. Prostitution and criminal street gang activity: knowingly owning, leasing or maintaining a building used for these is a nuisance; the Commonwealth's attorney, the Attorney General or (except for gang suits) any responsible citizen may sue to enjoin it, naming the owner or agent, and a court that finds a nuisance may order the building closed for a year unless the owner pays the costs and posts bond to abate it. Criminal blight: a locality may by ordinance require an owner to take corrective action against regular drug, prostitution or illegal-firearm activity on the property after notice and 30 days, or do the work itself and charge it as a lien; an owner who in good faith takes corrective action, or who starts and pursues a court action to remedy or end the tenancy of a tenant causing the blight, is treated as complying. Localities may also abate unsafe or unsanitary buildings and other public nuisances and charge the owner or occupant. Your remedies: illegal drug activity or another criminal or willful act threatening health or safety by the tenant, an occupant or a guest is an immediate nonremediable breach, so you may terminate at once and seek possession without waiting for a conviction. The tenant must also keep guests from disturbing neighbors' peaceful enjoyment (see No Disturbance or Nuisance).

title: Optional Lease Terms in Virginia
bodyText: A Virginia lease may include any term not prohibited by the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act or other law, including the rent, late charges, the length of the term, automatic renewal, the notice required to vacate or end the lease, and other provisions on the parties' rights and obligations (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1204). Some landlord rights exist only if the lease includes them, so leaving them out gives them up: late charges; electronic notices; submetering or ratio utility billing; charges for extra copies of tenant records; damages, costs and fees for an unjustified refusal of a showing; expedited deposit disposition for a fee; a holdover liquidated amount; a different notice period for ending a month-to-month tenancy; the lead-paint approval rule for painting or alterations in pre-1978 housing; and recovery of damages for an unreported absence of more than seven days. The library offers these as clauses where they serve you. An option to purchase changes the transaction. A lease with an option to buy residential property of one to four units is a transfer covered by the Virginia Residential Property Disclosure Act, so the owner must deliver that Act's disclosures before the contract is ratified, or the tenant-buyer may terminate within the Act's short periods (Va. Code Ann. §§ 55.1-701, 55.1-709). And a lease-option or rent-to-own contract under which the buyer occupies the home as a primary residence is a residential executory real estate contract: the Landlord and Tenant Act still applies; the buyer may exercise the option early without a fee or penalty; for a default in rent or other money only, you may end the lease only if it stays unpaid more than 30 days after a notice stating the amount and your intent; you may not forfeit the option payment (you may apply it to amounts owed); and the prevailing party may be awarded attorney fees. These rules cannot be waived. They do not apply to a vendor who owns no more than two single-family homes in Virginia (unless affiliated with an owner of another unit), a real estate licensee, or a bank or licensed mortgage lender (Va. Code Ann. §§ 55.1-3000 to 55.1-3002). The library does not offer an option-to-purchase clause for Virginia.

title: Ordnance, Demolition and Shared-Meter Disclosures
bodyText: This topic bundles three California disclosures; Virginia has the second in its own form and not the other two. Former ordnance locations: Virginia has no rule requiring you to tell a tenant that the property is near a former military ordnance or munitions site. The nearest Virginia disclosure is the one for property in a military air installation's noise or accident potential zone (see that clause). Demolition: in a multifamily building, if there is an existing plan, to take effect within six months, to displace tenants because of demolition or substantial rehabilitation (or conversion to office, hotel or motel use or a planned unit development), or an application to register the property as a condominium or cooperative has been filed, you must tell any prospective tenant in writing. The library's Owner and Manager Disclosure clause has a place for it; give it before the applicant signs. To end leases in a building of four or more residential units for demolition, rehabilitation or another change in use, you must give 120 days' written notice in a separate writing, not in the lease, and a lease cannot waive that notice except for a month-to-month tenancy (30 days' notice). A public housing authority planning a demolition application to HUD has its own six-month notice to tenants and to prospective tenants before they sign. Shared meters: Virginia has no rule requiring you to disclose that a tenant's own meter also measures service to common areas or other units. What it does say: billing tenants for shared-meter utilities needs a clear lease statement and an allocation method, and electricity or gas for owner-paid areas such as halls and laundry rooms is recovered through the rent, not a tenant's usage bill; in a building with electric or gas submeters or energy allocation equipment, the State Corporation Commission's rules also bar measuring owner-paid areas through a unit's equipment. If a tenant's meter serves anything outside the unit, the cautious course is to separate the circuit or disclose it in the lease and adjust the bill. See Owner and Manager Disclosure, Periodic Tenancies and Mass Nonrenewals, and Utilities Billed by Landlord.

title: Building Facilities You Supply
bodyText: Virginia has no statute on particular building facilities such as automatic garage door openers, gates, intercoms, mailboxes, window screens or shared laundry machines. They fall under the general duty: you must keep in good and safe working order all electrical, plumbing, sanitary, heating, ventilating, air-conditioning and other facilities and appliances, including elevators, that you supply or are required to supply, comply with building and housing codes that materially affect health and safety, and keep common areas of a multifamily building clean and structurally safe. A "facility" is anything built, installed or established to perform a particular function, and the premises include facilities held out for tenants' general use or promised to the tenant. So list in the lease what you supply and what you do not (see Items Not Supplied by Landlord): once you supply a facility, you must maintain it. You may adopt reasonable rules for shared facilities, for example laundry hours, if they apply fairly to all tenants and the tenant gets a copy; a rule adopted later that substantially changes the tenant's bargain needs the tenant's written consent. You and the tenant may agree in writing, in good faith, that the tenant will handle common-area cleaning, trash and water or heat supply duties and specified repairs, but not in a way that reduces your duties to other tenants. Your liability for failing these duties is for the tenant's actual damages caused by your failure to use ordinary care.

title: Parking Rules, Towing Notices and Vehicle Information
bodyText: Virginia has no separate parking-rules notice law. It prescribes no heading or format for parking rules, does not limit the vehicle information you may ask for, and does not tie a parking permit to the lease term. Parking rules are governed by the general rules-and-regulations law: a rule binds a tenant only if it serves the tenants' convenience, safety or welfare, protects the property or fairly distributes facilities, is reasonably related to that purpose, applies fairly to all tenants, is explicit, is not meant to evade your own obligations, and the tenant got a copy at signing or when it was adopted. A rule adopted or changed during the lease binds the tenant on reasonable notice if it is not a substantial modification of the bargain; a substantial change (taking away a space, adding a charge) needs the tenant's written consent, and no lease term may be changed unilaterally. So attach the parking rules to the lease and get the tenant's signed acknowledgment. Towing rules that reach tenants: you may tow a vehicle parked without permission only if signs at every entrance clearly say unauthorized vehicles will be towed and give the police nonemergency number or the tow operator's number (unless a local towing ordinance applies instead). In an apartment or townhome lot you own and maintain, a resident's vehicle that you know is associated with the resident by permit, registry or other identification, and that meets the lease's vehicle requirements, may not be towed for an expired registration or inspection sticker until 48 hours after the towing operator posts a dated written notice on it; the operator must send you a copy and repays the towing and storage charges if it skips the notice. Vehicle information: tenant information you hold may be released only with the tenant's prior written consent or under a listed exception. If the property is in a homeowners' or condominium association, the association may require you to give it the tenants' names, contact and vehicle information, so get the tenant's written consent in the lease. See Rules and Regulations and Towing From Rental Property.

title: Rights a Virginia Lease Cannot Waive
bodyText: Virginia's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act has one general rule for waivers: a lease may not make the tenant agree to waive or give up rights or remedies under the Act. The same section lists seven more terms a lease may not contain: a waiver of the 120-day notice for a condominium or cooperative conversion or rehabilitation; a confession of judgment; an agreement to pay your attorney fees except as the Act provides; a release or limit of your liability to the tenant arising under law, or an indemnity for it; in public housing, a firearm ban unless federal law requires it; prepaid deposit and insurance premiums above two months' rent; and a waiver of Servicemembers Civil Relief Act rights before a dispute arises (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1208). A prohibited term is unenforceable. Putting one in the lease carries no penalty by itself, but if you bring an action to enforce it, the tenant may recover actual damages and reasonable attorney fees. No locality, board or court may waive or change the Act either (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1201). A lease can change a rule of the Act only where the Act itself says so, and these are the main openings: a different notice period for ending a month-to-month tenancy; electronic notices; damages, costs and fees for a tenant's unjustified refusal of a showing; a written agreement that the tenant will do some of your duties and specified repairs; a deposit refund other than by one check to all tenants, if every tenant agrees in writing; an expedited deposit disposition for a fee, if the tenant asks in a separate writing; a charge for extra copies of tenant records; submetering or ratio utility billing; a holdover liquidated amount within the statutory cap; and use of the home for something other than a residence. A clause outside those openings that takes away a tenant's right under the Act does not hold, however it is worded. The rows on individual waivers (habitability, notices, showings, deposits, casualty and mitigation, exculpation, jury trial, confession of judgment) apply this rule and point here.

title: Entry for Scheduled Services
bodyText: Virginia has no rule allowing entry without notice for regularly scheduled services, even if the lease says so conspicuously. Routine maintenance you schedule that the tenant did not request needs at least 72 hours' notice unless that is impractical; the work must be done within 14 days after the notice is delivered, and the notice must state the last date it may be done. A pesticide application inside the unit needs 48 hours' written notice unless the tenant asked for it or agrees to a shorter period. No notice is needed for maintenance the tenant requests, or in an emergency. Because each notice must name a last date within a 14-day window, a schedule printed in the lease does not replace the notice for each visit. What the lease can do is list the services the tenant agrees to, so the tenant may not unreasonably refuse entry to supply them; the optional Entry for Regularly Scheduled Services clause does this and keeps the per-visit notice. Enter only at reasonable times, and don't use access to harass the tenant (see Landlord's Access).

title: Pesticide Notices to Tenants
bodyText: Before applying an insecticide or pesticide inside a tenant's unit, give the tenant written notice at least 48 hours ahead, unless the tenant agrees to a shorter period or asked for the treatment. A tenant with concerns about a specific product must tell you in writing at least 24 hours before the scheduled application. For treatments anywhere else on the premises (hallways, common areas, grounds), post conspicuous signs where the product will be applied at least 48 hours before. The tenant must prepare the unit as your written instructions direct and, if pests are found, follow your written instructions to eliminate them after the treatment. If the tenant doesn't, and the breach materially affects health and safety and can be fixed by repair, replacement or cleaning, you may give a written notice that you will do the work, then do it and send an itemized bill for the actual and reasonable cost, due as rent on the next rent due date (in an emergency, do it first and bill after), or give a notice to remedy the breach. The lease's access clause already states the 48-hour notice, the shorter-period and tenant-request exceptions, the 24-hour concern notice and the preparation duty (see Landlord's Access). Whether a shorter period the tenant agrees to in the lease itself, before any treatment is scheduled, satisfies the statute is unsettled, so get the tenant's agreement to a shorter period for each treatment, in writing. Pesticide applicators have their own licensing and use rules under the Board's regulations, which are not covered here; use a licensed pest control business.

title: No Pet Information Sheet Required
bodyText: Virginia has no requirement that you give a tenant a government fact sheet about pets and eviction, or any pet information sheet, whether or not you know the tenant has a dog or cat, and Virginia law has no special rule for a tenant's animals in an eviction (see Tenant's Belongings and Animals After an Eviction). Good practice instead: put your pet rules, any pet deposit and pet rent in the lease (see Pets), ask for an emergency contact who can take the animals if the tenant can't, and if an animal is left behind or without care, call animal control rather than removing it yourself (see Tenant's Animals Left Without Care). Assistance animals follow their own rules (see Service and Assistance Animals).

title: No Plain-Language Consumer Statement Rule
bodyText: Virginia has no plain-language statute for leases of the kind some states have: no readability test, no required statement of consumer restrictions listing every waiver or limitation in the lease, no Attorney General preapproval of lease forms, and no dollar threshold for such a rule. The nearest Virginia rules are different in kind. You must give the tenant, with the written lease, the state's Statement of Tenant Rights and Responsibilities, which the Department of Housing and Community Development writes in plain language in at least 14-point type, and both parties sign the Department's acknowledgment form; you may not sue on a lease violation until the statement has been provided (Va. Code Ann. §§ 36-139, 55.1-1204). The lease must itemize, beginning on its first page, the deposit, periodic rent and one-time charges under a set sentence (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1204.1). Those rules describe the tenant's rights and your charges; they do not list waivers, because a Virginia lease may not contain waivers of the tenant's rights under the Act in the first place. The separate question of general readability is covered in the guidance on the absence of a plain-language lease rule.

title: No Virginia Rule on Political Canvassing or Signs in Rentals
bodyText: Virginia has no statute giving candidates, campaign workers or canvassers a right to enter a rental building or complex, and none giving tenants a right to post political signs or distribute campaign literature; your lease rules on signs, solicitation and common areas govern, applied evenly. One election-law rule touches apartments: the local registrar may use a multifamily residential building not usually open to the public as an occasional voter registration site, but only if the public has free access to the site during registration hours; the statute gives no right of access to the building (Va. Code Ann. § 24.2-412). Tenant organizing is different: retaliation against a tenant for organizing or joining a tenants' organization is prohibited (edu-tenant-organizing-va). Flags: edu-no-flag-display-rule-va.

title: Pools at Rental Properties
bodyText: Virginia has no pool safety notice for leases and no state rule written for pools at rental properties, but several rules reach them. Construction: a pool built under the current Building Code, including its barrier, must meet the International Swimming Pool and Spa Code as Virginia adopts it (for example, pool showers with heated water need anti-scald controls and may not exceed 120°F). Maintenance: under the state Maintenance Code, pool, hot tub and spa barriers must be maintained as the building code or ordinance under which they were built requires. Local fence ordinances: a city, county or town may require a fence completely around any outdoor man-made swimming or bathing pool (or other outdoor structure holding water more than two feet deep), at least four feet high, reaching within two inches of the ground and at least five feet from the pool's edge, with gates that fasten at least four feet up and stay fastened when the pool is not in use; such an ordinance may apply to existing pools and can carry a fine of up to $300 or 30 days in jail per day of violation. A town or city may also regulate and inspect pools operated by clubs and associations. Health rules: the Board of Health's lodging pool regulations, including the lifeguard requirement, cover only pools that hotels and other transient lodging provide for guests. A separate Board regulation does reach apartment and condominium pools: the owner of a pool, spa or hot tub at least 24 inches deep that is used collectively by numbers of people, including one owned or operated by an apartment or a condominium, must test the water at least once a day, post the latest results and the water quality standards on durable waterproof material where users can readily see them, keep the disinfectant, pH and temperature within the regulation's ranges, and keep a test kit at the pool. A pool at a rental home that only the tenant's household and guests use is a private residential pool and is exempt. Since July 1, 2026 the Board must also adopt broader regulations for pools operated for public use (water treatment, safety equipment, staffing, incident response and more), which will not apply to private residential facilities as the Board defines them; none had been adopted as of November 7, 2026, so check for them before relying on this row. Practical steps for a pool you provide: keep barriers, self-closing gates and latches working, post your pool rules, and give them to tenants as written rules under the lease. See Rules and Regulations.

title: No Tenant Right to Install Air Conditioners
bodyText: Virginia gives tenants no right to install a window or portable air conditioner, and no rule requires a lease that limits them to say so in any particular way. You may allow, condition or prohibit them in the lease or in reasonable written rules. Your own cooling duties depend on what you provide. If you supply air conditioning you must keep it in good and safe working order and supply reasonable air conditioning; central air conditioning that you supply and that is operating, or that you represent as operating, when the lease takes effect is an essential service, so a willful or negligent failure to supply it gives the tenant the essential-service remedies. If you furnish cooling in an apartment building, the state Maintenance Code requires cooling from May 15 to October 1 that keeps habitable rooms at 77°F or cooler, unless it is hotter outside than the locality's summer design temperature and the system is running at full capacity. If you allow tenant-owned units, the tenant must use them and the unit's electrical system reasonably and is responsible for damage the tenant negligently causes (for example, water damage from a poorly installed window unit), but you may not charge a fee for maintenance or repair unless the tenant's violation made it necessary. A window unit must not block a bedroom window that serves as the required emergency escape opening, which the Maintenance Code says must stay operational from inside without keys or tools. See Heat: Season, Temperature and Remedies and Rules and Regulations.

title: No Possession Bond
bodyText: Virginia has no bond a tenant can give at the start of a lease promising to deliver possession at the end of the term, and no way to get possession on an agreed or confessed judgment. A Virginia lease may not authorize anyone to confess judgment on a claim arising out of the lease; such a term is unenforceable, and if you try to enforce it the tenant may recover actual damages and attorney fees (see No Confession of Judgment in a Lease). To get the home back when the tenant stays past the end of the lease, you file an unlawful detainer (eviction) case. If the tenant stays without your consent, you may recover actual damages, attorney fees and court costs unless the tenant proves staying was reasonable, and the lease may set liquidated damages of up to 150 percent of the daily rent for each day the tenant stays past the date in your notice (100 percent for public housing and other HUD-regulated units; see Holdover Liquidated Damages (Optional)). The security deposit is your advance protection for unpaid rent and damage. The bonds Virginia does have in eviction cases run the other way: a tenant who appeals (unless indigent) must pay the rent and charges owed into court, and then pay you the rent by the fifth of each month while the appeal is pending.

title: No Private Well Testing Rule for Rentals
bodyText: Virginia does not require a landlord to test a private well that serves a rental, or to give tenants well test results, at move-in or at any other time. Testing happens at construction: a new drinking-water well needs a health department construction permit and inspection, and before the health department issues its inspection statement the disinfected well must produce a water sample that tests negative for coliform bacteria (or be fitted with treatment shown to work). Some counties and cities may by ordinance require drinking-water testing before a building permit is issued for a home that will use a private well. Other testing programs: on request, the Department of Health will test a private well in an area with a confirmed oil release for oil contamination (at the requester's cost unless the release poses a potential risk to the well's users), and utilities must test private wells within 1.5 miles of the coal ash ponds at four named power stations on the well owner's behalf, at the utility's cost, and replace or treat a well whose water exceeds federal drinking-water limits. The well owner may refuse that testing. Your duties to the tenant are the general ones: supply running water and reasonable amounts of hot water at all times, keep the plumbing you supply in good and safe working order, and keep the unit fit and habitable. A well that fails can leave the tenant without running water, which is an essential service and a listed condition for rent escrow and other remedies. If you have well test results, tell the tenant about any known problem with the water before signing; periodic testing for bacteria and nitrates is good practice for a rental on a well. See Repair Duties and Tenant Remedies.

title: Promises to Repair or Improve
bodyText: Virginia has no rule that your promise to clean, repair or improve a rental must be in writing, carry a completion date, or be made before the lease is signed. A promise that is part of your agreement, written or oral, is a lease term: the Act's rental agreement includes oral agreements, and the premises include facilities whose use you promised the tenant. If you don't keep a promise that is part of the lease, the tenant may sue for damages and an injunction, with attorney fees unless you prove you acted reasonably, and may end the lease on written notice for a material breach you don't remedy within 21 days (the statute can be read to require that the breach also affect health and safety). A material breach of the lease is also grounds for rent escrow. Writing it down protects you as well: no one can sue on a lease for more than a year unless it, or a note of it, is in writing and signed by the person being held to it, and an oral promise is harder to prove either way. The Virginia Consumer Protection Act reaches a rental covered by the Act only for misrepresentations and fraudulent practices, and those include misrepresenting that repairs have been made and any false promise in the transaction. What to do: list every promised repair, cleaning or improvement in the lease or a signed addendum with a target date, and don't promise work you won't do.

title: No Proposition 65-Style Chemical Warning
bodyText: Virginia has no counterpart to California's Proposition 65. No Virginia law lists chemicals known to cause cancer or reproductive harm, and none requires you to post a sign or give a tenant a written warning that a building, unit, parking garage or anything in it may expose occupants to such chemicals. Specific hazards have their own Virginia rules and rows instead: the federal lead-based paint disclosure for pre-1978 housing, mold (move-in report and remediation), prior methamphetamine manufacture, defective drywall, and smoke and carbon monoxide alarms. The State Department of Health is the state's toxic substance information agency, but its duties do not reach landlords. Keep the unit fit and habitable and deal promptly with any hazard you know of (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1220).

title: No Property Tax Statement for Tenants
bodyText: Virginia does not require you to tell a tenant what share of the rent goes to property taxes, in the lease or on request, and has no renter's property tax credit for which a tenant would need such a statement. Local real estate tax relief for people 65 and older or permanently and totally disabled covers homes they own and occupy; an interest held under a lease or term of years does not qualify. One related rule applies to rent-to-own deals. A lease option or rent-to-own contract under which the buyer lives in the home as a primary residence is a residential executory real estate contract (unless the seller owns no more than two single-family homes in Virginia, or is a real estate licensee or a licensed lender), and it is also subject to the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act. The Board of Housing and Community Development publishes best-practice provisions for these contracts that include the property's most recent tax assessment and the property tax for the year before the deal; the statute makes those best practices, not mandatory lease terms. If you choose to tell tenants about property taxes, keep it accurate; a statement in the lease does not by itself let you pass a tax increase through (see Property Tax Pass-Throughs).

title: Questions You May and May Not Ask Applicants
bodyText: Virginia has no general statute barring a landlord from asking about a protected characteristic, but several rules limit what you ask and how. Disability: the Fair Housing Board's regulation makes it unlawful to ask whether an applicant, anyone who will live in the unit, or anyone associated with them has a disability, or to ask about the nature or severity of a disability. You may ask every applicant, whether or not disabled, about the ability to meet the requirements of tenancy, about eligibility for housing or a priority reserved for people with disabilities, whether the applicant currently uses or is addicted to an illegal controlled substance, and whether the applicant has been convicted of illegally manufacturing or distributing a controlled substance (18VAC135-50-200). For a reasonable accommodation request, verification is limited to what the law allows (edu-assistance-animals-va).
