Statements: any written or oral statement, including an application form, that indicates a preference, limitation or discrimination based on race, color, religion, national origin, sex, elderliness, familial status, source of funds, sexual orientation, gender identity, military status or disability is unlawful (Va. Code Ann. § 36-96.3; 18VAC135-50-110). Questions the law expressly allows: an application may ask for the number, ages, sex and familial relationship of the applicants and intended occupants, and for criminal convictions with written consent to a record check (Va. Code Ann. § 36-96.2). Criminal records: an application may not require disclosure of a sealed arrest, charge or conviction, and one that asks about criminal history must say that sealed records need not be disclosed (Va. Code Ann. § 19.2-392.15). Questions about religion, national origin, sexual orientation, gender identity, military status or source of funds aren't themselves banned by statute, but an answer you didn't need can become evidence if you later deny the applicant. The cautious course: ask only what your written criteria use, ask every applicant the same questions, ask about assistance programs only to process the payment, and don't ask about disability at all except as the regulation allows.

title: Use of the Home and Unlawful Purposes
bodyText: Unless the lease says otherwise, a Virginia tenant must occupy the unit only as a residence (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1232); the library's residential-use clause states that. No Virginia criminal or nuisance statute makes a lease void or annulled when the premises are used for an unlawful purpose. Your remedy is termination under the Act: a criminal or willful act that poses a threat to health or safety, or illegal drug activity, allows immediate termination and a fast-track possession case (edu-expedited-criminal-eviction-va), and other unlawful uses that breach the lease follow the ordinary noncompliance notices. The nuisance laws act on the property, not the lease: a building used for prostitution or criminal street gang activity can be enjoined and closed for up to a year, a drug nuisance can be closed after a conviction, and you face criminal exposure if you knowingly permit drug or gambling use (Va. Code Ann. §§ 18.2-258, 18.2-329, 48-7, 48-12, 48-16; edu-criminal-activity-va). A nuisance closure order is in addition to, not instead of, your right to terminate.

title: No Recycling Notice Rule
bodyText: Virginia has no rule requiring you to tell tenants where and how to recycle on the premises. What applies: You must provide and maintain appropriate receptacles and conveniences for collecting, storing and removing garbage, rubbish and other waste and arrange for its removal, and the tenant must put waste in the receptacles you provide, in a clean and safe manner. A locality may by ordinance require people, tenants included, to separate solid waste for collection and recycling, but such an ordinance may not make an apartment owner or manager liable when tenants fail to comply, and may carry only civil penalties. Localities also set collection times and container placement, with notice before any civil penalty. If the locality charges the building for recycling or trash collection, you may divide those fees among the tenants as rent if the lease clearly says so (use the Utilities Billed by Landlord clause). Recycling rules you adopt, such as which bins to use, bind tenants as rules and regulations if they meet the usual test and tenants get a copy at signing or when adopted. Telling tenants how your recycling works, in the rules or a move-in sheet, is good practice. Local ordinances vary and are not covered here.

title: Religious Displays by Tenants
bodyText: Virginia has no statute written for tenants' religious or cultural displays, but its Fair Housing Law defines religion to include any outward expression of religious faith, including religious dress and grooming and the carrying or display of religious items or symbols (Va. Code Ann. § 36-96.1:1). Treating a tenant differently in the terms, conditions or privileges of a rental because of religion is a discriminatory housing practice (Va. Code Ann. § 36-96.3). So a rule that bans or singles out religious items, such as a mezuzah on a doorframe, a religious wreath or a small symbol on a door, can be discrimination, and enforcing a neutral rule more harshly against religious items than against other decorations is risky. Neutral rules on decorations, signs and common areas that apply equally to everything are not barred by statute, but no Virginia case on how they apply to religious displays was looked at here. The cautious course: write decoration rules neutrally, enforce them evenly, and allow small religious items on or beside the unit's own door unless they cause damage or a safety problem. Cultural displays without a religious element have no specific protection, though treating them differently because of a tenant's national origin is barred. Flags: edu-no-flag-display-rule-va.

title: No Bar on Demanding Rent for a Unit Needing Repairs
bodyText: Virginia has no rule that bars you from demanding or collecting rent, or from giving a nonpayment notice, just because the unit has code violations or defects. Unrepaired conditions instead limit what you can collect through the tenant's remedies. Defense in an eviction: in a nonpayment case or a suit for rent while the tenant is in possession, the tenant may defend on a condition that is a fire hazard or a serious threat to life, health or safety (such as no heat, water, light or electricity, inadequate sewage disposal, rodents) or a material breach by you, if you were told in writing, or by a government violation or condemnation notice, and failed to fix it within a reasonable time (more than 30 days is presumed unreasonable). The court may then reduce the rent, end the lease at the tenant's request or order the repair. Rent escrow: the tenant may instead pay rent into court and ask the court to abate it (see Rent Escrow: How It Works and How the Money Is Released). Repair and deduct: if you take no reasonable steps within 14 days of written notice of such a condition, the tenant may hire a licensed contractor and deduct the cost, up to the greater of one month's rent or $1,500. Rent stops or is refunded in these cases: if you willfully fail to deliver possession, rent abates until you do; if you willfully or negligently fail to supply an essential service and the tenant moves to reasonable substitute housing after written notice, the tenant is excused from rent for that period; if the unit is condemned after the tenant warned you of a serious code violation, you must refund rent paid after the condemnation (see Condemned Units: Rent and Refunds); and a tenant who finds a serious threat at move-in may end the lease within seven days and get all rent and deposits back. Retaliation rules also protect a tenant who complains to a code official. See Repair Duties and Tenant Remedies.

title: Rent Increases During the Lease
bodyText: Virginia has no rent control, but three rules limit how rent can rise during a lease. The rent due each payment period must be itemized beginning on the first page of the lease, under the statutory sentence that no additional rent may be charged unless listed there or added later by a separate addendum; any money owed under the lease other than a deposit is rent. No one-sided change to the lease is valid without notice and both parties' written consent. So you may not raise rent mid-lease by notice alone, and a clause letting you do so does not work in Virginia. What does work is a fixed schedule agreed at signing: state each rent amount and the period it covers (for example, one amount for months 1 to 12 and a higher one for months 13 to 24) in the first-page list itself, so every amount is listed. The library's optional Scheduled Rent Changes clause does this. Whether a formula increase, such as one tied to a price index, counts as listed rent is not settled, so the library offers no index or formula clause for Virginia; build expected cost increases into the scheduled amounts or adjust at renewal. At renewal, a landlord with more than four Virginia units must give written notice of a rent increase at least 60 days before the lease ends (90 days, with a tenant response deadline, from July 1, 2027); for a month-to-month or holdover tenancy after a lease, a new rent set by written notice takes effect on the next rent due date at least 30 days later. Retaliation: until January 1, 2027, raising rent to similar market rentals is not retaliation; from January 1, 2027, an increase made under the lease's terms, or to market rent, is also not retaliation, so a scheduled increase written into the lease is protected.

title: Counterclaims and Rent Paid Into Court in Eviction Cases
bodyText: In a Virginia eviction (unlawful detainer) case in general district court, these rules govern counterclaims and rent paid into court. Counterclaims are optional: before trial the tenant may file any money claim against you within the court's limit, whether or not it comes from the lease, and the court may hear it with your case or separately. No rule requires the tenant to deposit rent before raising a defense, and the habitability defense in a nonpayment case does not depend on paying rent into court. Continuances: if the tenant asks for a continuance or a contested trial, the court must, at your request, order the tenant to pay the rent due as of the first court date into the court escrow account before granting it, unless the court finds the tenant has a good-faith defense. The court may give up to one week to pay; if the tenant doesn't pay in full, or later fails to pay future rent into escrow, the court must at your request enter judgment and possession for you. On your motion the court may release escrowed money to pay your mortgage or other expenses of the unit; otherwise none is paid out within 10 days of judgment unless you both agree. No escrow is ordered when you ask for the continuance. You may also ask for possession at the first hearing and a continuance of up to 120 days to fix final rent and damages, unless the tenant contests the amount at that hearing. Appeals: either side has 10 days to appeal to circuit court, where any party may ask for a jury. A tenant appealing a residential eviction must post a bond by paying into the general district court the rent, late charges, attorney fees and other charges due under the lease (indigent tenants excepted), or the appeal fails. During the appeal the tenant pays rent to you by the fifth of each month; if not, the circuit court enters judgment and possession on your written motion without a hearing. Money in the court account goes to you unless the court finds the tenant likely to win a money counterclaim. No rent deposit is tied to a jury demand. Where a court runs the eviction diversion program, an eligible tenant pays at least 10 percent of the amount due, to you or into court, at the first docket call and the rest on a three-month plan. The tenant's own rent escrow case has separate payment rules (see Rent Escrow: How It Works and How the Money Is Released), and paying everything owed into court can redeem the tenancy (see The Tenant's Right of Redemption).

title: Collecting Rent and the Duty to Repair
bodyText: Virginia has no statute saying that a lease, assignment of rents, deed, deed of trust or other security instrument may not let someone collect the rent free of the duty to keep the unit fit and habitable. Related rules reach much the same result. The repair duties fall on the landlord, which means the owner, lessor or sublessor, and an owner includes a mortgagee in possession; a managing agent who doesn't disclose the owner is treated as the landlord (Va. Code Ann. §§ 55.1-1200, 55.1-1220). A lease can't waive the tenant's rights or limit your liability, and a written agreement for the tenant to take on some of your duties is valid only if made in good faith and not to evade your obligations (Va. Code Ann. §§ 55.1-1208, 55.1-1220). When you sell in good faith and tell the tenant, you are released only for later events, and the new owner takes on the duties and must return any deposit owed (Va. Code Ann. §§ 55.1-1224, 55.1-1226). Whether a lender or receiver that only collects rent under an assignment, without taking possession, owes the repair duties is not settled by statute; the recording statute in the commercial-tenancy chapter, which perfects an assignment of rents without taking possession, lets the tenant keep paying you until told in writing to pay the assignee (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1403). If you assign rents to a lender, keep the repair and utility duties funded and make sure tenants know whom to pay and whom to ask for repairs.

title: Rent Receipts
bodyText: You must give the tenant a written receipt whenever rent is paid in cash or by money order (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1204). Virginia's landlord-tenant law requires no receipt for rent paid by check, card or electronic transfer, and Virginia's general law of contracts and payments gives a debtor no separate right to demand a receipt from a creditor; the only general receipt rule found concerns a person presenting a check or note for payment, who must sign a receipt on it on demand (Va. Code Ann. § 8.3A-501). Instead, on a tenant's written request you must give a written statement of all charges and payments over the tenancy or the past 12 months, whichever is shorter, within 10 business days; from July 1, 2027, the same statement must also go with every termination notice for nonpayment, and a landlord with four or more units (or any landlord receiving rental or utility assistance for the tenant) must give it within 10 business days of a written request for tenant records (Va. Code Ann. §§ 55.1-1202, 55.1-1204, 55.1-1209). Virginia has no rule that a receipt for a later month presumes earlier rent was paid. Cautious course: give a dated receipt for every in-person payment, keep a running ledger, and keep copies; the payment rules are in Rent Payments, Receipts and Statements.

title: No Virginia Rule on Reporting Rent to Credit Bureaus
bodyText: Virginia has no statute on reporting rent payments to credit bureaus: none requires you to offer positive rent reporting, none bars you from reporting, none requires a tenant's election in the lease, and none requires notice to the tenant before you report late rent. The tenant-records rule lets you release a summary of a tenant's rent payment record, including the periodic rent amount, to a third party without the tenant's consent (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1209), so sharing payment history with a reporting service doesn't breach Virginia's confidentiality rule; other tenant information still needs written consent. If you report, federal credit reporting law governs the accuracy of what you furnish and disputes about it (not covered here). From July 1, 2027, if you use a consumer report in screening, your pre-application notice must name the reporting agency and tell applicants of their right to a free copy and to dispute it (edu-tenant-screening-va). The cautious course for an opt-in program: describe it in a separate written election the tenant signs, report accurately, and tell tenants how to dispute an entry.

title: Taxes on Residential Rent
bodyText: Virginia does not tax residential rent: there is no state or local tax on the rent a tenant pays under a lease for a home the tenant lives in, apart from the local business license tax on rental receipts that a locality levying it on January 1, 1974 may keep (below). The taxes that touch rentals are for short stays. The state sales tax treats charges for accommodations furnished to transients for less than 90 continuous days, in a hotel, motel, inn, campground, short-term rental or any other place that regularly furnishes rooms to transients, as taxable retail sales; accommodations furnished for more than 90 continuous days are exempt. Counties may levy a transient occupancy tax on rooms rented out for continuous occupancy of fewer than 30 consecutive days, and it does not apply to rooms rented and continuously occupied by the same person or group for 30 days or more; cities and towns with charter taxing powers may tax transient room rentals, limited to rooms intended for occupancy by transients. The operator, or the booking platform that facilitates the sale, collects and remits the tax and must state it separately on the bill. Localities generally may not impose a business license tax on an owner for the business of renting residential real property, other than hotels, motels, campgrounds, bed and breakfasts, lodging houses, rooming houses and boardinghouses, though a locality that imposed such a tax on January 1, 1974 may keep it. Property taxes on the rental are assessed to the owner; whether a lease may pass them on is covered in Property Tax Pass-Throughs.

title: Local Rental Inspections
bodyText: Virginia localities inspect rental units through the Building Code powers state law gives them; the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act otherwise supersedes local landlord-tenant ordinances. A rental inspection ordinance can cover units inside a rental inspection district that the governing body has found blighted, deteriorating or in need of inspection to prevent deterioration, or an individual unit outside a district that it finds blighted, deteriorating or in violation of the Building Code. A district may not cover the whole locality. After the first inspection, the building department may inspect a unit in a district no more than once a calendar year, plus follow-up inspections until violations are fixed. In a multifamily development of more than 10 units it inspects a sample of at least two units and no more than 10 percent, and may not charge inspection fees for more than 10 units unless the sample shows violations affecting safe, decent and sanitary conditions. A unit that passes with no such violations must be exempted for at least four years, and a unit with a certificate of occupancy issued in the last four years is exempt for four years from that date; a sale can bring a new inspection, and a later violation can cost the exemption. The locality may also exempt units managed by a real estate licensee, a property manager or managing agent, or a manager it recognizes as professional. Outside these programs, the locality may inspect and enforce the Building Code for existing buildings generally, and after a tenant's complaint the building department must enforce the unsafe-structure provisions if it finds there may be a violation. Rental inspection fees charged against the building are local government fees you may allocate among tenants if the lease clearly says so (see Utilities Billed by Landlord). Entry: inspectors must make a reasonable effort to get the owner's, occupant's or tenant's consent, and where a complaint alleges an immediate and imminent threat and entry is refused, they may ask a magistrate or court for an inspection warrant. Virginia law does not say whether a lease clause can give an inspector the tenant's consent to enter, so do not rely on one: give the tenant notice of the inspection and ask the tenant to agree to it. Your own right of entry to inspect, on notice and at reasonable times, still applies, and the tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent. A rental inspection ordinance does not change landlord and tenant rights under the Act. See also Local Landlord-Tenant Rules and Rent Control.

title: No Ending a Lease Because Repairs Cost Too Much
bodyText: Virginia has no rule that lets you, or the tenant, end a lease because repairs would cost too much compared with the rent or the property's value. Your duty to make all repairs and keep the premises fit and habitable does not depend on cost. A tenancy can end over the property's condition only in these ways: (1) fire or casualty damage that substantially impairs the tenant's use or needs the tenant out for repairs lets either side end the lease, though from January 1, 2027 you may end it only after meeting or trying to meet with the tenant and offering any substantially similar unit in the same complex available within a reasonable time, unless the tenant's violation caused the damage (see Fire or Casualty: The Tenant's Options and the casualty clause); (2) if complying with the building or housing code needs alteration, remodeling or demolition that would effectively deprive the tenant of the unit, the retaliation rules do not stop you from ending a month-to-month tenancy on the required notice and suing for possession; (3) a month-to-month tenancy otherwise ends on 30 days' written notice before the next rent due date unless the lease sets a different notice period, a week-to-week tenancy on seven days' notice, and a fixed term ends when it expires; and (4) you and the tenant may agree in writing to end early. If a repair needs the unit empty but the home is worth fixing, you may instead move the tenant on 30 days' written notice for up to 30 days to a comparable unit or hotel at your cost while rent continues. A unit condemned after the tenant reported the code violation makes you liable for damages and refunds (see Condemned Units: Rent and Refunds). The library offers no clause reserving a right to end the lease because repairs are expensive.

title: No Small-Landlord Exemption From Repair Remedies
bodyText: Some states let a landlord with only a few units opt out of tenants' rent escrow or repair remedies by giving a notice. Virginia has no such exemption and no exemption notice. The Residential Landlord and Tenant Act applies to occupancy in all single-family and multifamily dwelling units, and its repair remedies (rent escrow, repair by a licensed contractor, ending the lease for your breach, and the habitability defense to a nonpayment case) apply to every landlord the Act covers, whatever the number of units. Virginia's size-based rules concern other things, such as card payments, limits on redemption and renewal notices (see Landlord Portfolio Size Rules), and the Act's exclusions are kinds of occupancy, such as transient lodging or employee housing, not small landlords (see Who the Virginia Residential Landlord and Tenant Act Covers). A lease cannot make the tenant give up these remedies, so don't add an exemption or waiver notice.

title: Repair Requests and Notice
bodyText: Most Virginia tenant repair remedies start with the tenant's written notice to you: ending the lease for your breach, damages or substitute housing when you fail to supply an essential service, rent escrow, and repair by a licensed contractor after 14 days. For rent escrow and for the habitability defense in your nonpayment case, a violation or condemnation notice from a state or local agency also counts. The habitability defense uses the Act's general meaning of notice, under which you also have notice of a condition you actually know about, were told about verbally, or have reason to know exists, so a tenant may be able to raise that defense without a written request. The tenant must also promptly tell you about insects or pests and about moisture or visible mold. The lease may say where repair requests go (notice to you is served at your place of business where the lease was made or any place you hold out for receiving it) and, if it says so, allow notices in electronic form, though any tenant may ask to use paper. A lease cannot make the tenant give up a right or remedy under the Act, so a term requiring written repair requests cannot cut off a defense or remedy the Act bases on your knowledge, a verbal report or a government notice. No Virginia law says that a lease accepting phone or verbal repair reports gives up your right to written notice where a remedy requires it, and whether such a term would be read as accepting oral notice is unsettled. Cautious course: name your repair contact and the methods you accept, act on every report however it arrives, confirm urgent phone reports in writing, and keep a log. Whoever relies on a notice that was not in writing must prove it was given.

title: Fees Allowed and How They Must Appear
bodyText: Virginia requires the lease to itemize, beginning on its first page, every charge that makes up the security deposit, the rent due each period and any one-time charge due before the lease starts or with the first payment, under a statutory sentence that no other deposit or rent will be charged unless listed or added by a later addendum (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1204.1). Because rent means all money other than the deposit owed under the lease, recurring fees (pet rent, amenity, insurance or utility charges billed by you) belong in that list. Several charges exist only if the lease provides for them: a late charge, the bad-check processing fee of up to $50, utility submetering or ratio billing charges, an expedited deposit-disposition fee, a charge for extra copies of tenant records, and deposit deductions for other damages or charges (Va. Code Ann. §§ 55.1-1200, 55.1-1204, 55.1-1209, 55.1-1212, 55.1-1226). You can't add a fee during the term without the tenant's written consent (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1204). Pass-through charges are limited to actual cost where the law says so: payment-processing fees (and only if you offer a fee-free way to pay), utility billing service charges, and insurance programs (with administrative fees). You may not charge a fee for maintenance or repair of the unit unless the tenant's violation made it necessary (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1208). Virginia has no separate rule on common-area fees or a required total-monthly-payment label. Use the library's Fee Disclosure Statement clause; the library does not add a second fee list for Virginia, so every fee has one place in the lease.

title: State Tenant Rights and Responsibilities Statement
bodyText: Virginia has a state-published guide: the Statement of Tenant Rights and Responsibilities, written by the Department of Housing and Community Development in plain language and at least 14-point type, with the statewide legal aid telephone number and website, and posted on the Department's website with a printable acknowledgment form. When you offer a prospective tenant a written lease, you must give the Statement with it, and both parties sign the Department's acknowledgment form; if the tenant will not sign, record the date or dates you gave it and that the tenant did not sign. The form must be current on the date you deliver it, so download it fresh. Give the tenant a copy of the Statement with the signed lease within 10 business days after the lease takes effect. Until the tenant has received the Statement, you may not file or keep up any court action, including an eviction, for a lease violation. After the tenancy starts you may, but need not, give the Statement again and offer the acknowledgment. The Act does not say whether a renewal lease offered to a current tenant counts as an offer to a "prospective tenant"; the cautious course is to give the current Statement and acknowledgment with every new or renewal lease. The library's Statement of Tenant Rights and Responsibilities clause records that you gave it. Manufactured home lot rentals have their own Department statement.

title: No Code Variance Notice to Tenants
bodyText: Virginia has no rule that you give tenants, or attach to the lease, a copy of a code variance or modification that applies to the rental. Virginia's housing standards come from the Uniform Statewide Building Code, whose maintenance part (the Virginia Maintenance Code) governs existing rental buildings; there is no separate state sanitary code for rentals. The code's equivalent of a variance is a modification: on the owner's written application, the local code official may approve a modification of any provision if the spirit and intent of the code are observed and public health, welfare and safety are assured. The decision must be in writing and kept in the enforcing agency's permanent records, and a certificate of occupancy notes when modifications were issued under a building permit. Anyone aggrieved by the department's application of the code or its refusal of a modification may appeal to the local board of Building Code appeals. A modification does not reduce your duties under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act to meet codes materially affecting health and safety and to keep the unit fit and habitable, and the tenant may still complain to the building department. Keep a copy of any modification with your property records.

title: No Special Seasonal Tenancy Rules
bodyText: Virginia has no special rules for seasonal tenancies. What matters is whether the occupant lives in the unit as a primary residence. A guest in a hotel, motel, extended stay facility, vacation residential facility (including a time-share), boardinghouse or similar transient lodging who does not live there as a primary residence is not a tenant under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, and the owner may use self-help eviction. Someone who lives in such lodging as a primary residence for 90 consecutive days or less is also outside the Act, but the owner must give a five-day written notice of nonpayment before self-help. Once a person has lived there as a primary residence for more than 90 consecutive days, or has a written lease for more than 90 days, the Act applies in full. Campgrounds are outside the Act. A seasonal lease of an ordinary house or apartment to a tenant who lives there is a normal tenancy under the Act, with the same deposit, notice, repair and eviction rules; a fixed seasonal term ends on its date without a renewal duty for a landlord with four or fewer Virginia units, while a larger landlord must give the 60-day renewal or nonrenewal notices (see Renewals and Rent Increases). Your duty to supply heat "in season" still applies. Rentals of fewer than 30 consecutive days are short-term rentals that localities may regulate and register, and they can carry the local transient occupancy tax; lodging furnished to transients for less than 90 continuous days is subject to sales tax (see Taxes on Residential Rent).

title: Security Deposit Cap
bodyText: Virginia caps the security deposit at two months' periodic rent, whatever the deposit is called; a pet deposit is part of it, and there is no separate allowance for furniture, pets or a short or long term (Va. Code Ann. §§ 55.1-1200, 55.1-1226). The deposit plus any damage insurance and renter's insurance premiums the tenant pays before the tenancy begins may not together exceed two months' rent, and you may not require both a deposit and damage insurance premiums that together exceed that amount (Va. Code Ann. §§ 55.1-1206, 55.1-1208). You may add a monthly amount as rent to recover later renter's insurance premiums. To raise the deposit during the tenancy (for example after a rent increase), do it only by a written addendum the tenant signs, and keep the total within two months of the current periodic rent (Va. Code Ann. §§ 55.1-1204, 55.1-1204.1). The full deposit rules are in Virginia Security Deposit Rules.

title: Where the Security Deposit Is Held
bodyText: Virginia does not require a landlord to keep security deposits in a separate, trust, escrow or interest-bearing account, to tell the tenant where the deposit is held, or to pay interest on it. Two exceptions apply. If a real estate licensee collects the deposit for you as your agent, it must go into the licensee's escrow account by the end of the fifth business banking day after receipt (unless the parties to the lease agree otherwise in writing) and stay there until paid out under the lease, the management agreement or the law; the licensee may not commingle it with the firm's own money, and if the licensee ends the management agreement it may transfer the escrowed funds to you without your consent, provided it gives each tenant written notice that the funds have been transferred (except after a foreclosure) (Va. Code Ann. § 54.1-2108.1). And rent paid more than one month ahead must be placed in an escrow account at a federally insured depository by the fifth business day (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1205). Even without an account rule, keep each deposit identifiable: you must keep two years of deduction records that tenants may inspect, you must hand deposits to a buyer when you sell, and whoever holds your interest when the tenancy ends must return any deposit owed (Va. Code Ann. §§ 55.1-1213, 55.1-1226).

title: Security Deposit Rules Cannot Be Waived
bodyText: Virginia's security deposit rules are part of the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, so a lease may not make the tenant waive them (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1208). That covers the two-month cap, the limited list of things a deposit may be applied to, the 45-day itemized disposition, the right to attend the move-out inspection, notice of deductions during the tenancy, and the record-keeping duty (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1226). The Act adds its own cap on what may be collected before the tenancy starts: a lease may not make the tenant agree to prepay a deposit plus damage-insurance and renter's-insurance premiums totalling more than two months' rent. A buyer or other successor to your interest must return a deposit owed to the tenant regardless of any agreement between you and the successor. The Act itself allows three changes: the deposit may be applied to other damages or charges the lease provides for; with every tenant's written agreement, the refund need not be one check payable to all tenants; and, if the lease provides and the tenant asks in a separate writing, you may make an expedited disposition for an administrative fee (the library's optional expedited-disposition clause). A willful failure to follow the deposit rules means the court orders the deposit returned with actual damages and reasonable attorney fees (or credited against rent the tenant owes). See the guidance on Virginia's security deposit rules.

title: Security Deposits When a Rental Is Sold
bodyText: When you sell a rental, you must transfer every security deposit you hold, with any interest it has earned, to the buyer at the time of the transfer, and tell each tenant of the sale with the buyer's name, address and phone number (Va. Code Ann. §§ 55.1-1213, 55.1-1216). If a managing agent holds the deposits under a written management agreement, you must ask the agent in writing to pay them to you before settlement; the agent then transfers them to you and tells each tenant in writing that the deposit has been transferred to the new owner. Whoever holds the landlord's interest when the tenancy ends, however it was acquired, must return any deposit owed, even if the deposit was never passed on and whatever the sale contract says; this binds a foreclosure buyer too (Va. Code Ann. §§ 54.1-2108.1, 55.1-1226). After a good-faith sale and notice to the tenant, the seller is relieved of liability for later events unless otherwise agreed (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1224). The full sale rules are in Selling or Losing a Rented Property.

title: Consequences of Mishandling a Security Deposit
bodyText: If you willfully fail to follow Virginia's deposit rules, the court must order the whole security deposit returned to the tenant, with the tenant's actual damages and reasonable attorney fees. If the tenant owes you rent, the court instead credits an amount equal to the deposit against the rent due (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1226). There is no double or treble penalty, and missing the 45-day itemization does not by itself forfeit your right to deduct; but a late or missing itemization is the usual evidence of a willful failure, so meet every deadline. Short of willfulness, a tenant can still sue for the amount wrongly kept, and anyone harmed by a practice the landlord-tenant law prohibits may sue for an injunction and damages (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1259). A lease term that breaks the deposit cap is unenforceable, and if you sue to enforce it the tenant recovers damages and attorney fees (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1208). A misrepresentation or fraudulent practice about a deposit can also bring a claim under the Consumer Protection Act. Separate rules apply to application deposits (wrongfully withheld amount plus attorney fees, Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1203) and to unlawful lockouts, where the court may end the lease at the tenant's request and order the whole deposit returned (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1243.1).

title: No Rule on Posting Deposit Standards
bodyText: Virginia does not require you to post or give tenants the standards you use to set deposit amounts, even if you charge different tenants different deposits, and it has no building-size trigger for such a rule. Three limits still apply. Every deposit, however labelled and including a pet deposit, is capped at two months' periodic rent. Fair housing law bars different deposit terms because of race, color, religion, national origin, sex, elderliness, source of funds, familial status, sexual orientation, gender identity, military status or disability, so a higher deposit for a tenant paying with a housing voucher or other assistance is unlawful, unless you own no more than four rental units in Virginia (and no more than a 10 percent interest in more than four), which exempts source of funds alone; an owner who lives in a building of up to four units, and some owners of up to three single-family houses who rent without a broker, are exempt more broadly (Va. Code Ann. §§ 36-96.2, 36-96.3; edu-source-of-funds-va). And from July 1, 2027, before you take any payment or information from an applicant, you must tell the applicant in writing or by posting the fees and any application deposit you charge and whether they are refundable, together with your selection criteria (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1203). Cautious course: set deposits by written criteria you apply the same way to every applicant (for example credit or rental history), and keep a record of why each amount was set.

title: Locks, Peepholes and Security Devices
bodyText: No Virginia statute makes every landlord install particular locks, deadbolts or peepholes in an existing rental, or rekey the locks between tenants. Three sets of rules do apply. First, a city or county may adopt an ordinance requiring a landlord who rents five or more units in one multifamily building to install: deadbolt locks meeting the Building Code's standard for new multifamily construction, and peepholes, on each unit's exterior swinging entrance door (no peephole is needed in a door with a glass panel); manufacturer's locks and removable metal pins or charlie bars on exterior sliding glass doors at the levels the ordinance names; and code-compliant locking devices on all exterior windows. The ordinance must give you a reasonable time to comply. Second, apartment buildings built under the current construction code must have locks on sliding doors that are one story or less above grade, shared by two units or otherwise reachable from outside (pins or charlie bars are an alternative), and a 180-degree door viewer on each unit's entrance door unless the door has a vision panel. Third, the state Maintenance Code requires security devices that the building code required or that you provided to be maintained, unless the building official approves their removal; and exit doors and required bedroom escape windows must stay openable from inside as the code in effect at construction requires, so window bars over an escape opening must release from inside without a key, tool or special force. Tenants also have lock rights: a tenant may install security devices such as chain latches you approve, if they cause no permanent damage and you get duplicate keys and instructions; and a tenant with a non-ex parte court order excluding a co-tenant may have the exterior locks changed, and you may not give keys to the excluded person. Rekeying between tenants is not required but is good practice. If you own more than 200 units on the same property you must have written key-control policies (see Key-Control Policies for Large Properties). See also Tenant-Installed Security Systems and Cameras and Domestic and Sexual Violence Protections.

title: No Work Card Rule for Senior Housing Staff
bodyText: Virginia has no work-card, permit or registration requirement for staff of senior or 55-and-older rental housing, and no special background-check rule for employees of independent senior apartments. Three related rules apply. If you own more than 200 rental units on the same piece of property (financial institutions and real estate licensees are excepted), you must require a pre-employment criminal history records check for any applicant for a job with access to unit keys or key codes, and keep written key-control policies (see Background Checks for Employees With Key Access). A licensed assisted living facility, which provides care and is not an ordinary rental under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, may not hire people convicted of certain barrier crimes and must run background checks on its employees under the social services licensing laws. And housing for older persons (housing under a program for the elderly, housing solely for people 62 or older, or housing intended for people 55 or older where at least 80 percent of occupied units have at least one such resident and the owner publishes and follows policies showing that intent) is exempt from the fair housing ban on familial-status discrimination; that exemption concerns residents, not staff.

title: No Criminal Penalty for Denying an Assistance Animal
bodyText: Virginia doesn't make it a crime for a landlord to refuse an assistance animal or a guide, hearing or service dog in housing; the consequences are civil, and they are serious. Under the Virginians with Disabilities Act, a person with a guide, hearing or service dog is entitled to full and equal access with the dog to all housing accommodations, may not be charged extra for the dog, and is liable for damage the dog does (Va. Code Ann. § 51.5-45). A person whose rights are abridged may sue in circuit court for an injunction, compensatory damages (not pain and suffering) and attorney fees; punitive damages are not available; the suit must be brought within one year, and it is barred unless the suit is filed, or a written statement of the claim is sent to you by registered mail, within 180 days of the violation (Va. Code Ann. § 51.5-46). Refusing a reasonable accommodation for an assistance animal is also a discriminatory housing practice under the Virginia Fair Housing Law: a private suit within two years can bring compensatory and punitive damages without the usual state-law cap, plus attorney fees, and in a suit by the Attorney General the court may add a civil penalty of up to $50,000 for a first violation and $100,000 for a later one (Va. Code Ann. §§ 36-96.17, 36-96.18). The public-places section of the Act (restaurants, hotels, lodging places, places of public accommodation) is not the housing rule; rented homes come under the housing section. Separately, it is a misdemeanor to willfully impede or interfere with the work of a dog you know is a guide or leader dog (Va. Code Ann. § 3.2-6588); that crime targets interference with the dog, not a refusal to rent, and no Virginia case applying it to housing was looked at here. Lease pet rules must exempt assistance animals (assistance-animal-accommodation-va, edu-assistance-animals-va).

title: Misrepresenting an Assistance Animal
bodyText: Virginia's misrepresentation crime doesn't reach housing. Fitting a dog with a harness, collar, vest or sign, or using a disability identification card, to pass the dog off as a service or hearing dog is a misdemeanor only when done to fraudulently gain public access under the public-places section (Va. Code Ann. § 51.5-44.1); renting a home is not public access. In housing, the law reaches the documentation instead: a mental health provider, licensed or certified professional, peer-support member, caregiver or other person who provides fraudulent supporting documentation of a disability or disability-related need commits a prohibited practice under the Virginia Consumer Protection Act (Va. Code Ann. § 36-96.3:1). No Virginia statute makes a tenant's false assistance-animal request a crime or a lease default in itself. What you may do: where the disability or need isn't obvious or known, ask for reliable documentation from a person with a therapeutic relationship, evaluate it case by case, and deny a request where there is no disability or disability-related need (edu-assistance-animals-va). If documents later prove false, the ordinary lease remedies for false statements in an application apply (rental-application-accuracy); the cautious course is to act only on clear evidence and to document it.

title: No Landlord Duty on Registered Sex Offender Occupancy
bodyText: Virginia puts no duty on a landlord about where a registered sex offender lives: no law bars renting to an offender, none makes it a crime to rent to two offenders living together, and none requires you to check the Registry or tell other tenants. The residence limit falls on the offender: an adult convicted of certain sexual offenses against a child, committed together with an abduction, burglary or similar crime, may not live within 500 feet of a child day center or a primary, secondary or high school, or of a qualifying public park next to a school, and violating that is the offender's felony (Va. Code Ann. § 18.2-370.3). Registry information about offenders is public on the State Police website, and any person may sign up for electronic notice of registrations in the same or a neighboring ZIP code (Va. Code Ann. §§ 9.1-913, 9.1-914). Using Registry information for purposes the law doesn't authorize, or to intimidate or harass someone, is prohibited, and a willful violation is a misdemeanor (Va. Code Ann. § 9.1-918); the law lists protecting the public as an authorized use, so the cautious course is to use it only for screening and safety, not to publicize a tenant's status. Criminal records in screening follow the general rules (edu-tenant-screening-va): you need not rent to someone whose convictions for harm to persons or property make the person a clear and present threat. Registered sex offender status isn't a protected class under the Virginia Fair Housing Law. No lease statement about sex offenders is required (edu-no-sex-offender-disclosure-va).

title: No Font-Size or Single-Family Occupancy Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Virginia has no single-family residence occupancy disclosure and no general font-size or first-page rule for residential leases. The layout rules that do apply are specific: (1) The itemized list of the security deposit, rent per period and one-time charges must begin on the first page of the written lease, with the statutory sentence immediately above it (see Fee Disclosure Statement). (2) The statement of tenant rights and responsibilities you must give with the lease is the state's own form, printed in at least 14-point type, and the parties sign the state's acknowledgment form. (3) Some documents must be separate from the lease: a notice ending tenancies to rehabilitate or change the use of a multifamily building with at least four units must be a separate writing, not part of the lease; a tenant's request for expedited deposit processing must be a separate written document. (4) A termination notice from a public housing authority, or from a private landlord to a tenant receiving a Housing Choice Voucher or other tenant-based rental assistance, is not effective unless its first page shows legal aid contact information in type no smaller or less legible than the rest of the notice. Manufactured home lot leases have their own bold-type flood-insurance statement; that rule is for lot rentals under the Manufactured Home Lot Rental Act, not dwelling leases.

title: No Shoreline Access Disclosure
bodyText: No Virginia statute requires a lease of waterfront property to tell the tenant about public access along the shore, public rights in the water, or where the owner's boundary lies, and none requires a shoreline notice in the lease. What Virginia law says about the shore: the beds of the bays, rivers and creeks and the shores of the sea that were never granted away belong to the Commonwealth and may be used by all the people for fishing, fowling, hunting and taking oysters and other shellfish, and a waterfront owner's land and rights reach the mean low-water mark but no farther (Va. Code Ann. §§ 28.2-1200, 28.2-1202). Where a public body has nourished a beach and the public already has a right to use the adjacent land, the public keeps that right on the new land too (Va. Code Ann. § 28.2-1202). A lease can give the tenant no more than you own, so don't describe a beach, pier or water area as private or exclusive unless it is. Building a pier, bulkhead or other structure in or over state waters, wetlands or coastal sand dunes needs permits, and local wetlands and dune ordinances apply; those rules govern the work, not the lease. If you lease a one-to-four-unit home with an option to buy, the Residential Property Disclosure Act's buyer-beware statement applies, and it tells the buyer to check for Chesapeake Bay resource protection areas and flood zones (Va. Code Ann. §§ 55.1-701, 55.1-703).

title: Notice Before Showings Cannot Be Waived
bodyText: Virginia sets no fixed number of hours' notice for showing the home to buyers, lenders or new tenants. The rule is that, except in an emergency or where it is impractical, you give the tenant notice of your intent to enter and enter only at reasonable times; the 72-hour rule applies only to routine maintenance the tenant has not requested (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1229). So there is no showing-notice period for a lease to shorten, and a clause waiving notice altogether, or allowing showings at unreasonable times, would take away a right the Act gives the tenant, which a lease may not do (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1208). Virginia has no separate-document procedure for such a waiver. The tenant may not unreasonably withhold consent to a showing. If the lease says so, a tenant who without reasonable justification refuses a showing for sale or lease owes you damages, costs and reasonable attorney fees; the library's access clause includes this. You may promise a set notice period in the lease (for example, 24 hours) if you want a clear standard; that adds to the tenant's protection and is lawful. You may not abuse the right of access or use it to harass the tenant.

title: Federal Government Shutdowns and Rent
bodyText: Virginia's one shutdown protection is in eviction court. A federal employee or contractor tenant who is furloughed or unpaid during a federal government closure and brings written proof to the first court date gets a 60-day continuance of your nonpayment case, unless you have served a notice for a non-rent breach. It covers employees of the United States government, independent contractors for it, and employees of its contractors, and only rent that came due after the closure began. Written proof is a federal paystub showing zero earnings for a closure pay period, a furlough or nonessential-status letter, or a signed letter from the contractor's officer, owner or human resources director tying the missed pay to the closure. The rule does not apply if you and the tenant have a separate signed agreement to hold off legal action or defer filing for 60 days or more, and it does not change other lease terms. If you rent a one-to-four-family home and your tenant is affected, you can get a 60-day stay of foreclosure by asking your lender, with the tenant's written proof, within 90 days of the closure or of its end, whichever is later. Nothing else changes: rent stays due on the lease date, Virginia has no shutdown grace period, late-fee moratorium or bar on filing, and nothing covers state or local government employees. A written payment agreement of 60 days or more is the practical alternative. See Declared Disasters and Emergencies and Eviction (Unlawful Detainer) Process.

title: No Local Bans on Long-Term Renting
bodyText: No Virginia locality may enact or enforce an ordinance that prohibits renting a residential dwelling unit for a lease term of 30 consecutive days or longer, and any local restriction on such rentals must be reasonable and may not go beyond the requirements for an owner-occupied home, or a home rented for 12 months or longer, in the same zoning district. So a single-family zone cannot be closed to long-term renting, and the owner does not have to live on the lot. What zoning can still do: limit the number of unrelated people who may live in a single-family dwelling, with fines of up to $2,000 for a conviction (and more if the violation is not abated) but no jail; no such fine accrues against an owner or managing agent while their court action against a tenant to end an overcrowding condition under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act is pending. Rentals of fewer than 30 days are short-term rentals, which localities may regulate through zoning and an annual registry. From July 1, 2027, a locality may require owner occupancy of an accessory dwelling unit or the main home only when the permit application is filed (see Accessory Dwelling Units). Private restrictions are not affected: recorded covenants, condominium instruments and property owners' association declarations may still limit leasing, and those rules bind your tenant through the association (see Homeowner / Condominium Association Compliance). See also Local Landlord-Tenant Rules and Rent Control.

title: Smart Locks and App-Based Entry
bodyText: Virginia has no statute written specifically for smart locks, keypad codes or app-based entry in rental housing, and no rule letting a domestic violence survivor ask a device-account manager to cut off another person's access. The general rules apply to electronic access just as to keys. Entry: using a code or app to enter does not change the entry rules. You may enter without consent only in an emergency; otherwise, unless it is impractical, you must give notice of your intent to enter (at least 72 hours for routine maintenance the tenant did not request), enter at reasonable times, and not use access to harass. An unlawful or unreasonable entry lets the tenant seek an injunction or end the lease, with damages and attorney fees. Lockouts: you may not deactivate a tenant's code or app access to keep the tenant out without a court order for possession. A willful lockout lets the tenant petition the general district court, with a hearing within five days, and recover actual damages, statutory damages of $5,000 or four months' rent, whichever is greater, and attorney fees. Court orders: when a tenant with a non-ex parte order excluding a co-tenant gives you a copy, you may not give keys to the excluded person; treat the excluded person's codes and app credentials the same way and remove them. Records: entry logs and account data about a tenant are tenant records, which you may release to third parties only in the cases the Act allows, such as with the tenant's prior written consent. Large properties: if you own more than 200 units attached to the same property, your written key policies must cover electronic key codes, including their deactivation. Any charge for a smart-lock or app service is rent and must appear in the lease's first-page fee disclosure or a later addendum. See Key-Control Policies for Large Properties, Entry, Access and Temporary Relocation and No Self-Help Eviction.

title: No Smoke-Drift Statute
bodyText: Virginia has no statute on tobacco or other smoke drifting between units, so there is no smoke-drift duty for a lease to waive, and no statute that lets you waive one. A clause making the tenant release you from claims about a neighbor's smoke still does not hold to the extent it releases liability you have to the tenant under law, because a lease may not exculpate or limit your liability to the tenant arising under law or waive the tenant's rights under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, which include your duty to keep the premises fit and habitable (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1208). What you can do is ban smoking: no Virginia statute limits a residential smoking ban, and the library's smoking policy clause bans smoking anywhere on the property; the tenant must also keep guests from disturbing neighbors' peaceful enjoyment and follow your reasonable rules. The Virginia Indoor Clean Air Act is narrow: smoking is banned in elevators regardless of capacity (including apartment elevators), but apartment hallways and lobbies are not on its lists, and it has no general smoke-free workplace rule for areas where building staff work. Localities may not set stricter smoking rules than the Act except as it allows. If the building is in a property owners' association or condominium, the association may adopt reasonable rules restricting smoking, including inside attached units, which bind your tenant through the association's rules.

title: No Eviction Defense for Late Benefit Payments
bodyText: Virginia has no eviction defense, continuance or stay for a tenant who fell behind because a Social Security payment, public assistance check, housing voucher payment or other government benefit arrived late. The ordinary nonpayment rules apply (see The Notice for Unpaid Rent). What can help such a tenant: before or at the first court date the tenant, or anyone on the tenant's behalf, may pay everything owed and have the case dismissed; a tenant who presents a written commitment from a local government or nonprofit to pay the full amount within 10 days gets a 10-day continuance; and later the tenant may still cancel the eviction by paying all amounts claimed at least 48 hours before it (see The Tenant's Right of Redemption). Where the general district court runs the Eviction Diversion Program, an eligible tenant who pays at least 10 percent at the first hearing gets a three-month court payment plan. A tenant who asks for a continuance without a good-faith defense must, at your request, pay the rent due into court. The only income-interruption continuance in Virginia law is for federal employees and contractors unpaid in a federal government closure (see Federal Government Shutdowns and Rent). If the tenant uses a housing voucher or other rental assistance, the termination notice must show the statewide legal aid phone number and website on its first page, and a public housing authority must include income-recertification information with its nonpayment notice.

title: Housing Vouchers and Source of Funds
bodyText: Virginia's Fair Housing Law protects source of funds: any source that lawfully provides funds to or on behalf of a renter, including any assistance, benefit or subsidy program run by a government or a private body, so housing vouchers are covered. You may not refuse to rent or negotiate, set different terms, say a unit is unavailable, or advertise a preference ("no vouchers", "no Section 8") because of a person's source of funds (Va. Code Ann. §§ 36-96.1:1, 36-96.3). Exemptions: an owner who owns no more than four rental units in Virginia at the time may decline based on source of funds, unless the owner, individually or through a business entity, owns more than a 10 percent interest in more than four Virginia rental units; and any owner may deny or limit a rental if the assistance source isn't approved within 15 days after the person submits the request for tenancy approval (Va. Code Ann. § 36-96.2). The general exemptions for a private owner of up to three single-family houses renting without a broker and for an owner-occupied building of up to four units also apply, but never to discriminatory advertising. Voucher tenants also get a notice protection: a private landlord's notice of termination to a tenant receiving tenant-based rental assistance is not effective unless its first page shows the statewide legal aid telephone number and website address (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1202). From January 1, 2027, refusing to renew a tenant who receives tenant-based rental assistance is listed as retaliation when it follows a protected complaint or other protected act, unless you fail to renew for good cause (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1258). No Virginia statute requires the lease to say anything about source of funds or vouchers. Local governments can't add their own landlord-tenant rules (edu-local-preemption-va), though a locality may keep enforcing, and amend consistently with state law, a fair housing ordinance it had on January 1, 1991 (Va. Code Ann. § 36-96.21). Screening tip: apply any income test to the tenant's share of the rent (edu-tenant-screening-va). See edu-fair-housing-va for the other protected classes.

title: No Special District Statement
bodyText: Virginia has no rule that a lease state, or that you tell a tenant, that the property lies in a special taxing, service, assessment or improvement district, or that the tenant knows of a district's charges or plans. Localities may create service districts to provide additional, more complete or more timely government services in part of the locality, and other districts and authorities (such as community development authorities and transportation improvement districts) exist, but none of their statutes requires a statement to tenants. If you want a tenant to share a district charge billed to the building, the only route the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act describes is the local government fee allocation (see Passing Local Government Fees to Tenants), and any such charge must be in the lease's first-page fee list or a later signed addendum. A lease with an option to buy a property of one to four units is a transfer under the Residential Property Disclosure Act, so its seller-side disclosure rules apply to that option; those rules are outside this row.

title: No Sprinkler Disclosure Rule
bodyText: Virginia does not require you to tell a prospective or current tenant whether the building has fire sprinklers, in the lease or anywhere else, and the lease disclosures Virginia does require do not include one. There is also no Virginia grant, loan or tax credit aimed at sprinkler retrofits, and no credit you could pass to a tenant. Two general programs can help with the cost as part of a larger project: housing revitalization zone grants, for qualifying rehabilitation or new construction of housing units in a zone a locality has designated, count fire suppression systems among eligible improvement costs, and enterprise zone real property investment grants, for commercial, industrial or mixed-use buildings in an enterprise zone, do the same. Both have minimum investment levels and caps. If you describe the building's fire protection in a listing or lease, describe it accurately: a misstatement of a material fact to a prospective tenant can be a deceptive practice. See Fire Sprinklers in Rental Buildings and Virginia Required Lease Disclosures and Their Timing.

title: Leases That Must Be in Writing
bodyText: Virginia's statute of frauds draws the line at one year. No one can be sued on a lease for more than a year unless the lease, or a memorandum or note of it, is in writing and signed by the person being sued or that person's agent; the writing need not state the consideration. An agreement that cannot be performed within a year, and a promise to answer for another person's debt (such as a guaranty of the tenant's rent), need a signed writing too. An electronic record and electronic signature satisfy these writing and signature rules when both sides have agreed to do business electronically. Two other length rules matter. An unwritten contract for a term of more than five years in real estate is void against later buyers for value without notice and creditors. And even a written lease is void against later buyers for value without notice and lien creditors until it is recorded where the property lies; the tenant's possession alone is not notice to a buyer (see Recording a Lease). The Residential Landlord and Tenant Act adds its own one-year rule: if one side never signs and delivers the written lease but the lease takes effect because the landlord accepted rent, or the tenant accepted possession or paid rent, without reservation, a lease written for more than one year is effective for only one year. A lease for one year or less may be oral, but you must still offer a written lease, and if you offer none the law creates a 12-month tenancy on statutory terms. The statute of frauds does not mention assignments or surrenders of leases; put them in a signed writing, and an early termination of a residential lease by agreement must be in writing under the Act.

title: Statutory Caps on Landlord Charges
bodyText: These are the limits the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act puts on what you may charge a tenant. Dollar and percentage caps: security deposit, however named, no more than two months' periodic rent; deposit plus damage-insurance and renter's-insurance premiums paid before the tenancy starts, together no more than two months' periodic rent; application fee no more than $50 ($32 for public housing or other HUD-regulated housing), plus actual third-party screening costs; late charge no more than the lesser of 10 percent of the periodic rent or 10 percent of the remaining balance, and only if the written lease provides for it; bad-check processing fee as the lease specifies, up to $50; sheriff's or process server's service of a notice or process, up to $12; utility late charge under submetering or ratio billing, up to $5, not due sooner than 15 days after the bill; and holdover liquidated damages up to 150 percent of the per diem of the monthly rent per day (the per diem itself for HUD-regulated housing). Actual-cost caps: card or electronic payment fees no more than the third party's actual charge (and only if a no-fee method is offered); utility billing service charges limited to the third-party provider's actual costs; extra copies of tenant records at actual cost, if the lease provides; insurance you obtain for the tenant at its actual cost plus administrative fees; repairs after a tenant's breach at actual and reasonable cost; a new lock for a tenant with a court order excluding a co-tenant at your actual cost. Reasonable-charge limits: a carbon monoxide alarm the tenant asks for; removal of tenant-installed security devices and repair at move-out; copying utility billing records (until July 1, 2027); and the costs of selling or storing abandoned property, taken from the sale proceeds. Zero: no fee for maintenance or repair unless the tenant's violation of the Act made it necessary, and from July 1, 2027, for a landlord with more than four units, no additional late fees while a tenant keeps to a statutory payment plan. There is no cap on rent itself, on rent increases, or on pet deposits apart from the deposit cap.

title: Tenant's Legal Rights to End a Lease Early
bodyText: Virginia law lets a tenant end a lease early only in these situations, and a lease cannot take any of them away. (1) Military orders: permanent change of station, temporary duty over three months, discharge, orders to government quarters, or a stop-movement order of 30 days or more, on written notice effective at least 30 days after the next rent due date, with no liquidated damages (see Military Tenants: Right to End the Lease); federal law adds its own rights. (2) Family abuse, sexual assault, stalking or trafficking: 28 days' written notice with a protective order or a conviction, warrant, summons, information or indictment, rent owed through that date and no liquidated damages (see Domestic and Sexual Violence Protections). (3) Your breach: a 21-day cure notice ending the lease at least 30 days after you receive it, or a 30-day notice for a breach that can't be remedied or a repeated intentional breach (see Tenant's Remedies When You Breach). (4) Unfit at move-in: written notice within seven days, with a full refund. (5) Willful failure to deliver possession: five days' written notice. (6) Fire or casualty that substantially impairs the home: vacate and give written notice within 14 days (21 days from January 1, 2027). (7) Visible mold disclosed in the move-in report: the tenant may end the tenancy. (8) Missing pre-signing disclosures: within the first 30 days for military air zones, or within 60 days after discovering an uncleaned meth lab or defective drywall. (9) Unlawful or harassing entry, or a court order in a lockout, escrow or habitability case ending the lease at the tenant's request. Virginia has no right to end a lease because you made a fraudulent misrepresentation; a misled tenant's routes are the Consumer Protection Act and general contract law. Virginia also has no rule that leaving a required statement out of the lease forfeits rent or other money you are owed. When a sole tenant dies the lease ends by law (see When a Sole Tenant Dies). Otherwise early termination is by written agreement, or the tenant owes rent until the term ends or you re-rent, with your duty to mitigate.

title: No Radiator Cover Rule
bodyText: Virginia has no rule requiring radiator covers or guards on steam or hot-water radiators, on a tenant's request or otherwise, and no lease rider about them. Your general duties still apply: you must keep the heating system you supply in good and safe working order, the state Maintenance Code requires heating equipment to be kept in safe working condition, and you are liable for a tenant's actual damages caused by a failure to use ordinary care. Where a unit has exposed radiators or steam pipes and a young child or a person with limited mobility will live there, providing covers on request is a reasonable precaution. If the building was built before 1978, a painted radiator is a building component under Virginia's lead rules, so any work that disturbs old paint on it should follow lead-safe practices. See Heat: Season, Temperature and Remedies and Lead-Based Paint.

title: No Duty to Supply a Stove or Refrigerator
bodyText: Virginia law does not require you to provide a stove, oven, refrigerator or other kitchen appliance in a rental unit. The Residential Landlord and Tenant Act even contemplates units without them: a tenant whose unit lacks a refrigerator, stove or sink and who shares one with other units is a roomer, and still a tenant under the Act. Once you supply an appliance, you must keep it in good and safe working order, and the state Maintenance Code requires cooking appliances you provide to be maintained in safe working condition and able to perform their intended function. A stove or refrigerator is not on the Act's list of essential services, so its failure is handled under your general repair duty and the tenant's notice, rent escrow and repair remedies rather than the essential-service remedy (unless the problem also cuts off gas or electricity you supply). List the appliances you include in the lease (see Appliances & Equipment Included), and say plainly which ones are not included. See Repair Duties and Tenant Remedies.

title: No Special Student Housing Rules
bodyText: Virginia has no special landlord-tenant rules for student housing. A privately owned apartment or house rented to students is an ordinary residential tenancy under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, with the same deposit, notice, repair and eviction rules as any other, whether or not the tenants are students and whether the lease runs for a school year or a calendar year. Two exclusions in the Act can reach student living. Residence at a public or private institution is outside the Act if it is incidental to educational or similar services the institution provides, which covers a college's own residence halls; whether housing a private company runs under contract with a school is "incidental" to the school's services is not settled, so treat a privately run building as covered unless a lawyer advises otherwise. Occupancy by a member of a fraternal or social organization in the part of a structure operated for the organization's benefit is also outside the Act. Virginia has no statute on parent guarantors or co-signers for student leases; a guaranty is a contract governed by the general rules for promises to answer for another's debt, which must be in writing and signed. College dormitories have their own fire-safety rules, including smoke alarms and, for tall buildings, sprinklers. With several student tenants on one lease, see Joint & Several Liability.

title: Voucher Inspections and Refusing a Voucher
bodyText: Virginia has no rule written specifically about refusing a voucher holder because the program must inspect the unit first, or about a tenant who refuses a program inspection. The source-of-funds rules decide it. If you own more than four Virginia rental units (or more than a 10 percent interest in more than four), you may not refuse to rent, set different terms, or say a unit is unavailable because a person pays with a housing voucher or other assistance. Refusing the program's inspection or its required paperwork can look like refusing the voucher itself, so take part in the process as you would in any applicant's screening. You may deny or limit the rental if the program has not approved the tenancy within 15 days after the applicant submits the request for tenancy approval. An owner of four or fewer units (and no more than a 10 percent interest in more than four) may decline based on source of funds, and an owner who lives in a building of up to four units, and some owners of up to three single-family houses who rent without a broker, are exempt more broadly (see Housing Vouchers and Source of Funds). Once a voucher tenant has moved in, the program's own inspections and the family's duty to allow them are set by federal program rules (not covered here). Your own entry follows the Act: the tenant may not unreasonably refuse entry to inspect or repair, and you give notice and enter at reasonable times (see Landlord's Access). Deficiency deadlines and payment abatement are in Voucher Payments When a Unit Fails Inspection.

title: Voucher Payments When a Unit Fails Inspection
bodyText: Virginia law has no rule on how rent is split or reduced between a subsidized tenant and the housing agency when a unit fails an inspection or is partly unfit. For a Housing Choice Voucher unit, federal rules govern the agency's share. After an agency inspection other than the initial inspection (which has its own rules) finds a deficiency and the agency notifies you in writing, you must fix a life-threatening deficiency within 24 hours and any other within 30 calendar days or an extension it approves. The agency may withhold its payments once it has notified you; if you fix the problem in time it must resume them and pay what it withheld. If you don't, it must abate its payments, including amounts it had withheld, and if the unit still fails 60 days after its abatement notice (or a longer period it sets), it must terminate the payment contract. Abated payments are not made up after you repair. You may not end the family's tenancy because the agency withheld or abated its payment; the family does not owe the agency's share, and the agency's failure to pay is not a lease violation by the tenant. During an abatement the family may end the tenancy by notifying you and the agency. If the family or a guest caused the deficiency (beyond ordinary use), the agency may waive your duty to fix it, and then it may not withhold or abate your payment. These rules apply to payment contracts signed on or after June 6, 2024, or renewed after that date; older contracts follow the earlier version of the federal rule. Virginia's own remedies still apply to the tenant's share: in a rent escrow case or a habitability defense the court may reduce rent by an equitable amount. Whether a court's reduction reaches the agency's share is unsettled. For public housing and other units regulated by HUD, HUD's regulations control where they conflict with the Act. Fix deficiencies within the deadlines, keep repair records, and never bill the tenant for an agency share that was withheld or abated.

title: Late Fees and Housing Subsidies
bodyText: Virginia has no statute on late fees tied to the part of the rent a housing subsidy pays; the general limit applies (a late fee only if the written lease provides for it, capped at the lesser of 10 percent of the periodic rent or 10 percent of the remaining balance due and owed by the tenant). Federal rules control where they conflict with Virginia's landlord-tenant law for public housing and other HUD-regulated units (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1201). In the Housing Choice Voucher program the family is not responsible for the part of the rent the housing assistance payment covers, the housing authority's failure to pay is not a lease violation, and during the lease term you may not end the tenancy for it (24 C.F.R. § 982.310), so a late fee for a late or missing assistance payment can't be charged to the tenant; the HUD tenancy addendum also overrides any conflicting lease term. Cautious course: charge any late fee only on the tenant's own share and work it out from that share; check the program's own rules for public housing and project-based units. Virginia also has HUD-unit rules elsewhere: a $32 application fee cap (exclusive of actual third-party screening costs), a holdover penalty no higher than the daily rent, and the statewide legal aid number on the first page of a termination notice to a voucher tenant (Va. Code Ann. §§ 55.1-1202, 55.1-1203, 55.1-1253). Treating voucher holders worse because of their source of funds is unlawful unless you own no more than four rental units in Virginia (and no more than a 10 percent interest in more than four); an owner who lives in a building of up to four units, and some owners of up to three single-family houses who rent without a broker, are exempt more broadly (Va. Code Ann. §§ 36-96.2, 36-96.3; edu-source-of-funds-va).

title: Receivership and Repair Orders for Substandard Property
bodyText: Virginia allows a court-appointed receiver for substandard residential property only in a narrow case: a locality that has adopted a derelict-building ordinance may ask the circuit court to appoint the locality or a land bank entity as receiver to repair property containing residential dwelling units, but only if the property has been properly declared both a derelict building and blighted under the spot blight law, the owners have not complied with either, the locality has made good-faith efforts to get compliance, the repairs are needed to meet the Building Code, and they would not change the zoning use. A derelict building is one that might endanger public health, safety or welfare and for more than six months has been vacant, boarded up and not lawfully connected to electric, water or sewer service, so this remedy does not reach an occupied rental. The receiver contracts for the repairs within a period the court sets, never more than two years; its costs and reasonable attorney fees become a lien collectible like delinquent real estate taxes and can be enforced by a court-ordered sale. The owner may redeem before the two-year period ends or the sale is confirmed by paying the lien in full with the taxes, penalties, interest, attorney fees, costs and recorded liens, and the court must let the owner or a recorded lender make the repairs instead if they show they can finish in a reasonable time under a court schedule.
