Short of receivership, localities enforce repair through Building Code notices, fines and prosecution; may repair or secure an unsafe building after notice and charge the cost as a lien; may abate spot blight and nuisances at your cost; and, from July 1, 2026, may sue on a tenant's behalf over serious habitability failures. Tenants have their own rent escrow remedy, where a court can release escrowed rent to pay for repairs. There is no tenant-initiated receivership.

title: Property Tax Pass-Throughs
bodyText: Virginia has no statute written for real estate tax escalation clauses in residential leases. General lease law recognizes a tenant's covenant to pay taxes: in any lease, a covenant by the lessee "to pay the taxes" means the lessee will pay all taxes, levies and assessments on the leased premises, or on the lessor on account of them. And if a tax collector takes the owner's taxes from a tenant, the tenant may credit that payment against rent, unless the tenant is bound by an express contract to pay those taxes. For a residential tenancy under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, three rules make a mid-lease tax pass-through hard to use. The rent due each payment period must be itemized beginning on the first page of the lease, under the statutory sentence that no additional rent may be charged unless listed there or added later by a separate addendum; any money owed under the lease other than a deposit is rent. No one-sided change to the lease is valid without notice and both parties' written consent. And the local government fee allocation the Act allows covers fees and charges assessed against the building, such as stormwater or trash fees, not the real estate tax. The cautious course is to build expected taxes into the rent and adjust at renewal (with the 60-day notice a landlord with more than four Virginia units owes, 90 days for a rent increase from July 1, 2027), or, for a month-to-month or holdover tenancy, by written notice taking effect on the next rent due date at least 30 days later. The library offers no tax escalation clause for Virginia. An increase to the rent charged for similar market rentals is not retaliation, and from January 1, 2027 neither is an increase made under the lease's terms (see Renewals and Rent Increases).

title: Tenancies at Will
bodyText: The Residential Landlord and Tenant Act mentions a tenancy at will only once, and does not define it or set a separate notice to end one. Its one rule is that a notice from either side changing any term of a tenancy at will is itself a notice to vacate, and must be given as the lease or the law requires. So you cannot change the terms of an at-will arrangement and expect the tenant to stay on the new terms: the change ends the tenancy, and the tenant may choose to leave. Most arrangements with no fixed end date are not tenancies at will under the Act. Unless the written lease says otherwise, a tenancy is week-to-week for a tenant who pays weekly rent and month-to-month in all other cases, and either side ends it with written notice at least 7 days (week-to-week) or 30 days (month-to-month, unless the lease sets a different period) before the next rent due date. If you never offer a written lease, the law creates a 12-month tenancy. Where a true tenancy at will exists (for example, occupancy with permission but no agreement on rent or term), the Act sets no notice period, so the cautious course is written notice at least 30 days before the next rent due date, and a court eviction (unlawful detainer) if the occupant stays; never use self-help. A former owner who stays in a single-family home after a foreclosure sale becomes a tenant at sufferance, whom the buyer may end with a written termination notice given at least three days before termination; that rule is for foreclosure buyers, and a tenant in the home has other protections (see Selling or Losing a Rented Property).

title: When a Tenant Files for Bankruptcy
bodyText: Virginia has no statute of its own on what happens to an eviction when the tenant files for bankruptcy; federal bankruptcy law controls. The filing automatically stops most collection and eviction steps against the tenant, including starting or continuing an eviction case, enforcing a judgment, and any act to get possession, until the bankruptcy court lifts the stay or an exception applies. Two exceptions matter most. First, if you got a judgment for possession before the tenant filed, the stay does not block the eviction, unless the tenant files a certification that state law would let the tenant cure the entire monetary default after the judgment and deposits 30 days' rent with the bankruptcy court clerk, and then within 30 days certifies that the default has been cured; you may object, and the court holds a hearing. Because a Virginia tenant can cancel an eviction by paying all amounts claimed at least 48 hours before it, expect tenants to be able to use this certification. Second, an eviction based on endangering the property or illegal drug use on it can go forward 15 days after you file and serve a certification, unless the tenant objects and the court finds otherwise. A lease term ending the lease because the tenant files for bankruptcy or becomes insolvent is not enforceable in the bankruptcy. In a chapter 7 case, a residential lease the trustee does not assume within 60 days is deemed rejected; a trustee who assumes a lease in default must cure the default. Do not collect pre-filing rent, send collection notices or change the locks while the stay is in effect; ask the bankruptcy court for relief from the stay instead, or consult a bankruptcy lawyer.

title: Disclosing Tenant Information
bodyText: Virginia bars you and your managing agent from releasing information about a tenant or prospective tenant to a third party unless the person gave prior written consent or a listed exception applies: a matter of public record; a summary of the rent payment record; an unremedied material noncompliance notice or a termination notice where the tenant moved out; a request from a law-enforcement or public safety official in the performance of duties; a civil subpoena; the commissioner of the revenue; a contract purchaser who agrees in writing to keep it confidential; your lender for financing; the tenant's commanding officer, military housing officer or military attorney; your attorney or collection agency; an emergency; a new managing agent; or the census. Information an applicant gives you with an application is stricter: it may be released only in response to a subpoena. You may keep records with a third-party service provider and aren't liable under this rule for a breach of the provider's data unless you were grossly negligent or acted intentionally (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1209). Reference requests from other landlords are not a listed exception, so get the tenant's written consent first, except for a summary of rent payments, which you may share. A victim's protective order or other evidence is covered too (edu-dv-confidentiality-va). Full rules on records, copies and the 2027 ledger statement are in edu-tenant-records-va.

title: Housing Your Employees
bodyText: If you house an employee, whether the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act applies depends on the arrangement. The Act does not cover occupancy by your employee whose right to live in a unit in a multifamily building depends on employment in and about the premises (for example, a resident manager or maintenance worker), or by a former employee whose occupancy has continued less than 60 days. It also does not cover anyone who pays no rent under a rental agreement. An employee who pays rent for a single-family home, or for a unit not tied to work on the premises, is an ordinary tenant with all the Act's rights. Virginia has no statute requiring a signed disclosure of an employee's occupancy and vacating conditions, or an offer of a lease when the job ends. Put the terms in writing anyway: that occupancy depends on the job, what the employee pays (if anything), and how much time the employee will have to leave when the job ends. If a former employee does not leave, remove him through the courts with an unlawful detainer case, never by self-help; once a former employee's occupancy has continued 60 days or more, treat him as a tenant under the Act. Farm and fishing employers housing migrant workers must have a state permit for a migrant labor camp and follow the Board of Health's camp regulations. If an employee will have keys or key codes to other tenants' units, the key-control and background-check rules for large properties may apply (see Background Checks for Employees With Key Access).

title: Tenant's Insurance and Claims
bodyText: Virginia lets you require renter's insurance or damage insurance as the lease specifies, and sets rules on premiums, notices and policy summaries (see Renter's Insurance and Damage Insurance Rules). It has no rule on how insurance claims are handled between you and the tenant: no statute requires a tenant to claim on the tenant's own policy, to name you as an additional insured or interested party, or to waive subrogation against you, and none forbids those terms. They are contract terms, within these limits. A lease cannot make the tenant release or limit your liability under law, or indemnify you for it, so a tenant's policy is no substitute for repairs that are yours to make or for damage you or your agents cause. You may recover damage the tenant's side causes through the deposit, a repair bill due as rent, or damages; whether the tenant then claims it on the tenant's own policy is between the tenant and the insurer. If you buy renter's insurance for tenants, the policy must cover the tenant as an insured, and the summary or certificate you give before signing must say whether it contains a waiver of subrogation. You may recover the tenant's prorated share of other insurance you carry for the premises as rent, and funds you hold in escrow for a self-insurance program may pay its claims. Your own insurance does not cover the tenant's belongings, and if the lease does not require renter's insurance you must give the tenant a written notice saying so before signing (see Renter's Insurance and Flood Notice). If you want the tenant to name you on the policy, say so in the lease and keep the requirement to liability coverage for the tenant's own acts.

title: Online Tenant Portals
bodyText: Virginia law allows an online tenant portal but limits what you can require through it. Payments: you must accept rent and the security deposit by check and money order, so a portal cannot be the only way to pay. You may not charge any fee for collecting or processing a payment unless you also offer a payment method with no added fee, and a fee for card or electronic payment may not exceed the actual out-of-pocket cost a third party charges you. A landlord with four or fewer Virginia units need not accept debit or credit cards. Notices and signatures: notices may go electronically (for example through a portal or by e-mail) only if the lease provides for it, and a tenant may at any time elect paper notices; the sender must keep proof of electronic delivery. The electronic transactions law that gives electronic signatures and records their effect applies only between parties who have agreed to do business electronically; an agreement to do so buried in a standard-form lease does not count unless it is conspicuously displayed and separately consented to, and a tenant who agreed may still refuse to handle later transactions electronically, a right that cannot be waived. So keep paper and in-person methods available for anyone who declines the portal. Records: if you make tenant records available to each tenant by an electronic portal, you may not charge the tenant for access to it; an electronic copy of the lease kept for the tenant must be free. From July 1, 2027, a landlord with four or more Virginia units (or one receiving rental or utility assistance for the tenant) must answer a written request for records within 10 business days with a statement of all charges and payments, on paper or through a free portal. The library offers no separate portal clause; use the Acceptable Forms of Payment and Electronic Notices clauses.

title: Rent Escrow: How It Works and How the Money Is Released
bodyText: Your repair duties and the full list of tenant remedies are in Repair Duties and Tenant Remedies; this explains rent escrow, the remedy that holds rent in court. A tenant may file a tenant's assertion in the general district court if the unit has a material breach of the lease or the law, or a condition that threatens life, health or safety (such as no heat or water, no electricity, rodents, or lead paint you know about), and you failed to fix it within a reasonable time after the tenant's written notice or a government violation or condemnation notice. More than 30 days is presumed unreasonable. Until January 1, 2027 the tenant gets no relief without paying the rent into court within five days of each due date. From January 1, 2027 the tenant pays rent that comes due during the case into the court escrow account, need not first pay past-due rent, late charges or fees, and a missed escrow payment does not end the case, but you may then give a nonpayment notice and seek possession, and you may get a money judgment for what the lease says is owed. You win if you show the condition does not exist, has been fixed, was caused by the tenant, the tenant's family or their guests, or that the tenant unreasonably refused you entry to fix it. The first hearing is within 15 calendar days after you are served, sooner for emergencies such as no heat in winter. How the money comes out: escrowed rent is paid out only by court order after a hearing with notice to both sides, on a joint motion by you and the tenant, or when the inspector certifies that the court-ordered work is done. The court may pay it to you or to the tenant, keep the escrow running until the repair is made, reduce the rent (you must show why it should not be reduced), release money to you or a contractor you choose to make the repair (making sure it is spent on the repair), pay your mortgage to stop a foreclosure, or pay a creditor to prevent or satisfy a mechanic's lien. If the condition is not fully fixed within six months and you made no reasonable attempt to fix it, the court must give all the escrowed money to the tenant, and a new six-month period begins. If the tenant wins, the court may order you to pay the tenant's court costs and attorney fees. The escrow law has no penalty for a tenant who files in bad faith; that penalty (your costs, repair costs the tenant caused, and attorney fees) applies to a bad-faith habitability defense in your nonpayment case, and the court must sanction any court paper not grounded in fact. Escrow does not freeze evictions: no Virginia rule bars every eviction while a unit is unfit or rent is in escrow, but you may not retaliate against a tenant for a code complaint or a court action about the Act. A tenant who uses escrow for a breach cannot also use another remedy in that part of the Act for the same breach.

title: Tenant Organizing and Tenant Associations
bodyText: Virginia protects tenant organizing through its retaliation rule rather than a free-standing right to organize. Until January 1, 2027, you may not retaliate by raising rent, decreasing services, bringing or threatening an action for possession, or ending a periodic tenancy after you know a tenant has organized or become a member of a tenant organization; rent increases to market rates and service cuts that apply to all tenants are allowed (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1258). From January 1, 2027, the protection also covers participating in lawful activities of a tenants' organization and reaches more retaliatory acts: raising rent or fees, selectively decreasing services or enforcing rules, materially changing lease terms without consent, threatening, harassing or coercing the tenant, filing or threatening a possession action, ending a periodic tenancy, or refusing to renew a tenant with rental assistance; you are not liable where an exception applies, such as rent default when the case is filed or a termination notice given before the tenant organized. The tenant may recover actual damages and raise retaliation as a defense to a possession case (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1258). Manufactured home lot tenancies have a parallel retaliation section with its own wording; for example, until January 1, 2027 it bars only selective rent increases (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1314). Virginia law gives tenants no specific right to meet in common areas, to distribute literature, or to have you recognize or bargain with an association, so your common-area rules govern if applied evenly. In publicly supported housing of 10 or more units with affordability restrictions, a locality may require the owner to give the tenant association, along with tenants and the locality, 24 months' written notice before an affordability restriction ends (Va. Code Ann. §§ 36-176, 36-177). Related: edu-retaliation-va.

title: Screening Rental Applicants in Virginia
bodyText: Virginia regulates tenant screening in several statutes rather than one. Identity: you may copy an applicant's driver's license or similar photo identification (but not a U.S. government-issued identification where copying it would violate federal law) and may require a Social Security number or an IRS individual taxpayer identification number; application fees are capped (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1203; edu-application-fees-va). Criminal history: an application may require disclosure of criminal convictions and written consent to a criminal record check, and you may collect the exact out-of-pocket cost of the check; you need not rent to someone whose record of convictions involving harm to persons or property would make the person a clear and present threat to others' health or safety, and the fair housing law doesn't reach conduct based on a conviction for illegal manufacture or distribution of a controlled substance (Va. Code Ann. § 36-96.2). Sealed records: you may not require an applicant to disclose a sealed arrest, charge or conviction or deny an application solely because the applicant won't disclose one, and an application that asks about criminal history must tell applicants that sealed records need not be disclosed; a willful violation is a misdemeanor for each violation (Va. Code Ann. § 19.2-392.15). Screening companies must delete records they know have been sealed and must date their criminal-history reports with a warning that records may have been sealed since (Va. Code Ann. § 19.2-392.16). Eviction cases dismissed or nonsuited without an order of possession are expunged (edu-eviction-record-expungement-va). Family abuse: you must consider evidence that an applicant is a victim of family abuse to offset an otherwise qualified applicant's low credit score (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1203). COVID-era rule: a landlord with more than four Virginia units may not take adverse action based solely on payment history or a nonpayment eviction from the COVID-19 period, and must give a written denial notice (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1245; edu-portfolio-size-rules-va). From July 1, 2027, before you request or collect any payment or information, you must tell applicants in writing or by posting your fees and deposit and whether refundable, your selection criteria, automatic-denial criteria, other criteria that may lead to denial, the name and address of any consumer reporting agency you use, and the applicant's right to a free copy of the report and to dispute it (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1203). Fair housing: apply the same criteria to everyone and don't use a protected class, including source of funds, as a criterion (edu-fair-housing-va, edu-source-of-funds-va, edu-protected-class-inquiry-va). Federal credit reporting law: if you deny or take other adverse action based even in part on a consumer report, give the applicant notice of the action, the reporting agency's name, address and telephone number, a statement that the agency didn't make the decision, notice of the right to a free copy within 60 days and to dispute the report, and any credit score you used. Virginia has no rule that criminal checks wait for a conditional offer, no look-back limit, no rule on minimum-income tests and no statutory shield from negligence claims for renting to a person with a record. The cautious course: write your criteria down and apply them uniformly; tie any denial for criminal history to the statute's clear-and-present-threat standard, looking at the nature and age of the offense; and, because source of funds is protected, apply any income test to the tenant's share of the rent rather than the full rent (no Virginia case on income tests was looked at here).

title: Changing Lease Terms and Fees
bodyText: During a lease, no one-sided change to its terms is valid unless notice is given as the lease or the law requires and both you and the tenant agree to the change in writing (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1204). Rules and regulations are the one thing you may change during the term on your own: a new or changed rule binds the tenant after reasonable notice if it does not substantially modify the tenant's bargain; if it does, it needs the tenant's written consent. When the term ends and the tenant stays on as a holdover or month-to-month tenant with your agreement and no new lease, the old lease terms continue except rent, and a new rent amount set by written notice takes effect only on the next rent due date at least 30 days after the notice. To change other terms of a periodic tenancy, end it with the required notice and offer a new lease. In a tenancy at will, a notice changing any term is itself a notice to vacate and must be given as the lease or the law requires. Fees: the Act sets no separate, longer notice for raising a fee the lease already provides; an increase made under the lease's own terms is a change the tenant agreed to. Every security deposit and rent charge (and fees billed with rent are rent) must appear in the first-page fee list or in a later signed addendum, so a new or higher charge not covered by the lease needs an addendum the tenant signs. Raising rent after a tenant's protected complaint can already be retaliation, unless the new rent is what similar market rentals charge; from January 1, 2027 the rule also covers fees, and an increase made under the lease's terms is not retaliation. Landlords with more than four Virginia units also have renewal-notice deadlines for rent increases and nonrenewals; see Renewals and Rent Increases.

title: No Tenant Protection Exemption Notice
bodyText: Some states make a landlord whose property is exempt from a statewide rent cap or just-cause eviction law give the tenant a written exemption notice. Virginia has no such law, so there is nothing to be exempt from and no exemption notice to give. Virginia's own exclusions work without any notice: the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act does not apply to the occupancies it lists, such as transient lodging (see "Who the Virginia Residential Landlord and Tenant Act Covers"), and a landlord with four or fewer Virginia rental units needs no statement to fall outside the rules that apply only to larger landlords (see "Landlord Portfolio Size Rules"). Don't put a sentence in a lease saying the property is exempt from tenant protections: the Act applies unless a statute excludes the tenancy, and a lease term by which the tenant gives up the Act's rights is unenforceable (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1208).

title: No Rent Cap or Just-Cause Notice
bodyText: Virginia has no statewide rent cap and no just-cause eviction law, so there is no tenant-protection-act notice for a Virginia lease to carry. Cities and counties cannot add one: the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act supersedes local landlord-tenant ordinances, and no statute authorizes local rent control (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1201; see "Local Landlord-Tenant Rules and Rent Control"). You may raise rent at renewal with the notice Virginia requires and may end a periodic tenancy or decline to renew without giving a reason, as long as the real reason is not retaliation, discrimination or another reason the law forbids (see "No Just-Cause Eviction Rule" and "Landlord Portfolio Size Rules"). Two narrow price limits exist: during a declared state of emergency no one may lease housing at an unconscionable price in the emergency area (Va. Code Ann. §§ 59.1-526, 59.1-527), and a manufactured home community may not raise a tenant's lot rent at renewal while a locality's code-violation notice stays unresolved (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1320). Virginia also gives tenants of a house or apartment no general right to buy it when you sell; you must tell the tenant about a sale and who the buyer is (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1216). Tenant purchase notices apply only in two settings: a manufactured home park owner must give lot tenants a yearly notice of a resident entity's right of first refusal and opportunity to buy the park, and notice within five business days of signing a sales contract (Va. Code Ann. §§ 55.1-1308.3, 55.1-1308.4); and a building converted to condominium or cooperative ownership must give its tenants formal notice and 60 days to buy their units (Va. Code Ann. §§ 55.1-1982, 55.1-2164).

title: Virginia Tenant Rules With End Dates
bodyText: No core Virginia tenant protection is on a dated repeal clock. The Residential Landlord and Tenant Act and the Manufactured Home Lot Rental Act carry no sunset, and Virginia has no rent-cap or just-cause law that could expire. Many sections show a heading such as "Effective until July 1, 2027": those are scheduled amendments, where a new version takes over on that date, not repeals. One narrow rule does end on a date. A landlord who owns more than four Virginia rental units (or more than a 10 percent interest in more than four) may not take adverse action against an applicant based solely on payment history or an eviction for nonpayment from the COVID-19 period (March 12, 2020, through 30 days after the Governor's COVID-19 state of emergency ended), and a denial needs a written notice giving the applicant a chance to say that was the reason; the rule drops out of the Act on the later of July 1, 2028, or seven years after the COVID-19 state of emergency expired (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1245; see "Landlord Portfolio Size Rules"). Keep following it until then. The Eviction Diversion Program, which began as a pilot with an end date, is now printed in the Code with no end date (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1260). Check the current Code before relying on any rule near a version date.

title: No Duty to Translate a Virginia Lease
bodyText: Virginia doesn't require you to translate a lease or any notice, and sets no rule for leases negotiated in another language. One notice comes with a translation option: if a tenant asks for a translation of the renter's insurance and flood notice you must give when the lease doesn't require renter's insurance, you may help the tenant get a translator or refer the tenant to an electronic translation service; doing so is not a breach of your duties and doesn't make you liable for the translation's accuracy, and you may not charge for the help or referral (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1206). The same rule applies to manufactured home lot rentals. The Department of Housing and Community Development must translate the forms and documents it is required to create for landlords and tenants, including its model forms, into the five non-English languages most commonly spoken in Virginia and post them on its website (Va. Code Ann. § 36-139.02); offering a tenant the translated version of the Statement of Tenant Rights and Responsibilities (tenant-rights-statement-va) is a good practice. In federally assisted housing covered by the Violence Against Women Act, the notice of occupancy rights and certification form must be made available in multiple languages. If you negotiate in another language, a translated copy reduces later disputes about what was agreed.

title: Trespass Warnings and Barring Persons
bodyText: Virginia's criminal trespass law makes it a Class 1 misdemeanor for a person, without authority of law, to go or remain on the lands, buildings or premises of another, or any part of them, after being forbidden to do so orally or in writing by the owner, lessee, custodian, their agent or another person lawfully in charge, or by signs posted where they can reasonably be seen. As owner you may forbid non-tenants (for example, people with no tenant's invitation) from common areas and grounds. Inside a unit, the tenant is the lessee and decides who may visit. For a tenant's guest or invitee, the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act sets the procedure: you may bar the guest from the premises for conduct on your property that violates the lease, a local ordinance, or state or federal law by a written notice served personally on the guest that describes the conduct, with a copy served on the tenant. Once the guest has been served, you may apply to a magistrate for a trespass warrant, in addition to your remedies against the tenant, and the tenant may ask the general district court to review the bar. The Act does not say whether a tenant's guest can be barred from common areas by a simple trespass warning outside this procedure, so the cautious course is to follow it whenever the person is a tenant's guest or invitee. Your locality may by ordinance let you designate the local police in writing as a person lawfully in charge of the property, so officers can give trespass warnings on your behalf. Do not post No Trespassing signs on land you have no authority over, which is itself a misdemeanor. If a barred person is a household member barred because of family abuse, special protections apply (see Domestic and Sexual Violence Protections).

title: No Truth in Renting Act
bodyText: Virginia has no Truth in Renting Act, and no rule requiring a truth-in-renting notice in the lease. Its counterpart is the state's Statement of Tenant Rights and Responsibilities, a plain-language summary the Department of Housing and Community Development publishes and you must give with every written lease you offer, with an acknowledgment form both parties sign (see State Tenant Rights and Responsibilities Statement). Virginia also does not penalize you simply for offering a lease that contains a forbidden term. Such a term is unenforceable, and if you sue to enforce it the tenant may recover actual damages and reasonable attorney fees. Among the terms a Virginia lease may not contain: a waiver of the tenant's rights or remedies under the Act, a confession of judgment, an agreement to pay your attorney fees except as the Act provides, a release or limit of your liability to the tenant or an indemnity for it, and upfront deposits and insurance premiums above two months' rent (see Lease Terms Virginia Prohibits). Using a void penalty or liquidated damages clause in a lease, or trying to collect under one, can also be a prohibited practice under the Consumer Protection Act (see Virginia Consumer Protection Act and Rentals). Remove any clause you know is unenforceable.

title: No Unbundled Parking Rule
bodyText: Virginia has no unbundled-parking rule. Nothing requires you to include parking in the rent, to offer it separately, or to let a tenant decline it and pay less, and nothing caps what you charge for a space. How a parking charge must be handled: money owed to you under the lease is rent under the Virginia Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, so a monthly parking charge is rent and belongs in the itemized charges that must begin on the first page of the lease (or in a later addendum). You cannot add a parking charge or change parking terms during the lease without the tenant's written consent, and a parking rule adopted mid-lease that substantially changes the tenant's bargain needs the tenant's written consent. Zoning is a separate matter: near transit stations, localities may not require more than half a parking space per apartment in new multifamily development, which may leave fewer spaces to go around. To offer parking separately, write it into the lease as an optional add-on with its own charge listed in the fee disclosure, and assign the space with the Assigned Parking Space(s) clause. See Fees Count as Rent and Fee Disclosure Statement.

title: No Unconscionability Statute for Leases
bodyText: Unlike many states, Virginia's Residential Landlord and Tenant Act has no unconscionability section letting a court refuse to enforce an unfair lease term or settlement. Virginia's statutory unconscionability rules are elsewhere and do not cover a lease of a home: the Uniform Commercial Code rules for sales of goods and for leases of goods (a "lease" there means a lease of goods, not of real property), the rule for cooperative interests in the Real Estate Cooperative Act, the computer-information statute, and the rules for marital and mediation agreements. Two other statutes reach part of the ground. During a declared disaster, the Post-Disaster Anti-Price Gouging Act makes it unlawful to lease or offer to lease necessary goods and services, which include housing, at an unconscionable price within the emergency area. And the Consumer Protection Act bars a landlord's misrepresentations and fraudulent practices, including using a void penalty clause or waiver of defense in a lease. Whether a court may still refuse an unconscionable lease term under general contract law is a matter of case law. In practice the Act's own list of prohibited terms, and the rule that a lease cannot waive the tenant's rights under the Act, do most of the work an unconscionability statute does elsewhere.

title: Interest on Unpaid Rent and Damages
bodyText: Virginia's landlord-tenant law sets no interest rate on unpaid rent or damages and doesn't require the lease to state one. General law fills the gap. Where there is an obligation to pay interest but no agreed rate, the legal rate of 6 percent a year applies (Va. Code Ann. § 6.2-301). In a suit, the court may award interest on the amount it awards from a date it fixes; if the judgment says nothing, it bears the judgment rate from entry. The judgment rate is 6 percent, or, for a judgment on a contract, the rate lawfully charged on the contract if that is higher (Va. Code Ann. §§ 6.2-302, 8.01-382). So a lease rate can raise what a judgment for damages earns, but two cautions apply. Interest charged on late rent is a charge for late payment, and every late charge is capped at the lesser of 10 percent of the periodic rent or 10 percent of the remaining balance due, so interest and a late fee on the same rent must together stay inside that cap (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1204). And Virginia's 12 percent limit applies to interest on a loan or forbearance of money; whether a lease charge on overdue amounts is a forbearance is unsettled, so keep any lease rate at or below 12 percent (Va. Code Ann. §§ 6.2-300, 6.2-303). The library does not offer a Virginia clause charging interest on unpaid amounts.

title: Leasing When You Hold Only a Life Estate
bodyText: Virginia law has no usufruct; the closest Virginia interest is a life estate (for example, a parent who deeded a house to the children but kept the right to live in it or rent it out for life). If you lease property you hold only for your life, or under another interest that ends on an uncertain event, the lease does not simply end when your interest does: when you die or your interest ends, the tenant may stay through the end of the current year of the tenancy, paying rent. Rent payable in money is split between you (or your estate) and the people who take the property next, according to time (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1703). After that, the people who take the property (the remaindermen) are not bound by a lease they didn't sign. If you want a lease that runs past your own interest, the remaindermen must join it, or, where they can't consent (for example because they are minors or not yet born), a circuit court can approve a lease of the full property (Va. Code Ann. §§ 8.01-94, 8.01-95). Tell a prospective tenant that you hold a life estate, and name the remaindermen in your records, so the tenant knows who will be the landlord if your interest ends. The written owner and manager disclosure you give at the start of the tenancy must be kept current, and that duty binds whoever succeeds you as landlord (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1216).

title: Utility Allowances and Cost Caps on Utility Billing
bodyText: Virginia has no statute on utility allowances. A lease may include utilities in the rent, and a fixed allowance with the tenant paying any overage is a lawful term if you set it up so that you never collect more than the utility actually charged. The cost caps: if you bill tenants for electricity, gas, water or sewer that you buy from a utility, you stay outside utility regulation only if you charge each tenant just the part of your bill that comes from that tenant's use, plus the billing service charges the lease allows, and keep three years of billing records. In an apartment building that is not individually metered, the State Corporation Commission's submetering rules must also bar any charge above the utility's own rate, demand and customer charges and taxes; the Commission can penalize violations, and the tenant can sue for breach of the lease. Virginia has no rule like New Hampshire's that allows electricity in a master-metered building to reach tenants only through a fixed rent: submetering, allocation equipment and ratio billing are all allowed for electricity if the lease clearly says so (in an apartment building, submeters or allocation equipment must serve every unit as far as the building allows). Practical setup: use an allowance clause only for a utility on a utility-owned meter that serves only the rented home, bill the overage for the same period the utility bills you, give the tenant at least 15 days to pay after you deliver the bill, and let the tenant see the bills. Overage payments are rent under the Virginia Residential Landlord and Tenant Act. For a shared meter, use the Utilities Billed by Landlord clause and its allocation method instead. The library's optional Utility Allowance clause follows these rules.

title: Dividing Shared-Meter Utilities Among Tenants
bodyText: Virginia allows you to make tenants pay for utilities that are not separately metered to their unit, if the lease clearly says so. In a building where several units share one utility-owned meter, you may use a ratio utility billing system, in place of a rent increase, to divide the actual or anticipated water, sewer, electric, oil or natural gas bills among the tenants by square footage, occupancy, number of bedrooms or another method the lease states. You may instead install submeters or energy allocation equipment. You may also divide local government fees billed to the building (stormwater, recycling, trash collection, elevator or fire safety testing, rental inspection programs) the same way if the lease clearly says so. With submeters, allocation equipment or ratio billing you may charge the billing service fees the lease lists to cover your actual third-party billing costs and a late charge of up to $5, payable no sooner than 15 days after the bill is sent; with local government fees the service fees may cover your actual cost of administering the program; ratio-billed amounts' late charges, and allocated local government fees with their administrative charges, count as rent. Keep adequate billing records and let tenants inspect and copy them. A tenant in a ratio-billed unit may not install a plug-in solar device under the 2027 portable solar law. From July 1, 2027, your records must show how monthly billing fees are calculated and each tenant's billing fee payment history, and nonpayment termination notices and requested statements of charges must include the tenant's utility debits and credits. Unlike Connecticut, Virginia does not void a lease term that makes the tenant pay for utilities not metered to the unit. Use the library's Utilities Billed by Landlord clause.

title: Utility Deposits and Final Utility Bills
bodyText: Virginia has no separate rule for a utility deposit held by a landlord. Money you hold to secure the tenant's payments is a security deposit however it is labelled, so a utility deposit counts toward the two-month cap and follows the 45-day return rules (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-1226). What Virginia does allow is holding back part of the security deposit for the tenant's final water, sewer or other utility bill owed to a third-party provider under the lease. You may withhold a reasonable portion only if you told the tenant in writing of these rights and duties in the termination notice, in a written notice confirming the vacating date, or in a separate written notice at least 15 days before the deposit disposition. Once you pay the bill, you must send written confirmation and any balance within 10 days. If the tenant gives you written confirmation that the final bill is paid, refund within the 45 days, or within 10 days of the confirmation if it comes later; the same applies if you learn of payment another way. Water and sewer authorities may take their own deposit from a tenant who opens service in the tenant's name (Va. Code Ann. § 15.2-2119.4), public utilities must pay interest on customer deposits and return them after no more than a year of satisfactory credit (Va. Code Ann. § 56-247.1), and an unclaimed utility deposit is presumed abandoned one year after service ends (Va. Code Ann. § 55.1-2510).

title: No Separate Utility Disclosure Attachment
bodyText: Virginia requires no separate utility disclosure attached to the lease, and prescribes no utility exhibit, type size, page position or separate signature for one. What it does require: if you bill tenants through submeters, allocation equipment or ratio billing, or divide local government fees among them, the lease itself must clearly say so, and service charges for billing must be agreed in the lease. The lease must also itemize, beginning on its first page, the security deposit, the rent due each period and any one-time charges due before or with the first payment, under the statutory sentence that no other deposit or rent will be charged unless listed or added by a later addendum; utility amounts you bill are rent, so name them there and point to the utility clause. From July 1, 2027, a nonpayment termination notice must include the tenant's utility debits and credits when the lease provides for submetering, allocation or ratio billing. If the tenant will hold water and sewer service in the tenant's own name, a copy of the lease can serve as your authorization to the local provider. Use the library's Utilities Billed by Landlord clause and Fee Disclosure Statement; attaching a utility summary is good practice but not required.

title: Getting Notice of a Tenant's Utility Shutoff
bodyText: Water and sewer from a locality or water and sewer authority: you can be told about a tenant's unpaid bill without the tenant's permission. If you ask the provider in writing to be notified of a tenant's delinquent water or sewer bill and give an email address, it must email you when the bill is 15 days delinquent. Before it shuts off service it must give the tenant at least 10 business days' written notice with a copy to you, and on request it must give you information about a current or former tenant's account. Ask for this when you sign the owner's authorization for the tenant's account. Electricity and gas: no Virginia statute lets you, or lets the tenant authorize you, to receive a utility's disconnection notices for the tenant's account. The statutes require the utility to send its notices to its own customer: a copy of its disconnection policy, and notice of nonpayment by at least two methods (mail, email, text, phone call or door hanger) before a disconnection (one method for a utility run by a locality). The State Corporation Commission's disconnection and submetering rules do not provide one either. Whether a utility offers a third-party notice service that a tenant can use to name you is up to the utility's own terms of service, which this library has not reviewed; ask the utility. If one is offered, the lease can ask the tenant to name you, but the library has no clause for it. Separately, a tenant may name a third party to receive copies of your notices to the tenant; that runs the other way. See Local Utility Liens for a Tenant's Unpaid Bills and Utility Disconnection Rules.

title: Never Cut Off a Submetered Tenant's Utilities
bodyText: Never use a submeter, a disconnect switch or a load limiter to cut or reduce a tenant's electricity, gas or water because the tenant has not paid you, whether for rent or for utility charges you bill. Heat, central air conditioning you supply, running and hot water, electricity and gas are essential services, and a landlord who willfully, without a court order, interrupts or causes the interruption of one faces a court petition heard within five days. The court can order service restored, and at a full hearing the tenant recovers actual damages plus statutory damages of $5,000 or four months' rent, whichever is greater, and attorney fees, and may end the lease with the deposit returned. You also may not take possession by interrupting an essential service. If you fail to supply an essential service the lease requires, willfully or negligently, the tenant after written notice and reasonable time to fix it may recover reduced rental value or move to substitute housing rent-free for that period, plus attorney fees. The lawful route for unpaid utility charges you bill is the same as for rent: those charges are rent, so give a written nonpayment notice and, if needed, go to court; from July 1, 2027 that notice must list the tenant's utility debits and credits. Planned interruptions: Virginia has no rule on advance notice of a repair outage. Shut services off only as long as the work needs, tell tenants beforehand when you can, and follow the entry-notice rules if you need to enter units. The State Corporation Commission's submetering rules govern billing for submetered electricity and gas (bills on actual readings within 15 days of the utility's bill, a final reading on the move-out date) and give you no disconnection procedure of your own. See No Self-Help Eviction and Submetered Electricity and Gas: Lease Statement and Utility Rules.

title: Utilities in the Landlord's Name: Shutoffs and Tenant Remedies
bodyText: When a utility account is in your name, because the lease says you supply the utility or because one meter serves several units, keeping it paid is your job. Heat, running and hot water, electricity and gas (and central air conditioning you supply) are essential services. If service stops because you did not pay: the tenant, after written notice and a reasonable time for you to fix it, may recover the reduced rental value or move to substitute housing and owe no rent for that period, plus attorney fees; a lack of heat, running water, light or electricity also supports rent escrow in court, where rent can be abated, and a written repair demand that you must act on within 14 days. If you let service be cut off deliberately, the tenant can petition for an order restoring it and recover actual damages, statutory damages of $5,000 or four months of rent (whichever is greater) and attorney fees. Virginia's statutes give tenants no right to pay your utility bill and deduct it from rent (the repair-and-deduct remedy covers invoices from licensed contractors and pest control businesses only), no tenant rent-receivership for unpaid utilities, no damages for failing to identify tenants to the utility, and no duty on a master-meter owner to notify the utility. Water and sewer from a locality or authority on your account: if a bill goes unpaid the provider notifies you after 30 days and may shut off service after 60 days with at least 10 business days' written notice to you, unless health officers certify that shutting off the water would endanger the occupants. The statute does not require notice to each tenant. Commission-regulated electric and gas utilities must wait until the account is 60 days in arrears (45 days for a utility run by a locality), offer payment help, and not disconnect in extreme heat or cold or on Fridays, weekends or holidays (see Utility Disconnection Rules). The State Corporation Commission's disconnection and submetering rules say nothing about notifying each unit before a building's master-metered service is shut off, or about letting tenants keep service by paying; whether a utility does either is set in its own terms of service, which this library has not reviewed.

title: Utility Disconnection Rules
bodyText: Virginia's utility disconnection rules protect the utility's residential customer, whether that is you or your tenant. Weather and days: an electric utility may not disconnect a residential customer for nonpayment when the forecast low is 32 degrees Fahrenheit or below, or the forecast is 92 degrees or above, within the 24 hours after the scheduled disconnection; a gas utility may not when the forecast low is 32 degrees or below; and a water or wastewater utility may not when the forecast is 92 degrees or above. No residential disconnection for nonpayment may happen on a Friday, weekend, state holiday or the day before a state holiday. These rules cover State Corporation Commission-regulated utilities and utilities run by localities. Notice and arrears: a Commission-regulated electric, gas, water or wastewater utility may not disconnect for nonpayment until the account is 60 days in arrears and it has offered payment help, must give notice by at least two methods (mail, email, text, phone call or door hanger), and must give its disconnection policy, with payment-plan and energy assistance information, in English, Spanish and certain other languages. An electric or gas utility must also give 10 days' notice by mail, and a regulated water utility 10 days' written notice and no shutoff until 20 days after the bill was due. A utility run by a locality must wait until 45 days in arrears and give notice by at least one method. Local water and sewer: shutoff only after 60 days' delinquency and at least 10 business days' written notice (to a tenant account holder, with a copy to you), and not if health officers certify it would endanger the occupants. Emergencies: when the Governor declares a state of emergency for a communicable disease, these utilities may not disconnect residential customers for nonpayment for 30 days. There is no other mandatory moratorium for storms or declared disasters; utilities may suspend disconnections voluntarily. Serious medical conditions: under the Commission's rules, an investor-owned electric utility, electric cooperative, natural gas utility or public water or wastewater utility must, at the customer's request, delay a nonpayment disconnection at least 30 days beyond the notice when a Serious Medical Condition Certification Form signed by a physician or nurse practitioner is on file for the customer or a household member, or 15 days while the customer gets one; it must restore service cut off in the previous 14 days once the form is in; and a customer may use the delay twice in 12 months. What it means for you: a tenant must keep tenant-paid utilities on, and a loss of heat or water caused by the tenant's own failure to pay a utility the tenant is responsible for does not support rent escrow. If the account is yours, see Utilities in the Landlord's Name: Shutoffs and Tenant Remedies.

title: No Cutoff for Utilities the Tenant Did Not Transfer
bodyText: Virginia has no rule letting a lease authorize you to shut off a utility still in your name because the tenant has not moved it into the tenant's own name, and acting on such a clause is risky. Heat, running and hot water, electricity and gas are essential services; a landlord who willfully, without a court order, interrupts or causes the interruption of one while the tenant is in possession faces a five-day court hearing, an order to restore service, actual damages, statutory damages of $5,000 or four months of rent (whichever is greater) and attorney fees, and you may not use an interruption to get the unit back. Closing an account in your name so that service stops can be treated the same way. The library does not offer a cutoff clause for Virginia. What works instead: require in the lease that the tenant put the utilities in the tenant's own name by the move-in date (the optional Tenant Utility Accounts clause; for water and sewer, a copy of the lease serves as your authorization to the local provider), and keep service on until the tenant's account is open. If the tenant does not transfer, the failure is a lease breach: you may give a written notice that the lease will end in 30 days if the tenant does not fix it within 21, and recover what you paid for the tenant's use as damages. A tenant must keep tenant-paid utilities on during the tenancy. Ask the utility whether it can move the account straight from your name to the tenant's without a break in service.

title: No State Incentive for Renting to Veterans
bodyText: Virginia offers landlords no tax credit, grant or other state incentive for renting to veterans, and has no statute authorizing a veterans' rent concession. The real property tax exemption for veterans with a 100 percent service-connected, permanent and total disability applies to the veteran's own home and expressly excludes an interest held under a leasehold, so it does not reach a tenant or a landlord's rental property. What Virginia does have is a protection: military status (members of the uniformed forces and their reserve components, veterans, and certain dependents) is a protected class under the Virginia Fair Housing Law. You may not refuse to rent to someone, or discriminate in the terms, conditions or privileges of a rental, because of military status, and you may not make, print or publish any notice, statement or advertisement indicating a preference, limitation or discrimination based on military status. Because that advertising rule speaks of any preference based on military status, whether a rent discount or fee waiver offered only to veterans is lawful in Virginia is not settled. The cautious course is not to advertise or offer a veterans-only concession; if you want to help veterans, accept housing assistance they receive (refusing a lawful source of rent money is generally prohibited, subject to the Fair Housing Law's exemptions; see Housing Vouchers and Source of Funds), and follow the servicemember rules (see Servicemember Rights and Military Tenants: Right to End the Lease).

title: No Water Heater Temperature Rule
bodyText: Virginia has no rule telling you to set a water heater to a maximum (or minimum) temperature, before a new tenant moves in or at any other time. What the law does require: you must supply running water and reasonable amounts of hot water at all times, unless the unit is built so that the hot water comes from equipment under the tenant's exclusive control or from a direct public utility connection, and you must keep the water heater you supply in good and safe working order. The state Maintenance Code requires water heating facilities to be maintained, with a combination temperature and pressure-relief valve and its discharge pipe kept on every water heater. Limits on how hot water may be delivered at showers and tubs come from the plumbing codes that apply when the fixtures are installed; a plumber setting or replacing equipment follows them. Hot water is an essential service, so a willful or negligent failure to supply it gives the tenant the essential-service remedies, and a lack of hot water can support rent escrow, a defense to a nonpayment eviction, and repair by a licensed contractor after 14 days' written notice. Setting a safe temperature at turnover is still good practice, and a scald from equipment you control is judged under your duty of ordinary care. See Heat: Season, Temperature and Remedies and Repair Duties and Tenant Remedies.

title: No Waterbed Statute
bodyText: Virginia has no statute on waterbeds or other liquid-filled furniture. Nothing gives a tenant a right to have one, and nothing stops you from prohibiting them or allowing them on conditions. Put the rule in the lease, or in written rules given to the tenant at signing: a rule must protect safety, welfare or your property, be reasonably related to that purpose, apply fairly to all tenants and be clear. A rule you add after signing binds the tenant only with reasonable notice and only if it is not a substantial change to the bargain; otherwise the tenant must agree in writing. If you allow a waterbed, you may require renter's insurance as specified in the lease, which includes personal liability coverage. Any extra charge for allowing one is rent and must appear in the lease's first-page fee disclosure or a later addendum, and it may not be a charge for maintenance or repair. The tenant is responsible for damage the tenant deliberately or negligently causes to the premises, and you may recover it from the security deposit (less reasonable wear and tear) or as damages. If a waterbed is allowed, consider stating in the lease where it may be placed and that it must be of a type designed for the floor it sits on. See Rules and Regulations and Damage Caused by the Tenant.

title: Window Guards and Window Bars
bodyText: Virginia has no rule requiring you to install child window guards on a tenant's request, and no window-guard notice or rider for the lease. Window fall protection comes from the Building Code instead. New construction: in apartment buildings and in one- and two-family homes and townhouses, an operable window whose sill is less than 18 inches above the floor and more than 72 inches above the ground outside must meet one of the code's fall-protection options. Replacement windows: in an apartment building or other residential building with dwelling units, when you replace an operable window's sash and frame, and the sill is less than 36 inches above the floor, the drop outside is more than 72 inches and the window opens wide enough to pass a four-inch sphere, you must install window opening control devices meeting ASTM F 2090 (unless the window has a compliant fall prevention device); the device must still let the window open fully for emergency escape once released. Existing buildings must be kept as the code under which they were built requires, so fall protection devices installed under that code must be maintained. Security or burglar bars: bars, grilles or grates over a required bedroom escape window are allowed only if the opening stays big enough and the bars release or come off from inside without a key, tool or more force than it takes to open the window; where bars are added over escape openings in a renovation, smoke alarms are also required. Separately, a city or county may require landlords with five or more units in a multifamily building to put code-compliant locks on all exterior windows. If a tenant with young children asks for window stops or guards, providing ones that meet ASTM F 2090 (with an emergency release) is a sensible precaution. See Locks, Peepholes and Security Devices.

title: Notices That Must Be in Writing
bodyText: Under the Residential Landlord and Tenant Act, "notice" means a written notice given by regular mail or hand delivery, with the sender keeping a certificate of service as proof. A written notice may be on paper or electronic (electronic only if the lease provides for it, and a tenant may always insist on paper). A person is also treated as having notice of a fact he actually knows, was told orally, or has reason to know, but whoever relies on an unwritten notice must prove it was given, so put every notice in writing. Notices the Act expressly requires in writing include: your termination notices for a lease breach (ending the lease at least 30 days after receipt, with 21 days to cure a breach that can be remedied) and for unpaid rent (14 days; from July 1, 2027, a landlord with more than four Virginia units must offer a payment plan in that notice when no more than one month's rent plus late charges is owed); notices ending a week-to-week (7 days) or month-to-month (30 days, unless the lease sets a different period) tenancy, from either side; the 60-day notice an owner of a multifamily property must give before failing to renew, within a 30-day period, the greater of 20 or more, or half, of the month-to-month tenancies there (not needed for a tenant who has failed to pay rent); for a landlord with more than four Virginia units, renewal rent-increase and nonrenewal notices; the itemized security deposit disposition within 45 days; the 30-day notice of a temporary relocation for a repair; and the tenant's notice of your breach. Your notice of intent to enter for nonemergency access is a "notice" under the Act's definition, so give it in writing, and, unless impractical, give at least 72 hours' notice of routine maintenance the tenant did not request. From July 1, 2027, a termination notice for nonpayment of rent is not effective unless it includes a written statement of charges and payments over the tenancy or the past 12 months, whichever is shorter. Termination notices to public housing tenants, and private landlords' termination notices to tenants with a housing voucher or other tenant-based rental assistance, must carry legal aid contact information on the first page.

title: Checks Marked 'Paid in Full'
bodyText: Virginia follows the Uniform Commercial Code rule on checks marked 'paid in full' (Va. Code Ann. § 8.3A-311). If a tenant, or anyone else you have a claim against, gives you a check or other payment instrument for less than you claim, with a conspicuous statement, on the check or in a writing with it, that it is offered in full satisfaction of the claim, then cashing it settles your whole claim, the unpaid balance included. This applies only when the payment was offered in good faith and the amount was not yet fixed or was subject to a genuine (bona fide) dispute, so writing 'paid in full' on a short check for rent nobody disputes does not by itself settle the rent owed. Writing 'under protest' or 'without prejudice' when you endorse the check does not save the balance: the rule on reserving your rights does not apply to an accord and satisfaction (Va. Code Ann. § 8.1A-308(b)). There are two ways out. If you are an organization (for example an LLC) and, within a reasonable time before the check, sent the tenant a conspicuous statement that communications about disputed debts, including checks offered in full satisfaction, must go to a named person, office or place, the claim is not settled if the check or the writing with it was not received there. And whether or not you are an organization, the claim is not settled if you offer to repay the amount of the check within 90 days after it is paid; an organization that sent the statement just described cannot use this second way out. Neither way out works if you, or your agent responsible for the disputed debt, knew within a reasonable time before the check was collected that it was offered in full satisfaction. The cautious course: don't cash a check for less than you claim that is marked as payment in full of a disputed amount; return it, and if one is cashed by mistake, offer the money back within 90 days.

title: Duty of Good Faith
bodyText: Virginia's landlord-tenant statutes impose no general duty of good faith of the kind in the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act (the Virginia Residential Landlord and Tenant Act searched); good faith appears only in specific rules. Courts in many states read a covenant of good faith and fair dealing into every contract, a lease included; whether and how Virginia's courts do is case law this library has not reviewed, so act as if the duty applies. In practice: give notices, enter, handle the deposit, enforce lease terms and end a tenancy honestly and for the purpose the law or the lease gives you the right, not as a pretext.
